# State: timerId=null, fn fires once after 50ms silence
# t=0ms: call debounced() → clearTimeout(null) no-op → timerId=setTimeout(fn,50). timer fires at t=50ms
# t=30ms: call debounced() → clearTimeout(timer50) CANCELLED → timerId=setTimeout(fn,50). fires at t=80ms
# t=60ms: call debounced() → clearTimeout(timer80) CANCELLED → timerId=setTimeout(fn,50). fires at t=110ms
# t=110ms: fn() executes ✓. No earlier calls fired.
# Trace single call at t=0: clearTimeout(null) → setTimeout(fn,50) → fn fires at t=50ms ✓
# WHY reset timer: debounce means 'only fire after t ms of silence'; each new call restarts clock.
# Edge: no calls → fn never fires. Rapid calls → fn fires once after last call + t ms.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(1) per call. Space O(1): one timer reference.
#  Debounce: wait until activity stops. Throttle: fire at most once per interval.
#  Follow-up: leading debounce — fire immediately then ignore for t ms.

3160.title: FIND THE NUMBER OF DISTINCT COLORS AMONG THE BALLS  (Math)
3160.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  N balls (0 to limit). queries[i]=[ball,color]: paint that ball.
#  After each query, return the number of distinct colors among painted balls. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Unpainted balls have no color — don't count? Correct.
#  Can a ball be repainted? Yes — overwrites previous color."
#
# "Let me walk: queries=[[1,4],[2,5],[1,3],[3,4]] → [1,2,2,3] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Dict ball→color. After each query, scan all values for distinct count.
#  O(n) per query, O(n²) total.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _3160_FindDistinctColors_Brute:
    def queryResults(self, limit, queries):
        ball_color = {}; result = []
        for ball, color in queries:
            ball_color[ball] = color
            result.append(len(set(ball_color.values())))
        return result

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is the O(n) set scan for distinct colors.
#  color_count tracks how many balls have each color.
#  On each query: if ball had a color, decrement old color count (remove if 0).
#  Add new color to color_count. Distinct count = len(color_count).
#
#  Time: O(1) per query. Space: O(n)."
# Key insight: a color→ball-count map supports O(1) updates and distinct-color tracking — the size of the map is the distinct color count at any point.
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _3160_FindDistinctColors:
    def queryResults(self, limit, queries):
        ball_color = {}
        color_count = {}
        result = []
        for ball, color in queries:
            if ball in ball_color:
                old = ball_color[ball]
                color_count[old] -= 1
                if color_count[old] == 0:
                    del color_count[old]
            ball_color[ball] = color
            color_count[color] = color_count.get(color, 0) + 1
            result.append(len(color_count))
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the derived formula and confirm it on the example numbers."
#
# queries=[[1,4],[2,5],[1,3],[3,4]]:
# [1,4]: ball_color={1:4},color_count={4:1}. distinct=1 ✓
# [2,5]: color_count={4:1,5:1}. distinct=2 ✓
# [1,3]: old=4→count[4]=0 del. color_count={5:1,3:1}. distinct=2 ✓
# [3,4]: color_count={5:1,3:1,4:1}. distinct=3 ✓
#
# Deleting color_count[old] when it hits 0 keeps len(color_count) correct

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "O(1) per query. Space O(unique balls + colors).
#  color_count keys = currently active distinct colors — len gives the answer directly.
#  Follow-up: range coloring (paint balls l..r) — needs segment tree or lazy propagation.
#  Follow-up: undo queries — maintain a stack of (ball, old_color, new_color)."

10.title: REGULAR EXPRESSION MATCHING  (Dynamic Programming)
10.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Implement regex matching with '.' (any single char) and '*' (zero or more of preceding).
#  Full string must match. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: '.*' matches any sequence? Yes. 'a*' can match zero 'a's? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: s='aa', p='a*' -> true ✓. s='ab', p='.*' -> true ✓. s='aab', p='c*a*b' -> true ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Recursion: match char-by-char, handle '*' as zero or more of preceding.
#  O(2^(m+n)) without memo. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _10_RegexpMatching_Brute:
    def isMatch(self, s, p):
        if not p: return not s
        first = bool(s) and p[0] in {s[0], '.'}
        if len(p) >= 2 and p[1] == '*':
            return self.isMatch(s, p[2:]) or (first and self.isMatch(s[1:], p))
        return first and self.isMatch(s[1:], p[1:])

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DP on (i, j) = does s[i:] match p[j:] — O(mn). Walk-through:
#  dp[i][j] = True if s[i:] matches p[j:].
#  Base: dp[len(s)][len(p)] = True (both exhausted).
#  Fill backwards (i from len(s) down to 0, j from len(p) down to 0):
#    first_match = i < len(s) and (p[j] == s[i] or p[j] == '.').
#    If j+1 < len(p) and p[j+1] == '*':
#      dp[i][j] = dp[i][j+2]  (use '*' as zero occurrences)
#                OR (first_match AND dp[i+1][j])  (use '*' for one more match).
#    Else: dp[i][j] = first_match AND dp[i+1][j+1].
#  WHY OR condition for '*': '*' can match 0 times (skip pattern char+star) or
#  match current char and stay at same pattern position for the next s char.
#  Time: O(mn). Space: O(mn)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _10_RegexpMatching:
    def isMatch(self, s, p):
        m, n = len(s), len(p)
        dp = [False] * (n + 1)
        dp[n] = True
        for i in range(m, -1, -1):
            new_dp = [False] * (n + 1)
            new_dp[n] = (i == m)
            for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
                first_match = i < m and p[j] in {s[i], '.'}
                if j + 1 < n and p[j+1] == '*':
                    new_dp[j] = new_dp[j+2] or (first_match and dp[j])
                else:
                    new_dp[j] = first_match and dp[j+1]
            dp = new_dp
        return dp[0]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace isMatch('aab','c*a*b')."
# dp[i][j] = does s[:i] match p[:j]. dp[0][0]=T.
# p='c*a*b'. p[1]='*': dp[0][2]=dp[0][0]=T (c* matches empty). p[3]='*': dp[0][4]=dp[0][2]=T (a* matches empty).
# i=1 (s='a'): j=1: s[0]='a' vs p[0]='c'. No match. dp[1][1]=F.
# j=2 (p='c*'): p[1]='*'. dp[1][2] = dp[1][0](use c* zero times)=F OR (c matches a? No). dp[1][2]=F.
# j=3 (p='c*a'): s[0]='a'==p[2]='a' → dp[1][3]=dp[0][2]=T ✓
# j=4 (p='c*a*'): dp[1][4]=dp[1][2]=F OR (a*: s[0]='a'==p[2]='a' AND dp[1][2]=F)→F.
# Actually dp[1][4]=dp[1][3]=T (a* uses zero more → skip star). 
# Continue... dp[3][5]=T ✓ ('aab' matches 'c*a*b').


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(m*n). Space O(n): two rolling rows.
#  Follow-up: Wildcard Matching (#44) — '*' matches any sequence; simpler DP.
#  Follow-up: if '?' (any single char) is added — treat like '.' in this solution."

68.title: TEXT JUSTIFICATION  (Math)
68.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Arrange words into lines of exactly maxWidth chars. Spaces distributed as evenly as possible.
#  Extra spaces go to the LEFT. Last line: left-justified with single spaces. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: Each word fits in maxWidth? Yes per constraints.
#  At least one word? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: words=['This','is','an','example'], maxWidth=16.
#  Line 1: 'This    is    an' (total=16) ✓. Last: left-justified."
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Greedy packing: fit as many words per line as possible. Then distribute spaces.
#  O(n*maxWidth) time. This IS the optimal approach.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _68_TextJustification_Brute:
    def fullJustify(self, words, maxWidth):
        result = []; i = 0; n = len(words)
        while i < n:
            line_words = [words[i]]; line_len = len(words[i]); i += 1
            while i < n and line_len + 1 + len(words[i]) <= maxWidth:
                line_len += 1 + len(words[i]); line_words.append(words[i]); i += 1
            result.append(line_words)
        lines = []
        for idx, lw in enumerate(result):
            if idx == len(result) - 1 or len(lw) == 1:
                lines.append(' '.join(lw).ljust(maxWidth))
            else:
                total = maxWidth - sum(len(w) for w in lw)
                gaps = len(lw) - 1
                base, extra = divmod(total, gaps)
                line = lw[0]
                for j in range(1, len(lw)):
                    line += ' ' * (base + (1 if j <= extra else 0)) + lw[j]
                lines.append(line)
        return lines

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Greedy line filling + space distribution — O(n * L). Walk-through:
#  Greedily fill each line: pack as many words as fit (with single spaces between).
#  For each filled line:
#    If last line OR only one word: left-justify (spaces on right, single space between words).
#    Else: distribute remaining spaces evenly:
#      gaps = len(words) - 1. extra = maxWidth - sum(word lengths).
#      spaces_per_gap = extra // gaps. leftover = extra % gaps.
#      First 'leftover' gaps get one extra space.
#  WHY leftover to left gaps: problem specifies extra spaces go to left gaps first.
#  HOW to fill a line: maintain curr_width, keep adding words until next word would overflow.
#  Time: O(n * maxWidth). Space: O(maxWidth) per line."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _68_TextJustification:
    def fullJustify(self, words, maxWidth):
        result = []
        i = 0
        while i < len(words):
            line = [words[i]]; length = len(words[i]); i += 1
            while i < len(words) and length + 1 + len(words[i]) <= maxWidth:
                length += 1 + len(words[i]); line.append(words[i]); i += 1
            if i == len(words) or len(line) == 1:
                result.append(' '.join(line).ljust(maxWidth))
            else:
                spaces = maxWidth - sum(len(w) for w in line)
                gaps = len(line) - 1
                base, extra = divmod(spaces, gaps)
                row = line[0]
                for j in range(1, len(line)):
                    row += ' ' * (base + (1 if j <= extra else 0)) + line[j]
                result.append(row)
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the derived formula and confirm it on the example numbers."
#
# words=['This','is','an','example'], maxWidth=16:
# line=['This','is','an'], length=10. spaces=6, gaps=2. base=3,extra=0.
# row='This   is   an'. len=16 ✓
# Last line='example      '.ljust(16) ✓
#
# Single word line: 'word'.ljust(16) → padded with spaces ✓
#
# Base + (1 if j <= extra else 0) distributes extra spaces to left gaps

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n*maxWidth): O(n) lines, each O(maxWidth) to build. Space O(n) output.
#  Follow-up: minimize raggedness (aesthetic) — DP approach balances line lengths.
#  Follow-up: proportional fonts — use pixel widths instead of character counts."

115.title: DISTINCT SUBSEQUENCES  (Dynamic Programming)
115.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count distinct subsequences of s that equal t.
#  Same positions count as different even if same characters. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: t='rabbit', s='rabbbit' -> 3 ways ✓ (three different 'b' choices)"
#
# "Let me walk: s='babgbag', t='bag' -> 5 ✓"
#  Can the array be empty or contain a single element? Can values be negative?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Recursion: if s[i]==t[j]: use(i+1,j+1)+skip(i+1,j); else skip(i+1,j).
#  O(2^m) without memo. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _115_DistinctSubsequences_Brute:
    def numDistinct(self, s, t):
        from functools import lru_cache
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(i, j):
            if j == len(t): return 1
            if i == len(s): return 0
            result = dp(i+1, j)
            if s[i] == t[j]: result += dp(i+1, j+1)
            return result
        return dp(0, 0)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "2-D DP counting distinct subsequences. O(mn).
#  dp[i][j] = number of distinct subsequences of s[:i] that equal t[:j].
#  Base: dp[i][0] = 1 (empty t is a subsequence of any s — one way: delete everything).
#       dp[0][j] = 0 for j>0 (can't match non-empty t from empty s).
#  Transition:
#    If s[i-1] != t[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j]  (must skip s[i-1], can't use it).
#    If s[i-1] == t[j-1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (use this char to match t[j-1])
#                                   + dp[i-1][j]   (skip this char, find other matches).
#  WHY add both cases when chars match: we can either USE s[i-1] to match t[j-1],
#  OR skip it and find t[j-1] matched by an earlier char in s.
#  Answer = dp[m][n]. Time: O(mn). Space: O(mn)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _115_DistinctSubsequences:
    def numDistinct(self, s, t):
        n = len(t)
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)
        dp[n] = 1
        for ch in reversed(s):
            for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
                if ch == t[j]:
                    dp[j] += dp[j+1]
        return dp[0]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace numDistinct('rabbbit','rabbit')."
# dp[i][j] = ways s[:i] contains t[:j] as subsequence. dp[i][0]=1 (empty t always matched).
# Build dp row by row. s='rabbbit', t='rabbit'.
# i=1(r),j=1(r): s[0]=r==t[0]=r → dp[1][1]=dp[0][0]+dp[0][1]=1+0=1.
# i=2(a),j=1(r): s[1]=a≠r → dp[2][1]=dp[1][1]=1.
# i=2(a),j=2(a): s[1]=a==t[1]=a → dp[2][2]=dp[1][1]+dp[1][2]=1+0=1.
# i=3(b),j=3(b): s[2]=b==t[2]=b → dp[3][3]=dp[2][2]+dp[2][3]=1+0=1.
# i=4(b),j=3(b): s[3]=b==t[2]=b → dp[4][3]=dp[3][2]+dp[3][3]=1+1=2. (use 3rd or 4th b)
# i=5(b),j=3(b): dp[5][3]=dp[4][2]+dp[4][3]=1+2=3. (use 3rd,4th,or 5th b)
# dp[7][6]=3 ✓


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(m*n). Space O(n): one rolling array.
#  Right-to-left update is essential — prevents reuse of same s[i] across matches.
#  Follow-up: Edit Distance (#72) — related; counts edits instead of matching occurrences.
#  Follow-up: print all distinct subsequences — backtrack through the DP table."

123.title: BEST TIME TO BUY AND SELL STOCK III  (Dynamic Programming)
123.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  At most 2 transactions. Maximize profit. Can't hold two stocks simultaneously. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: Complete one transaction before starting next? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: prices=[3,3,5,0,0,3,1,4] -> buy@0,sell@3 + buy@1,sell@4 = 6 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all pairs of buy1<sell1<=buy2<sell2. O(n^4). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _123_StockIII_Brute:
    def maxProfit(self, prices):
        n = len(prices); best = 0
        for s1 in range(n):
            for e1 in range(s1, n):
                p1 = prices[e1]-prices[s1]
                for s2 in range(e1, n):
                    for e2 in range(s2, n):
                        best = max(best, p1+prices[e2]-prices[s2])
        return best

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "4-state DP — O(n). Walk-through:
#  At most 2 transactions. States: hold1, cash1, hold2, cash2.
#  hold1 = max profit after buying stock 1 (hold).
#  cash1 = max profit after selling stock 1 (cash after 1st tx).
#  hold2 = max profit after buying stock 2 (cash1 - price).
#  cash2 = max profit after selling stock 2 (answer).
#  For each price:
#    hold1 = max(hold1, -price).       ← buy as cheap as possible
#    cash1 = max(cash1, hold1+price).  ← sell at best price
#    hold2 = max(hold2, cash1-price).  ← buy second stock (uses profit from first)
#    cash2 = max(cash2, hold2+price).  ← sell second stock
#  Return cash2.
#  WHY 4 states: track the lifecycle of at most 2 buy-sell cycles independently.
#  WHY cash1-price for hold2: second buy uses whatever profit was made in first transaction.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _123_StockIII:
    def maxProfit(self, prices):
        buy1 = buy2 = float('-inf')
        sell1 = sell2 = 0
        for price in prices:
            buy1 = max(buy1, -price)
            sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + price)
            buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - price)
            sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + price)
        return sell2

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace 2-transaction stock on [3,3,5,0,0,3,1,4]."
# States: hold1=-inf, cash1=0, hold2=-inf, cash2=0.
# Day 0 (p=3): hold1=max(-inf,-3)=-3. cash1=max(0,-3+3)=0. hold2=max(-inf,0-3)=-3. cash2=max(0,-3+3)=0.
# Day 3 (p=0): hold1=max(-3,-0)=0. cash1=0. hold2=max(-3,0-0)=0. cash2=max(0,0+0)=0.
# Day 5 (p=3): hold1=0. cash1=max(0,0+3)=3. hold2=max(0,3-3)=0. cash2=max(0,0+3)=3.
# Day 7 (p=4): hold1=0. cash1=max(3,0+4)=4. hold2=max(0,4-4)=0. cash2=max(3,0+4)=4.
# Wait, optimal is buy@0,sell@3 (profit 3) + buy@1,sell@4 (profit 3)=6. Let me retrace...
# Return 6 ✓ after full trace: hold1=0 (buy@0), cash1=3 (sell@3), hold2=3-1=2 (buy@1), cash2=2+4=6.


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n): single pass. Space O(1): four state variables.
#  Follow-up: at most k transactions (#188) — generalize to 2k state variables or O(n*k) DP.
#  Follow-up: unlimited transactions (#122) — sum all positive consecutive differences."

132.title: PALINDROME PARTITIONING II  (Dynamic Programming)
132.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the minimum cuts to partition s into palindromes.
#  Each partition must be a palindrome. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: The whole string being a palindrome = 0 cuts? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: s='aab' -> 1 cut ('aa'|'b') ✓. s='a' -> 0 ✓. s='ab' -> 1 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all partitionings. O(2^n) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _132_PalindromePartitioningII_Brute:
    def minCut(self, s):
        from functools import lru_cache
        n = len(s)
        @lru_cache(None)
        def is_pal(i, j): return s[i:j+1] == s[i:j+1][::-1]
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(i):
            if i == n: return -1
            return min(1 + dp(j+1) for j in range(i, n) if is_pal(i, j))
        return dp(0)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "2-pass DP: palindrome table + min cuts — O(n²). Walk-through:
#  Pass 1: dp_palindrome[i][j] = True if s[i..j] is palindrome.
#    Expand: for center in 0..2n-1 (odd+even): expand while s[l]==s[r] → set dp[l][r]=True.
#  Pass 2: cuts[i] = min cuts for s[:i+1].
#    cuts[-1]=-1. For i in 0..n-1: cuts[i] = min over j in 0..i of (cuts[j-1]+1 if dp[j][i]).
#    If dp[0][i]: cuts[i]=0 (whole prefix is palindrome, 0 cuts).
#  Return cuts[n-1].
#  WHY -1 sentinel for cuts[-1]: cuts[j-1]+1 when j=0 → cuts[-1]+1 = 0 cuts (one palindrome).
#  WHY loop over all j: any j where s[j..i] is a palindrome is a valid last partition.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(n²)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _132_PalindromePartitioningII:
    def minCut(self, s):
        n = len(s)
        is_pal = [[False]*n for _ in range(n)]
        for i in range(n):
            is_pal[i][i] = True
        for length in range(2, n+1):
            for i in range(n-length+1):
                j = i+length-1
                is_pal[i][j] = (s[i]==s[j]) and (length==2 or is_pal[i+1][j-1])
        dp = list(range(-1, n))
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i+1):
                if is_pal[j][i]:
                    dp[i+1] = min(dp[i+1], dp[j]+1)
        return dp[n]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minCut on 'aab'."
# palindrome table: p[0][0]=T,p[1][1]=T,p[2][2]=T,p[0][1]='aa'=T,p[1][2]='ab'=F,p[0][2]='aab'=F.
# cuts[i] = min cuts for s[:i+1].
# cuts[0]: p[0][0]=T(whole prefix is palindrome) → cuts[0]=0.
# cuts[1]: p[0][1]=T('aa') → cuts[1]=0.
# cuts[2]: p[0][2]='aab'=F. Try j=0..2:
#   j=0: p[j][2]=p[0][2]=F. j=1: p[1][2]='ab'=F. j=2: p[2][2]='b'=T → cuts[2]=cuts[1]+1=1.
# Return 1 ✓ ('aa'|'b' → 1 cut).
# WHY enumerate all j: any palindrome ending at i is a valid last partition.
# DP cut: dp[i]=min cuts for s[0..i]. dp[i]=min(dp[j]+1) for all j where s[j+1..i] is palindrome. dp[0]=0,dp[1]=0('aa'),dp[2]=1('aab'→'aa'|'b'). Prune: dp[i]=0 if s[0..i] itself palindrome.
# DP with backtrack perspective: dp[i]=min cuts. path=[cut positions]. call(s,start): try cuts after each palindrome. Prune: skip non-palindrome substrings. backtrack: undo cut.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n^2). Space O(n^2) table + O(n) dp.
#  Follow-up: Palindrome Partitioning I (#131) — return all partitions; backtrack with table.
#  Follow-up: Palindrome Partitioning IV (#1745) — fixed 3 parts; use same palindrome table."

312.title: BURST BALLOONS  (Dynamic Programming)
312.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Burst balloon i: earn nums[i-1]*nums[i]*nums[i+1]. Pad array with 1s on both ends.
#  Burst all balloons to maximize total coins. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: After bursting i, its neighbors become adjacent? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[3,1,5,8] -> 167 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all permutations of burst order. O(n!). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _312_BurstBalloons_Brute:
    def maxCoins(self, nums):
        nums = [1] + nums + [1]; n = len(nums)
        from functools import lru_cache
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(l, r):
            return max((nums[l]*nums[k]*nums[r] + dp(l,k) + dp(k,r) for k in range(l+1,r)), default=0)
        return dp(0, n-1)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is the O(n!) permutation search.
#  Interval DP: dp[l][r] = max coins from open interval (l,r) where l,r are boundaries NOT popped.
#  Think backwards: k is the LAST balloon popped in (l,r).
#  dp[l][r] = max over k: dp[l][k]+nums[l]*nums[k]*nums[r]+dp[k][r].
#  Time: O(n^3). Space: O(n^2)."
# Key insight: choosing the LAST balloon popped in subrange (l,r) makes both halves independent subproblems — dp[l][r] = max over k of coins[l]*coins[k]*coins[r] + dp[l][k] + dp[k][r].
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _312_BurstBalloons:
    def maxCoins(self, nums):
        nums = [1] + nums + [1]
        n = len(nums)
        dp = [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
        for length in range(2, n):
            for left in range(0, n-length):
                right = left+length
                for k in range(left+1, right):
                    dp[left][right] = max(dp[left][right],
                        nums[left]*nums[k]*nums[right] + dp[left][k] + dp[k][right])
        return dp[0][n-1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace maxCoins on [3,1,5,8]."
# Add sentinels: [1,3,1,5,8,1]. dp[i][j]=max coins from bursting all balloons in (i,j) exclusive.
# dp[i][j]: try each k as LAST balloon burst in (i,j):
# dp[0][2]=dp[0][1]+1*3*1+dp[1][2]=0+3+0=3. (only balloon 1 in (0,2))
# dp[1][3]=dp[1][2]+3*1*5+dp[2][3]=0+15+0=15. dp[2][4]=1*5*8=40. dp[3][5]=5*8*1=40.
# dp[1][4]=max(dp[1][2]+3*1*8+dp[2][4]=0+24+40=64, dp[1][3]+3*5*8+dp[3][4]=15+120+...). 
# dp[0][5] (full range): try all k as last burst → max = 167 ✓
# WHY last burst: if k is last, its neighbors are the sentinels of the range → known coin value.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n^3). Space O(n^2).
#  The last-burst reversal is the key insight that gives clean substructure.
#  Follow-up: Minimum Cost to Merge Stones (#1000) — same interval DP skeleton.
#  Follow-up: Stone Game (#877) — similar range DP for game theory."

1000.title: MINIMUM COST TO MERGE STONES  (Dynamic Programming)
1000.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Merge exactly k consecutive piles at a time; cost = sum of the k piles.
#  Return minimum total cost, or -1 if impossible. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: When is it impossible? When (n-1) % (k-1) != 0.
#  Each merge reduces pile count by k-1, so we need (n-1) divisible by (k-1)."
#
# "Let me walk: stones=[3,2,4,1], k=2 -> 20 ✓. stones=[3,2,4,1], k=3 -> -1 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all orders of k-consecutive merges. O(n^k) -- exponential. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1000_MinCostMergeStones_Brute:
    def mergeStones(self, stones, k):
        n = len(stones)
        if (n-1) % (k-1): return -1
        from functools import lru_cache
        prefix = [0] * (n+1)
        for i in range(n): prefix[i+1] = prefix[i] + stones[i]
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(l, r, piles):
            if r-l+1 == piles: return 0
            result = min(dp(l,m,1)+dp(m+1,r,piles-1) for m in range(l,r,k-1))
            if piles == 1: result += prefix[r+1]-prefix[l]
            return result
        return dp(0, n-1, 1)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Interval DP: minimum cost to merge stones — O(n³). Walk-through:
#  If (n-1) % (k-1) != 0: return -1 (can never reduce to 1 pile with merges of k at a time).
#  dp[i][j] = min cost to merge stones[i..j] into minimum possible piles.
#  prefix = prefix sums for O(1) range sum.
#  For length in 2..n:
#    For i, j = all windows of this length:
#      dp[i][j] = min over all m (step k-1): dp[i][m] + dp[m+1][j].
#      If (j-i) % (k-1) == 0: dp[i][j] += prefix[j+1]-prefix[i].  ← merged down to 1 pile
#  Return dp[0][n-1].
#  WHY step k-1: each merge reduces k piles to 1, net reduction of k-1. So m advances by k-1.
#  WHY add prefix sum when (j-i)%(k-1)==0: this interval merges into exactly 1 pile at this step.
#  Time: O(n³). Space: O(n²)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1000_MinCostMergeStones:
    def mergeStones(self, stones, k):
        n = len(stones)
        if (n-1) % (k-1): return -1
        prefix = [0] * (n+1)
        for i in range(n): prefix[i+1] = prefix[i] + stones[i]
        dp = [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
        for length in range(k, n+1):
            for l in range(n-length+1):
                r = l+length-1
                dp[l][r] = float('inf')
                for m in range(l, r, k-1):
                    dp[l][r] = min(dp[l][r], dp[l][m] + dp[m+1][r])
                if (length-1) % (k-1) == 0:
                    dp[l][r] += prefix[r+1]-prefix[l]
        return dp[0][n-1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minimumCostMergeStones on stones=[3,2,4,1], k=2."
# Check: (n-1)%(k-1)=(4-1)%(2-1)=3%1=0 ✓ (can always merge to 1 pile).
# prefix=[0,3,5,9,10]. dp[i][j]=min cost to merge stones[i..j].
# len=2: dp[0][1]=3+2=5. dp[1][2]=2+4=6. dp[2][3]=4+1=5.
# len=3: dp[0][2]: try m=0: dp[0][0]+dp[1][2]=0+6=6. Try m=1: dp[0][1]+dp[2][2]=5+0=5.
#   (0..2)%1==0 → add prefix sum[0..2]=9. dp[0][2]=5+9=14.
# dp[1][3]: try m=1: dp[1][1]+dp[2][3]=0+5=5. Try m=2: dp[1][2]+dp[3][3]=6+0=6. min=5. add sum=7. dp[1][3]=12.
# len=4: dp[0][3]: try m=0: dp[0][0]+dp[1][3]=12. Try m=1: dp[0][1]+dp[2][3]=5+5=10. Try m=2: dp[0][2]+dp[3][3]=14.
#   (0..3)%1==0→add sum=10. dp[0][3]=10+10=20 ✓


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n^3/k). Space O(n^2).
#  The feasibility check (n-1)%(k-1)==0 saves all computation for impossible inputs.
#  Follow-up: Burst Balloons (#312) — same interval DP skeleton, different cost formula.
#  Follow-up: k=2 (classic stone merging) — solvable in O(n log n) with Hu-Shing algorithm."

40.title: Combination Sum II
40.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find all unique combinations in candidates that sum to target.
#  Each number can be used ONCE per combination. No duplicate combinations. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  candidates can have duplicate values (e.g. two 1s)? Yes — that's the key difference from Combination Sum I.
#  Order within a combination doesn't matter? Correct."
#
# "Let me walk: candidates=[10,1,2,7,6,1,5], target=8 → [1,1,6],[1,2,5],[1,7],[2,6] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Sort candidates. Backtrack: at each index, either skip or take it, advance index by 1 (no reuse).
#  Use a set of tuples to dedupe combinations. O(2^n) time with dedup overhead.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _40_CombinationSumII_Brute:
    def combinationSum2(self, candidates, target):
        candidates.sort()
        result = set()
        def backtrack(start, path, remaining):
            if remaining == 0:
                result.add(tuple(path)); return
            if remaining < 0: return
            for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
                path.append(candidates[i])
                backtrack(i+1, path, remaining-candidates[i])
                path.pop()
        backtrack(0, [], target)
        return [list(t) for t in result]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is the set-based dedup — wasteful since we generate duplicates first.
#  Instead: sort, then at each backtrack level skip candidates[i] if i>start and candidates[i]==candidates[i-1]
#  (skip duplicate siblings at the SAME recursion depth, not duplicate ancestors).
#  Also prune early when candidates[i] > remaining (sorted array).
#  Time: O(2^n) worst case but no dedup overhead. Space: O(n) recursion."
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _40_CombinationSumII:
    def combinationSum2(self, candidates, target):
        candidates.sort()
        result = []
        path = []
        def backtrack(start, remaining):
            if remaining == 0:
                result.append(path[:])
                return
            for i in range(start, len(candidates)):
                if i > start and candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]:
                    continue
                if candidates[i] > remaining:
                    break
                path.append(candidates[i])
                backtrack(i+1, remaining - candidates[i])
                path.pop()
        backtrack(0, target)
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the backtracking recursion tree (choose → recurse → undo) on the example."
#
# candidates=[1,1,2,5,6,7,10], target=8:
# start=0: take 1(idx0). start=1: take 1(idx1, ok i==start). remaining=6.
#   take 2→remaining=4. take 5→neg, skip(break since 5>4). take 6→neg.
#   backtrack: take 5(skip 2)... eventually [1,1,6] found.
# start=0: take 1(idx0), skip idx1(dup at same level after using idx0... wait idx0 used so start=1, i>start check)
# Final: [1,1,6],[1,2,5],[1,7],[2,6] ✓
#
# I>start check skips duplicate VALUES at the same tree level, not duplicate uses of one element

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(2^n) worst case, much better in practice with pruning. Space O(n) recursion + output.
#  Follow-up: Combination Sum (#39) — unlimited reuse, no duplicates in input.
#  Follow-up: Combination Sum III (#216) — fixed count k digits 1-9, no repeats."

43.title: Multiply Strings
43.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Multiply two numbers given as strings, return the product as a string.
#  Cannot convert to int directly (numbers can be arbitrarily large). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Either input could be '0'? Yes — handle that. No leading zeros in output except '0' itself."
#
# "Let me walk: num1='123', num2='456' → '56088' ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Simulate grade-school multiplication: multiply num1 by each digit of num2, shift, sum as strings.
#  O(m*n) digit multiplications + O(m+n) string additions = O(m*n*(m+n)) due to repeated string adds.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _43_MultiplyStrings_Brute:
    def multiply(self, num1, num2):
        if num1=='0' or num2=='0': return '0'
        def add_str(a, b):
            i,j,carry,res = len(a)-1,len(b)-1,0,[]
            while i>=0 or j>=0 or carry:
                d = carry + (int(a[i]) if i>=0 else 0) + (int(b[j]) if j>=0 else 0)
                res.append(str(d%10)); carry=d//10; i-=1; j-=1
            return ''.join(reversed(res))
        total = '0'
        for i in range(len(num2)-1, -1, -1):
            carry, row = 0, []
            for j in range(len(num1)-1, -1, -1):
                p = int(num2[i])*int(num1[j]) + carry
                row.append(str(p%10)); carry = p//10
            if carry: row.append(str(carry))
            row_str = ''.join(reversed(row)) + '0'*(len(num2)-1-i)
            total = add_str(total, row_str)
        return total

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Grade-school multiplication on digit arrays — O(mn). Walk-through:
#  result = [0] * (len(num1)+len(num2)).
#  For i from len(num1)-1 down to 0:
#    For j from len(num2)-1 down to 0:
#      product = (num1[i]-'0') * (num2[j]-'0').
#      pos1 = i+j.  pos2 = i+j+1  (position in result array).
#      sum_ = product + result[pos2].
#      result[pos2] = sum_ % 10.
#      result[pos1] += sum_ // 10  (carry into next position).
#  Strip leading zeros. Return ''.join(str(d) for d in result).
#  WHY i+j and i+j+1: multiplying digit at position i (from right in num1) and j (from right
#  in num2) contributes to position (i+j) in the result (like grade-school alignment).
#  The ones digit goes to pos2=i+j+1; carry goes to pos1=i+j.
#  Time: O(mn). Space: O(m+n)."
# Time: O(n) — optimal single-pass or O(n²) DP. Linear preferred.

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _43_MultiplyStrings:
    def multiply(self, num1, num2):
        if num1 == '0' or num2 == '0':
            return '0'
        m, n = len(num1), len(num2)
        result = [0] * (m + n)
        for i in range(m - 1, -1, -1):
            for j in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
                product = int(num1[i]) * int(num2[j])
                pos_low, pos_high = i + j + 1, i + j
                total = product + result[pos_low]
                result[pos_low] = total % 10
                result[pos_high] += total // 10
        result_str = ''.join(map(str, result)).lstrip('0')
        return result_str

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace multiply('123','456')."
# Simulate grade-school multiplication. result=[0]*5 (len=3+3-1=5... actually 6).
# result=[0,0,0,0,0,0]. 
# i=2(3),j=2(6): pos=4. 3*6=18. result[4]+=18→18. 
# i=2(3),j=1(5): pos=3. 3*5=15. result[3]+=15.
# i=2(3),j=0(4): pos=2. 3*4=12. result[2]+=12.
# i=1(2),j=2(6): pos=3. 2*6=12. result[3]+=12→27.
# ... After all: result=[0,0,1+0,6+2+1,3+0+2,8]. Then carry propagation.
# Carry from pos4: 56%10=6→pos4=6,carry=5. pos3: (15+12+12+5)%10=4,carry=4. ... final='56088' ✓


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(m*n). Space O(m+n).
#  Follow-up: Add Strings (#415) — simpler single-pass addition, same string-as-number idea.
#  Follow-up: if numbers can be negative, track sign separately and strip before multiplying."

45.title: Jump Game II
45.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Each nums[i] is the max jump length from index i. Find the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index.
#  Guaranteed reachable. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Return 0 if already at last index (n=1)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[2,3,1,1,4] → jump to idx1(3), then idx4 → 2 jumps ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i] = min jumps to reach i. For each i, try all reachable j and take min+1.
#  O(n²) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _45_JumpGameII_Brute:
    def jump(self, nums):
        n = len(nums)
        dp = [float('inf')]*n; dp[0]=0
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i+1, min(i+nums[i]+1, n)):
                dp[j] = min(dp[j], dp[i]+1)
        return dp[n-1]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Greedy BFS — O(n). Walk-through:
#  curr_end=0 (furthest we can reach with current jumps). farthest=0. jumps=0.
#  For i in 0..n-2:
#    farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]).  (update max reach from this position)
#    If i == curr_end:  (we've exhausted the current jump's reach)
#      jumps++.  (must take another jump)
#      curr_end = farthest.  (new boundary = best reach so far)
#  Return jumps.
#  WHY farthest tracks max reach: from any position i within [prev_end+1, curr_end],
#  we could jump to i+nums[i]. The best of all these is farthest.
#  WHY jump when i==curr_end: we've visited all positions reachable in 'jumps' steps.
#  The next step's boundary is 'farthest'.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _45_JumpGameII:
    def jump(self, nums):
        n = len(nums)
        jumps = 0
        current_end = 0
        farthest = 0
        for i in range(n - 1):
            farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])
            if i == current_end:
                jumps += 1
                current_end = farthest
        return jumps

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace jump on [2,3,1,1,4]."
# Greedy BFS: jumps=0, cur_end=0, farthest=0
# i=0: farthest=max(0,0+2)=2. i==cur_end → jumps=1, cur_end=2
# i=1: farthest=max(2,1+3)=4
# i=2: farthest=max(4,2+1)=4. i==cur_end → jumps=2, cur_end=4
# i=3: farthest=max(4,3+1)=4
# i=4: reached last index (4==n-1=4) → stop. Return 2 ✓
# WHY greedy: at each level boundary, commit to the jump that reaches farthest.
# Edge: [1] → single element, 0 jumps needed; return 0.
# Invariant: cur_end = boundary of current BFS level.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: Jump Game (#55) — just feasibility, not minimum jumps.
#  Follow-up: Jump Game VII (#1871) — string-based reachability with range constraints."

52.title: N-Queens II
52.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count the number of distinct solutions to the n-queens puzzle (just the count, not the boards). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Same constraint as N-Queens I: no two queens share row, column, or diagonal."
#
# "Let me walk: n=4 → 2 solutions ✓"
#  What should I return for the minimal edge case — empty input or a single element?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Backtrack row by row; for each row try every column, check column/diagonal sets for conflicts.
#  O(n!) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _52_NQueensII_Brute:
    def totalNQueens(self, n):
        count = [0]
        def backtrack(row, cols, diag1, diag2):
            if row == n:
                count[0] += 1; return
            for col in range(n):
                if col in cols or (row-col) in diag1 or (row+col) in diag2:
                    continue
                cols.add(col); diag1.add(row-col); diag2.add(row+col)
                backtrack(row+1, cols, diag1, diag2)
                cols.remove(col); diag1.remove(row-col); diag2.remove(row+col)
        backtrack(0, set(), set(), set())
        return count[0]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Backtracking counting solutions — O(n!). Walk-through:
#  Track cols, diag1, diag2 as sets (same as N-Queens I).
#  Place queens row by row:
#    For each col in 0..n-1:
#      If col not in cols AND (row-col) not in diag1 AND (row+col) not in diag2:
#        Mark all three. Recurse to next row.
#        If reached row n: count++.
#        Unmark all three.
#  Return count.
#  WHY same structure as N-Queens: identical constraint checks — only change is
#  incrementing a counter instead of recording board configurations.
#  Diagonal key: row-col is unique for each '/' diagonal; row+col for each '\' diagonal.
#  Time: O(n!). Space: O(n) recursion + O(n) sets."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _52_NQueensII:
    def totalNQueens(self, n):
        count = [0]
        full_mask = (1 << n) - 1
        def backtrack(row, cols, diag1, diag2):
            if row == n:
                count[0] += 1
                return
            available = full_mask & ~(cols | diag1 | diag2)
            while available:
                pos = available & (-available)
                available -= pos
                backtrack(row + 1, cols | pos, (diag1 | pos) << 1, (diag2 | pos) >> 1)
        backtrack(0, 0, 0, 0)
        return count[0]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace totalNQueens n=4."
# Same logic as Q51 but count solutions instead of storing boards.
# Row 0, col 0: → Row 1, col 2 → Row 2: no valid → backtrack.
# Row 0, col 0 → Row 1, col 3 → Row 2, col 1 → Row 3: col 3(clash), col 0(diag with (2,1)→|2-3|=1,|1-0|=1 yes diag), so no valid. Backtrack.
# Actually for n=4 there are exactly 2 solutions:
# Solution 1: queens at (0,1),(1,3),(2,0),(3,2).
# Solution 2: queens at (0,2),(1,0),(2,3),(3,1).
# Return 2 ✓
# WHY count not store: saves memory since only the count matters.
# path=[Q(r,c)...] builds queen positions. backtrack(row,path,cols,diag1,diag2): try each col → if safe: add to path, recurse. prune: skip if col/diagonal conflict. count valid paths.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n!) with small constant via bitmasks. Space O(n) recursion.
#  Follow-up: N-Queens I (#51) — same backtracking but must reconstruct and return boards.
#  Follow-up: count solutions for an n×n board with pre-placed queens — seed initial masks."

66.title: Plus One
66.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  digits represents a non-negative integer (most significant digit first). Add 1 and return the new digit array. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Handle carrying — e.g. [9,9] → [1,0,0]? Yes. No leading zeros in input."
#
# "Let me walk: digits=[1,2,3] → [1,2,4] ✓. digits=[9,9] → [1,0,0] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Convert digits to integer, add 1, convert back to a list of digits. O(n) time but uses big-int conversion.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _66_PlusOne_Brute:
    def plusOne(self, digits):
        num = int(''.join(map(str, digits))) + 1
        return [int(c) for c in str(num)]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is unnecessary string/int conversion of a potentially huge number.
#  Walk from the last digit: if it's < 9, just increment and return immediately.
#  If it's 9, set to 0 and carry to the next digit (continue left).
#  If all digits were 9 (carry propagates past index 0), prepend a 1.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(1) extra (O(n) for output array)."
# Key insight: carry propagates only through trailing 9s — the first non-9 digit absorbs the carry in O(1), making the common case sub-linear.
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _66_PlusOne:
    def plusOne(self, digits):
        for i in range(len(digits) - 1, -1, -1):
            if digits[i] < 9:
                digits[i] += 1
                return digits
            digits[i] = 0
        return [1] + digits

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace plusOne on [9,9,9]."
# Scan right to left: i=2: digits[2]=9+1=10 → set to 0, carry=1
# i=1: digits[1]=9+1=10 → set to 0, carry=1
# i=0: digits[0]=9+1=10 → set to 0, carry=1
# carry remains → prepend 1: [1,0,0,0] ✓
# Trace [1,2,3]: i=2: 3+1=4, no carry → [1,2,4]. Stop. ✓
# WHY handle carry with loop: avoids converting int and back; works for arbitrary length.
# Edge: [9] → [1,0]; [1,9,9] → [2,0,0].

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1) extra beyond output.
#  Follow-up: Add Binary (#67) — same carry logic in base 2.
#  Follow-up: Multiply Strings (#43) — same digit-array manipulation idea, harder operation."

97.title: Interleaving String
97.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Is s3 formed by interleaving s1 and s2, preserving the relative order of characters within each? Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  len(s1)+len(s2) must equal len(s3), else immediately false?  Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: s1='aabcc', s2='dbbca', s3='aadbbcbcac' → true ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Recursion: at each step, try consuming from s1 or s2 if it matches s3's next char. Memoize (i,j).
#  O(m*n) states, O(1) work each with memoization. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _97_InterleavingString_Brute:
    def isInterleave(self, s1, s2, s3):
        if len(s1)+len(s2) != len(s3): return False
        from functools import lru_cache
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(i, j):
            if i==len(s1) and j==len(s2): return True
            k = i+j
            res = False
            if i<len(s1) and s1[i]==s3[k]: res = res or dp(i+1,j)
            if j<len(s2) and s2[j]==s3[k]: res = res or dp(i,j+1)
            return res
        return dp(0,0)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "2-D DP on (i,j) = can s1[:i]+s2[:j] interleave to form s3[:i+j] — O(mn). Walk-through:
#  m=len(s1), n=len(s2). dp[i][j] = True if s3[:i+j] is a valid interleaving.
#  Base: dp[0][0]=True. dp[i][0]: only s1 used. dp[0][j]: only s2 used.
#  Fill: dp[i][j] = (dp[i-1][j] AND s1[i-1]==s3[i+j-1])  ← took from s1
#                 OR (dp[i][j-1] AND s2[j-1]==s3[i+j-1]).  ← took from s2
#  Answer: dp[m][n].
#  WHY s3[i+j-1]: s3's (i+j)-th character must be matched. Previous i chars from s1 and j from s2.
#  WHY both conditions: an interleaving can draw the next character from either string.
#  Space optimization: 1-D dp array updated row by row.
#  Time: O(mn). Space: O(mn) → O(n) with space optimization."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _97_InterleavingString:
    def isInterleave(self, s1, s2, s3):
        m, n = len(s1), len(s2)
        if m + n != len(s3):
            return False
        dp = [False] * (n + 1)
        dp[0] = True
        for j in range(1, n + 1):
            dp[j] = dp[j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[j-1]
        for i in range(1, m + 1):
            dp[0] = dp[0] and s1[i-1] == s3[i-1]
            for j in range(1, n + 1):
                dp[j] = (dp[j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]) or (dp[j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1])
        return dp[n]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace isInterleave('aab','dbbca','aadbbcbcac') — length check first: 3+5=8? No, len='aadbbcbcac'=10. Recalculate: s1='aabcc'? No: s1='aab'(3),s2='dbbca'(5),s3='aadbbcbcac'(10). 3+5=8≠10 → False. Use s3='aadbbcbca'(9)? Still. Correct: s3 must equal len(s1)+len(s2)."
# Use s1='aab',s2='dbbca',s3='aadbbcbcac'(10): 3+5=8≠10→return False.
# Canonical: s1='aabcc'(5),s2='dbbca'(5),s3='aadbbcbcac'(10) 5+5=10 ✓
# dp[i][j]=can s1[:i]+s2[:j] form s3[:i+j]. dp[0][0]=T.
# dp[0][j]: s2[:j]==s3[:j]. 'd'=s3[0]? s3[0]='a'≠'d'→dp[0][1]=F. All dp[0][j≥1]=F.
# dp[i][0]: s1[:i]==s3[:i]. s1='aabcc',s3='aadbb...'. 'a'==s3[0]='a'✓→dp[1][0]=T. 'aa'==s3[:2]='aa'✓→dp[2][0]=T. 'aab'?s3[2]='d'≠'b'→dp[3][0]=F.
# dp[2][1]: s3[2]='d'. s1[1]='a'≠'d'. s2[0]='d'==s3[2] AND dp[2][0]=T → dp[2][1]=T.
# Continue... dp[5][5]=True ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(m*n). Space O(n) with rolling array.
#  Follow-up: Edit Distance (#72) — similar 2D DP grid, different transition (insert/delete/replace).
#  Follow-up: return one valid interleaving path — backtrack through the DP table."

138.title: Copy List with Random Pointer
138.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Deep copy a linked list where each node has next AND a random pointer (can point anywhere or null).
#  Return the head of the new list, fully independent of the original. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  random can point to itself or be null? Yes — handle both."
#
# "Let me walk: list with random pointers crossing → produce an identical structure with new node objects ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Hash map old_node → new_node. First pass: create all new nodes with just val.
#  Second pass: wire next and random using the map. O(n) time, O(n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _138_CopyListWithRandomPointer_Brute:
    def copyRandomList(self, head):
        if not head: return None
        old_to_new = {}
        node = head
        while node:
            old_to_new[node] = Node(node.val)
            node = node.next
        node = head
        while node:
            old_to_new[node].next = old_to_new.get(node.next)
            old_to_new[node].random = old_to_new.get(node.random)
            node = node.next
        return old_to_new[head]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Two-pass to set random pointers — O(n). Walk-through:
#  Pass 1: copy nodes without random/next. Use a map: original→copy.
#  Pass 2: for each original node: copy.next = map[original.next]; copy.random = map[original.random].
#  WHY two passes: in pass 1 we don't know if the random-pointed node's copy exists yet.
#  Pass 2 fills all pointers once all copies exist.
#  In-place O(1) space trick:
#    Interleave: A→A'→B→B'→... (insert copy after each original).
#    Set random: curr'.random = curr.random.next.  ← curr.random is original; .next is copy
#    Separate: restore original list; extract copy list.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n) with map, O(1) with interleave."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _138_CopyListWithRandomPointer:
    def copyRandomList(self, head):
        if not head:
            return None
        old_to_new = {}
        current = head
        while current:
            old_to_new[current] = Node(current.val)
            current = current.next
        current = head
        while current:
            copy = old_to_new[current]
            copy.next = old_to_new.get(current.next)
            copy.random = old_to_new.get(current.random)
            current = current.next
        return old_to_new[head]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace copyRandomList([[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]])."
# Two-pass with hash map (original→copy).
# Pass 1: create all copy nodes. copies={orig_i: Node(val_i)}.
# Pass 2: wire next and random pointers.
# Node 0 (val=7, random=null): copies[0].next=copies[1], copies[0].random=None.
# Node 1 (val=13, random=0): copies[1].next=copies[2], copies[1].random=copies[0].
# ... Continue for all nodes. Return copies[head] ✓
# O(1) space alt: interleave copies in original list, set randoms, then split.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(n) for the map (O(1) extra possible with list interleaving trick).
#  Follow-up: Clone Graph (#133) — same hashmap-of-clones pattern for arbitrary graphs.
#  Follow-up: implement the O(1)-space interleaving variant for an interview follow-up."

202.title: Happy Number
202.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Repeatedly replace n with the sum of squares of its digits. If it reaches 1, it's happy.
#  If it loops forever without reaching 1, it's not happy. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  n is positive? Yes. Need to detect cycles to avoid infinite loop."
#
# "Let me walk: n=19 → 1²+9²=82 → 8²+2²=68 → 6²+8²=100 → 1²+0+0=1 → happy ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Use a set to track seen values; if we see a repeat before hitting 1, it's a cycle → not happy.
#  O(log n) per digit-square-sum computation, unknown but bounded number of iterations.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _202_HappyNumber_Brute:
    def isHappy(self, n):
        seen = set()
        def digit_square_sum(x):
            return sum(int(d)**2 for d in str(x))
        while n != 1 and n not in seen:
            seen.add(n)
            n = digit_square_sum(n)
        return n == 1

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Fast/slow pointer (Floyd's cycle detection on digit sums) — O(log n). Walk-through:
#  HOW digit sum works: sum_sq_digits(n) = sum of squares of each digit of n.
#  Floyd's cycle: slow = sum_sq_digits(n). fast = sum_sq_digits(sum_sq_digits(n)).
#  While slow != fast: slow = f(slow); fast = f(f(fast)).
#  If slow==1: it's a happy number (cycle ends at 1).
#  Else: it's in a cycle not containing 1 → not happy.
#  WHY Floyd's: non-happy numbers enter a cycle among values < 243 (since 9²*3=243 for 3-digit).
#  The slow/fast pointers detect the cycle without storing a set.
#  Alternative: hash set — if we see a repeated value, it's not happy.
#  Time: O(log n). Space: O(1) with Floyd's."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _202_HappyNumber:
    def isHappy(self, n):
        def digit_square_sum(x):
            total = 0
            while x:
                d = x % 10
                total += d * d
                x //= 10
            return total
        slow, fast = n, digit_square_sum(n)
        while fast != 1 and slow != fast:
            slow = digit_square_sum(slow)
            fast = digit_square_sum(digit_square_sum(fast))
        return fast == 1

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace isHappy(19)."
# 19 → 1²+9²=1+81=82
# 82 → 8²+2²=64+4=68
# 68 → 6²+8²=36+64=100
# 100 → 1²+0²+0²=1 → return True ✓
# WHY detect cycle: unhappy numbers loop (e.g., 4→16→37→58→89→145→42→20→4)
# Use fast/slow pointers or a seen set to detect the cycle.
# Edge: n=1 → immediately True; n=7 → path 7→49→97→130→10→1 → True.
# Say: "Digit sum helper: repeatedly sum squares of digits until 1 or cycle."

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(log n) per step (digit count), bounded total iterations. Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: Linked List Cycle (#141) — same Floyd's algorithm on an explicit list.
#  Follow-up: find the actual cycle length once detected — count steps after meeting point."

213.title: House Robber II
213.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Houses are arranged in a CIRCLE — first and last are adjacent. Can't rob two adjacent houses.
#  Maximise total robbed amount. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  n=1 → just return that house's value (no adjacency issue)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[2,3,2] → can't rob both house0 and house2 (adjacent in circle) → max(rob[1:], rob[:-1]) → 3 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Since first/last can't both be robbed, run House Robber I DP twice: once excluding house0, once excluding last house.
#  Take the max. O(n) time. This IS the optimal approach. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _213_HouseRobberII_Brute:
    def rob(self, nums):
        if len(nums)==1: return nums[0]
        def rob_line(houses):
            prev, curr = 0, 0
            for h in houses:
                prev, curr = curr, max(curr, prev+h)
            return curr
        return max(rob_line(nums[1:]), rob_line(nums[:-1]))

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Two runs of House Robber I — O(n). Walk-through:
#  Houses form a circle → house 0 and house n-1 are adjacent.
#  Two cases: either rob house 0 (then CAN'T rob house n-1), or don't rob house 0 (can rob n-1).
#  Case 1: run rob_linear on houses[0..n-2].
#  Case 2: run rob_linear on houses[1..n-1].
#  rob_linear(arr): dp where dp[i] = max(dp[i-2]+arr[i], dp[i-1]).
#    dp[0]=arr[0]. dp[1]=max(arr[0],arr[1]).
#    For i≥2: dp[i]=max(arr[i]+dp[i-2], dp[i-1]).
#  Answer = max(case1, case2).
#  WHY two cases: can't have BOTH house 0 and n-1 robbed. Split into two non-circular
#  subproblems, each handled by the linear rob.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _213_HouseRobberII:
    def rob(self, nums):
        if len(nums) == 1:
            return nums[0]
        def rob_line(houses):
            prev_max, curr_max = 0, 0
            for amount in houses:
                prev_max, curr_max = curr_max, max(curr_max, prev_max + amount)
            return curr_max
        return max(rob_line(nums[1:]), rob_line(nums[:-1]))

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace houseRobberII on [2,3,2]."
# Can't rob both house 0 and house n-1 (circular). Split into two linear problems:
# rob([2,3]) = max(2,3)=3. (skip last house)
# rob([3,2]) = max(3,2)=3. (skip first house)
# Return max(3,3)=3 ✓
# [1,2,3,1]: rob([1,2,3])=max(1,max(2,1+3),max(3,2))=4. rob([2,3,1])=max(2,max(3,2+1),max(1,3))=4. return 4 ✓
# WHY two linear solves: the circular constraint means house 0 and house n-1 can't both be robbed.
# Take the best of: rob(0..n-2) vs rob(1..n-1). Each is the standard linear rob problem.

# WHY DP terms: using state + recurrence/transition to combine prior results efficiently.
# dp[i]=max rob from 0..i. dp[0]=nums[0],dp[1]=max(dp[0],nums[1]),dp[i]=max(dp[i-1],dp[i-2]+nums[i]). Run twice: once skip first, once skip last. Answer=max of both runs ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: House Robber I (#198) — linear arrangement, no circular constraint.
#  Follow-up: House Robber III (#337) — tree-shaped arrangement, needs tree DP."

332.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
332.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Given flight tickets [from,to], reconstruct the itinerary starting from 'JFK' using all tickets exactly once.
#  If multiple valid itineraries exist, return the lexicographically smallest. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Guaranteed at least one valid itinerary exists (uses all tickets)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: tickets=[['MUC','LHR'],['JFK','MUC'],['SFO','SJC'],['LHR','SFO']] → ['JFK','MUC','LHR','SFO','SJC'] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Build adjacency list sorted lexicographically. DFS trying each destination in order, backtrack if stuck.
#  O(E²) worst case due to backtracking. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _332_ReconstructItinerary_Brute:
    def findItinerary(self, tickets):
        from collections import defaultdict
        graph = defaultdict(list)
        for a,b in sorted(tickets): graph[a].append(b)
        route = []
        def dfs(airport):
            while graph[airport]:
                nxt = graph[airport].pop(0)
                dfs(nxt)
            route.append(airport)
        dfs('JFK')
        return route[::-1]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DFS / Hierholzer's algorithm for Eulerian path — O(E log E). Walk-through:
#  Sort adjacency lists (for lexicographic ordering).
#  DFS from 'JFK': greedily visit the smallest available destination.
#  When a node has no more outgoing edges: append it to the result.
#  Reverse at the end.
#  WHY post-order append (Hierholzer): if we greedily follow edges but hit a dead-end early,
#  those dead-end nodes should go AFTER the nodes that circle back.
#  Post-order ensures: cycles are explored fully before backtracking.
#  WHY sort adjacency: Eulerian path is not unique — we want lexicographically smallest.
#  Sorting + taking smallest next ensures this.
#  Time: O(E log E) for sorting. Space: O(E)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict
class _332_ReconstructItinerary:
    def findItinerary(self, tickets):
        graph = defaultdict(list)
        for src, dst in tickets:
            heapq.heappush(graph[src], dst)
        route = []
        def visit(airport):
            while graph[airport]:
                next_airport = heapq.heappop(graph[airport])
                visit(next_airport)
            route.append(airport)
        visit('JFK')
        return route[::-1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace findItinerary on tickets=[['MUC','LHR'],['JFK','MUC'],['SFO','SJC'],['LHR','SFO']]."
# Build sorted adjacency: JFK→[MUC], MUC→[LHR], LHR→[SFO], SFO→[SJC].
# Hierholzer DFS from JFK:
# dfs(JFK): neighbor=MUC (pop). dfs(MUC): neighbor=LHR (pop). dfs(LHR): neighbor=SFO (pop).
#   dfs(SFO): neighbor=SJC (pop). dfs(SJC): no neighbors → append SJC. return.
#   dfs(SFO) done → append SFO. return.
#   dfs(LHR) done → append LHR. return. dfs(MUC) done → append MUC. return.
# dfs(JFK) done → append JFK. result=[SJC,SFO,LHR,MUC,JFK]. Reverse → [JFK,MUC,LHR,SFO,SJC] ✓
# WHY post-order append: dead-ends go last when reversed → correct Euler path.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(E log E): heap push/pop per edge. Space O(E).
#  Follow-up: Valid Arrangement of Pairs (#2097) — same Eulerian path idea, no lexicographic constraint.
#  Follow-up: Cracking the Safe (#753) — Eulerian circuit construction for de Bruijn sequences."

355.title: Design Twitter
355.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Design a simplified Twitter: postTweet, getNewsFeed (10 most recent from self+followees), follow, unfollow. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  getNewsFeed needs tweets ordered most-recent-first across all followed users? Yes.
#  A user follows themselves implicitly (sees own tweets)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: post(1,5), getNewsFeed(1)→[5]. follow(1,2), post(2,6), getNewsFeed(1)→[6,5] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Store all tweets globally with timestamps. getNewsFeed: filter tweets by followee set, sort by time, take top 10.
#  O(n log n) per feed call. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _355_DesignTwitter_Brute:
    def __init__(self):
        self.tweets = []  # (time, userId, tweetId)
        self.time = 0
        self.follows = {}
    def postTweet(self, userId, tweetId):
        self.tweets.append((self.time, userId, tweetId)); self.time += 1
    def getNewsFeed(self, userId):
        followees = self.follows.get(userId, set()) | {userId}
        relevant = [t for t in self.tweets if t[1] in followees]
        relevant.sort(key=lambda x: -x[0])
        return [t[2] for t in relevant[:10]]
    def follow(self, followerId, followeeId):
        self.follows.setdefault(followerId, set()).add(followeeId)
    def unfollow(self, followerId, followeeId):
        self.follows.get(followerId, set()).discard(followeeId)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Heap-based tweet feed + follow/unfollow maps — O(log U) per getNewsFeed. Walk-through:
#  follow_map[userId] = set of followees.
#  tweet_map[userId] = list of (timestamp, tweetId) in FIFO order (append order = timestamp order).
#  postTweet: append (global_time++, tweetId) to tweet_map[userId].
#  getNewsFeed(userId):
#    min-heap of size 10 (negate timestamp for max-heap behavior).
#    For each user in follow_map[userId] ∪ {userId}:
#      Add last tweet (tweet_map[user][-1]) to heap (with pointer to position in their list).
#    Extract top-10: pop max-timestamp tweet, add to result; if user has more tweets, push next.
#  follow/unfollow: add/remove from follow_map[userId].
#  WHY heap: efficiently merge multiple tweet lists to get top-10 globally.
#  Time: O(U log U) per getNewsFeed where U = followees. Space: O(total tweets)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict
class _355_DesignTwitter:
    def __init__(self):
        self.timestamp = 0
        self.user_tweets = defaultdict(list)
        self.user_follows = defaultdict(set)

    def postTweet(self, userId, tweetId):
        self.user_tweets[userId].append((self.timestamp, tweetId))
        self.timestamp += 1

    def getNewsFeed(self, userId):
        heap = []
        followees = self.user_follows[userId] | {userId}
        for uid in followees:
            tweets = self.user_tweets[uid]
            if tweets:
                idx = len(tweets) - 1
                time, tweetId = tweets[idx]
                heapq.heappush(heap, (-time, tweetId, uid, idx - 1))
        result = []
        while heap and len(result) < 10:
            neg_time, tweetId, uid, idx = heapq.heappop(heap)
            result.append(tweetId)
            if idx >= 0:
                time, tid = self.user_tweets[uid][idx]
                heapq.heappush(heap, (-time, tid, uid, idx - 1))
        return result

    def follow(self, followerId, followeeId):
        if followerId != followeeId:
            self.user_follows[followerId].add(followeeId)

    def unfollow(self, followerId, followeeId):
        self.user_follows[followerId].discard(followeeId)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace Twitter: follow(1,2), postTweet(1,5), getNewsFeed(1), unfollow(1,2), getNewsFeed(1)."
# userId→set of followees. userId→list of (timestamp,tweetId).
# follow(1,2): following[1]={2}. postTweet(1,5): tweets[1]=[(0,5)].
# getNewsFeed(1): self + followees = {1,2}. Merge tweet lists by timestamp desc.
#   tweets[1]=[(0,5)], tweets[2]=[]. Top 10 → [(5)] ✓. Return [5] ✓
# unfollow(1,2): following[1]={}.
# getNewsFeed(1): only {1}'s tweets → [5] ✓ (own tweet still there).
# WHY heap merge: n users × up to 10 tweets each → min-heap of size n for O(n log n) merge.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(F log F) per feed. Space O(n + F).
#  Follow-up: Merge k Sorted Lists (#23) — identical heap-merge pattern.
#  Follow-up: support retweets or likes — extend tweet tuple with metadata."

371.title: Sum of Two Integers
371.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Compute a+b WITHOUT using the + or - operators. Use bitwise operations instead. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Handle negative numbers via two's complement representation? Yes, within 32-bit bounds."
#
# "Let me walk: a=1,b=2 → 3 ✓ (via XOR+AND+shift simulation of addition)"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Bitwise addition: XOR gives sum without carry, AND+shift gives the carry. Repeat until no carry remains.
#  O(32) iterations max (bounded by integer width). This IS the standard approach. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _371_SumOfTwoIntegers_Brute:
    def getSum(self, a, b):
        mask = 0xFFFFFFFF
        while b & mask:
            carry = (a & b) << 1
            a = a ^ b
            b = carry
        return (a & mask) if (b > mask >> 1 or a & 0x80000000) else (a & mask)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Simulate addition with bit operations — O(1) (32-bit integers). Walk-through:
#  sum_no_carry = a ^ b  (XOR gives bits that differ → these are the sum bits without carry).
#  carry = (a & b) << 1  (AND gives positions where both bits are 1 → carry shifted left).
#  Repeat: a = sum_no_carry, b = carry. Stop when carry == 0.
#  WHY XOR for sum: 1+1=10 (carry), 1+0=1, 0+0=0 → XOR gives the no-carry part.
#  WHY AND then shift left: carry happens when both bits are 1 → affects the next bit position.
#  Iterate until no carry remains. In Python, mask to 32 bits to handle negatives.
#  Time: O(1) for 32-bit integers. Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _371_SumOfTwoIntegers:
    def getSum(self, a, b):
        mask = 0xFFFFFFFF
        while b != 0:
            carry = (a & b) << 1
            a = (a ^ b) & mask
            b = carry & mask
        return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF else ~(a ^ mask)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace getSum(1,2) without + operator."
# a=1=01, b=2=10.
# sum_no_carry=a^b=01^10=11=3. carry=(a&b)<<1=00<<1=0.
# carry=0 → stop. Return 3 ✓
# a=3=011, b=5=101: a^b=110=6. carry=(011&101)<<1=001<<1=010=2.
# a=6=110, b=2=010: a^b=100=4. carry=(110&010)<<1=010<<1=100=4.
# a=4=100, b=4=100: a^b=000=0. carry=(100&100)<<1=100<<1=1000=8.
# a=0, b=8: a^b=8. carry=0 → return 8 ✓ (3+5=8).


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(1) — bounded by 32 iterations max. Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: implement subtraction using getSum(a, getSum(~b, 1)) (two's complement negation).
#  Follow-up: Add Binary (#67) — string-based version of the same carry logic."

494.title: Target Sum
494.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Assign + or - to each number in nums so they sum to target. Count the number of ways. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  nums can include 0s (still counted as separate +/- choices even if value is 0)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[1,1,1,1,1], target=3 → 5 ways ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all 2^n sign assignments via backtracking, count those summing to target. O(2^n) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _494_TargetSum_Brute:
    def findTargetSumWays(self, nums, target):
        count = [0]
        def backtrack(i, total):
            if i == len(nums):
                if total == target: count[0] += 1
                return
            backtrack(i+1, total+nums[i])
            backtrack(i+1, total-nums[i])
        backtrack(0, 0)
        return count[0]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DP on sum offset — O(n * sum). Walk-through:
#  Map: sum ranges from -total to +total. Use offset=total to shift to [0, 2*total].
#  dp[s] = number of ways to reach sum s.
#  Initial: dp[total] = 1  (sum=0, shifted by total).
#  For each num: new_dp[s+num] += dp[s]; new_dp[s-num] += dp[s].
#  Return dp[total + target].
#  WHY sum offset: dp array can't have negative indices; shift by total to handle -sum..+sum.
#  WHY new_dp each step: assignments for current num must not interfere with each other.
#  Optimization: observe P-N=target and P+N=total → P=(total+target)/2 → subset sum problem.
#  Time: O(n * sum). Space: O(sum)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _494_TargetSum:
    def findTargetSumWays(self, nums, target):
        total = sum(nums)
        if abs(target) > total or (total + target) % 2 != 0:
            return 0
        subset_sum = (total + target) // 2
        dp = [0] * (subset_sum + 1)
        dp[0] = 1
        for num in nums:
            for s in range(subset_sum, num - 1, -1):
                dp[s] += dp[s - num]
        return dp[subset_sum]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace findTargetSumWays([1,1,1,1,1], target=3)."
# Sum=5. Subset with + signs: P. Subset with -: N=5-P. P-N=3 → P=4. Subset sum = 4.
# dp=[0]*6. dp[0]=1. Process each 1:
# After 1st '1': dp[1]+=dp[0]=1. dp=[1,1,0,0,0,0].
# After 2nd '1': dp[2]+=dp[1]=1. dp[1]+=dp[0]=1. dp=[1,2,1,0,0,0].
# After 3rd '1': dp[3]+=dp[2],dp[2]+=dp[1],dp[1]+=dp[0]. dp=[1,3,3,1,0,0].
# After 4th '1': dp=[1,4,6,4,1,0]. After 5th '1': dp=[1,5,10,10,5,1].
# dp[4]=5 ✓ (number of ways to choose 4 from 5 ones for '+' sign = C(5,4)=5).


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n*sum). Space O(sum).
#  Follow-up: Partition Equal Subset Sum (#416) — same subset-sum DP, simpler target.
#  Follow-up: Coin Change II (#518) — unbounded version (reuse allowed), forward iteration instead."

518.title: Coin Change II
518.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count the number of distinct combinations of coins that sum to amount.
#  Unlimited supply of each coin. Order doesn't matter (combinations, not permutations). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  amount=0 → 1 way (use no coins)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: amount=5, coins=[1,2,5] → 4 ways ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Recursive: for each coin, either use it (stay at same coin index) or skip to next coin.
#  Memoize (index, remaining). O(n*amount) states. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _518_CoinChangeII_Brute:
    def change(self, amount, coins):
        from functools import lru_cache
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(i, remaining):
            if remaining == 0: return 1
            if i == len(coins) or remaining < 0: return 0
            return dp(i, remaining-coins[i]) + dp(i+1, remaining)
        return dp(0, amount)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Unbounded knapsack DP — O(n * amount). Walk-through:
#  dp[i] = number of combinations to make amount i.
#  dp[0] = 1 (one way to make 0: use no coins).
#  For each coin (OUTER loop — processes one coin at a time to avoid permutations):
#    For i in coin..amount:
#      dp[i] += dp[i-coin].
#  Return dp[amount].
#  WHY coin as OUTER loop: ensures each coin is either not used or used any number of times,
#  but combinations (not permutations) are counted.
#  If amount were OUTER loop: [1,2] and [2,1] would be counted separately → permutations.
#  WHY unbounded: same coin can be used multiple times → no 'used' tracking per coin.
#  Time: O(n * amount). Space: O(amount)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _518_CoinChangeII:
    def change(self, amount, coins):
        dp = [0] * (amount + 1)
        dp[0] = 1
        for coin in coins:
            for a in range(coin, amount + 1):
                dp[a] += dp[a - coin]
        return dp[amount]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace change on amount=5, coins=[1,2,5]."
# dp[i] = number of ways to make amount i
# dp[0]=1 (empty combination). Initialize dp[1..5]=0
# coin=1: dp[1]+=dp[0]=1, dp[2]+=dp[1]=1, dp[3]+=dp[2]=1, dp[4]+=dp[3]=1, dp[5]+=dp[4]=1
# coin=2: dp[2]+=dp[0]=1→dp[2]=2, dp[3]+=dp[1]=1→dp[3]=2, dp[4]+=dp[2]=2→dp[4]=3, dp[5]+=dp[3]=2→dp[5]=3
# coin=5: dp[5]+=dp[0]=1→dp[5]=4 ✓? Wait: (1+1+1+1+1),(1+1+1+2),(1+2+2),(5),(1+1+3?)
# Actually dp[5]=4: (5),(1+2+2),(1+1+1+2),(1+1+1+1+1) ✓
# WHY outer loop over coins: ensures each coin used at most... wait it's unbounded, so 4 ways ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n*amount). Space O(amount).
#  Follow-up: Coin Change I (#322) — minimum coins instead of count of combinations.
#  Follow-up: Target Sum (#494) — 0/1 knapsack variant (reverse iteration, no reuse)."

567.title: Permutation in String
567.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Does s2 contain a contiguous substring that is a permutation of s1 (i.e. an anagram)? Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Case sensitive, lowercase letters only per constraints? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: s1='ab', s2='eidbaooo' → 'ba' at index 3 is a permutation of 'ab' → true ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each window of length len(s1) in s2, sort and compare to sorted(s1). O(n * k log k) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _567_PermutationInString_Brute:
    def checkInclusion(self, s1, s2):
        k = len(s1)
        target = sorted(s1)
        for i in range(len(s2)-k+1):
            if sorted(s2[i:i+k]) == target: return True
        return False

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is sorting each window — O(n*k log k).
#  Fixed-size sliding window with character frequency counts. Maintain a 'matches' counter of how
#  many of the 26 letters have matching counts between window and s1. Slide one char at a time,
#  updating counts and matches in O(1) per step.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(26) = O(1)."
# Key insight: a "matches" counter tracks how many of 26 letters have equal frequency — each character slide updates the counter in O(1), making the full sweep O(n).
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _567_PermutationInString:
    def checkInclusion(self, s1, s2):
        if len(s1) > len(s2):
            return False
        need = [0] * 26
        window = [0] * 26
        for ch in s1:
            need[ord(ch) - 97] += 1
        k = len(s1)
        for i in range(k):
            window[ord(s2[i]) - 97] += 1
        if window == need:
            return True
        for i in range(k, len(s2)):
            window[ord(s2[i]) - 97] += 1
            window[ord(s2[i - k]) - 97] -= 1
            if window == need:
                return True
        return False

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace checkInclusion('ab','eidbaooo')."
# need={a:1,b:1}. window size=2.
# [0..1]='ei': {e:1,i:1}≠need. Slide right.
# [1..2]='id': no. [2..3]='db': no. [3..4]='ba': {b:1,a:1}==need → return True ✓
# 'ab' in 'eidboaoo': check each window of size 2.
# Short circuit: track have/need count. have=0 (chars meeting required freq).
# When have==len(need): window contains permutation ✓

# WHY: DP/greedy isn’t needed because the window property is maintained by expanding and contracting while keeping the condition valid.
# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1) (26-letter arrays).
#  Follow-up: Find All Anagrams in a String (#438) — same technique, collect all start indices.
#  Follow-up: Minimum Window Substring (#76) — variable-size window instead of fixed."

647.title: Palindromic Substrings
647.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count how many substrings of s are palindromes (including single characters and the whole string if applicable). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Overlapping substrings all count separately? Yes — e.g. 'aaa' has 6 palindromic substrings."
#
# "Let me walk: s='abc' → 3 (a,b,c). s='aaa' → 6 (a,a,a,aa,aa,aaa) ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Check every substring for palindrome property. O(n²) substrings × O(n) check = O(n³). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _647_PalindromicSubstrings_Brute:
    def countSubstrings(self, s):
        n = len(s); count = 0
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i, n):
                sub = s[i:j+1]
                if sub == sub[::-1]: count += 1
        return count

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Expand around every center — O(n²). Walk-through:
#  For each center in 0..2n-2 (odd+even centers):
#    Odd center c: l=c//2, r=c//2.
#    Even center c: l=c//2, r=c//2+1.
#    While l>=0 and r<n and s[l]==s[r]: count++; l--; r++.
#  Return count.
#  WHY 2n-1 centers: n odd centers (each character) + n-1 even centers (between characters).
#  WHY expand outward: a palindrome expands from its center.
#  Each valid expansion = one palindromic substring.
#  Alternative: Manacher's algorithm → O(n) but complex.
#  DP: dp[i][j] = is s[i..j] palindrome? → O(n²) time and space.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _647_PalindromicSubstrings:
    def countSubstrings(self, s):
        n = len(s)
        count = 0
        def expand(left, right):
            nonlocal count
            while left >= 0 and right < n and s[left] == s[right]:
                count += 1
                left -= 1
                right += 1
        for center in range(n):
            expand(center, center)
            expand(center, center + 1)
        return count

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace how the left/right pointers move and why the invariant stays true."
#
# s='aaa': center=0: expand(0,0)→count=1('a'). expand(0,1)→s[0]==s[1]→count=2('aa'); left=-1 stop.
# center=1: expand(1,1)→count=3. expand(1,2)→count=4('aa'). center=2: expand(2,2)→count=5. expand(2,3)→out of bounds.
# Also center=0's odd expansion at full range: expand(0,0)→ -1,1 invalid since aaa needs center=1 for full match.
# Let me recheck: center=1,expand(1,1)→then left=0,right=2: s[0]=='a'==s[2]→count+=1('aaa'). Total=6 ✓
#
# Each center (single char and between-pairs) independently expands until mismatch or boundary

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²). Space O(1).
