#  Height-balanced: every node's subtree heights differ by at most 1. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Same as #108 but with a linked list instead of array? Yes — find the middle each time."
#
# "Let me walk: head=[-10,-3,0,5,9] → [0,-3,9,-10,null,5] or similar balanced BST ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Collect all values into an array; then apply #108 (sorted array to BST).
#  O(n) time, O(n) space for the array. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _109_ConvertSortedListToBST_Brute:
    def sortedListToBST(self, head):
        vals=[]; cur=head
        while cur: vals.append(cur.val); cur=cur.next
        def build(lo,hi):
            if lo>hi: return None
            mid=(lo+hi)//2; node=TreeNode(vals[mid])
            node.left=build(lo,mid-1); node.right=build(mid+1,hi)
            return node
        return build(0,len(vals)-1)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Slow/fast pointer to find middle, then recursively build BST — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  findMid(node): slow/fast pointers to find middle of linked list.
#    Return slow (middle node), also disconnect: prev.next = None to split list.
#  convert(head):
#    If head is None: return None.
#    If head.next is None: return TreeNode(head.val).
#    mid = findMid(head).
#    root = TreeNode(mid.val).
#    root.left = convert(head).  ← left half of list (up to mid)
#    root.right = convert(mid.next).  ← right half of list
#    return root.
#  WHY middle as root: BST property + sorted list → middle of current sublist = root gives balanced BST.
#  WHY disconnect list: separates the left and right halves for recursive calls.
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(log n) call stack."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _109_ConvertSortedListToBST:
    def sortedListToBST(self, head):
        if not head:
            return None
        if not head.next:
            return TreeNode(head.val)
        prev = None
        slow = fast = head
        while fast and fast.next:
            prev = slow; slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next
        prev.next = None
        node = TreeNode(slow.val)
        node.left = self.sortedListToBST(head)
        node.right = self.sortedListToBST(slow.next)
        return node

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace sortedListToBST on -10→-3→0→5→9."
# findMid(-10→...): slow ends at 0, disconnect: -10→-3 | 0→5→9. mid=0→root.
# Left subproblem: convert(-10→-3):
#   findMid: slow=-10, fast reaches end. mid=-3. disconnect: -10 | -3. mid=-3→root.
#   Left: convert(-10)→Node(-10). Right: convert(None)→None.
# Right subproblem: convert(5→9): mid=9? No, findMid: slow=5,fast=9→next=None. mid=5→root. Right=convert(9)→Node(9).
# Tree: 0(left=-3(left=-10), right=5(right=9)) ✓
# WHY slow/fast to find mid: splits list in half. Disconnecting isolates each half for recursion.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log n): O(log n) levels, each finding n midpoints total → O(n log n).
#  Space O(log n) recursion.
#  Array approach: O(n) time, O(n) space — better time at cost of space.
#  Follow-up: Convert BST to Sorted Linked List (#426) — reverse operation."

912.title: SORT AN ARRAY  (Merge Sort)
912.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Sort an array of integers. The follow-up asks for O(n log n) without built-in sort. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Return a new sorted array? Yes. Values can be negative? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[5,2,3,1] → [1,2,3,5] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Use Python's built-in sort. O(n log n). This IS the standard answer.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _912_SortAnArray_Brute:
    def sortArray(self, nums):
        return sorted(nums)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Merge sort — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Divide: split array in half recursively until single elements.
#  Conquer: merge two sorted halves into a sorted array:
#    Two pointers i (left half), j (right half). Compare; take smaller; advance that pointer.
#    Append remaining elements.
#  HOW recursion builds the answer: base case (1 element) is trivially sorted.
#  Each merge combines two sorted halves of size k → sorted array of size 2k.
#  At depth log n, we merge two halves of size n/2 → complete sorted array.
#  WHY merge sort for this problem: guaranteed O(n log n) unlike quicksort's O(n²) worst case.
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(n) for merge buffer."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _912_SortAnArray:
    def sortArray(self, nums):
        def merge_sort(arr):
            if len(arr) <= 1:
                return arr
            mid = len(arr) // 2
            left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
            right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])
            return merge(left, right)
        def merge(a, b):
            result = []; i = j = 0
            while i < len(a) and j < len(b):
                if a[i] <= b[j]: result.append(a[i]); i += 1
                else: result.append(b[j]); j += 1
            result.extend(a[i:]); result.extend(b[j:])
            return result
        return merge_sort(nums)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace sortArray([5,2,3,1]) using merge sort."
# Divide: [5,2] and [3,1]
# Recurse left: [5] and [2] → merge → [2,5]
# Recurse right: [3] and [1] → merge → [1,3]
# Merge [2,5] and [1,3]: compare 2 vs 1 → take 1; 2 vs 3 → take 2; 3 vs 5 → take 3; take 5
# Result: [1,2,3,5] ✓
# Merge call stack: sortArray([5,2,3,1])→sort([5,2])→sort([5]),sort([2])→merge→[2,5]; similarly [1,3]
# WHY merge sort: O(n log n) guaranteed; stable; O(n) extra space for merging.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log n). Space O(n) for merged arrays.
#  In-place merge sort: O(1) extra space but O(n log²n) time.
#  Follow-up: Sort List (#148) — bottom-up merge sort on linked list, O(1) space.
#  Follow-up: if values in bounded range, counting sort achieves O(n)."

1985.title: FIND THE KTH LARGEST INTEGER IN THE ARRAY  (QuickSort / QuickSelect)
1985.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Given an array of numeric strings, find the kth largest integer (by numeric value).
#  Return as a string. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Strings represent non-negative integers with no leading zeros? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=['3','6','7','10'], k=4 → 4th largest = '3' ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Sort by numeric value descending; return kth element. O(n log n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1985_FindKthLargestInteger_Brute:
    def kthLargestNumber(self, nums, k):
        return sorted(nums, key=lambda x: int(x), reverse=True)[k-1]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Sort as integers, return k-th largest — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Convert strings to integers for correct numeric comparison (not lexicographic).
#  Sort descending. Return nums[k-1].
#  WHY convert to int: '100' > '99' numerically but '99' > '100' lexicographically
#  (comparing char '9' vs '1'). Must compare as integers.
#  Alternative O(n) QuickSelect: partial sort, stop when pivot is at position n-k.
#  Picks answer without fully sorting → O(n) average.
#  Time: O(n log n) sort or O(n) avg QuickSelect. Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import heapq
class _1985_FindKthLargestInteger:
    def kthLargestNumber(self, nums, k):
        def cmp_key(s):
            return (len(s), s)
        heap = []
        for num in nums:
            heapq.heappush(heap, cmp_key(num))
            if len(heap) > k:
                heapq.heappop(heap)
        return heap[0][1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace kthLargestNumber(['3','6','7','10'], k=4)."
# These are string representations of integers; sort by numeric value
# Sorted numerically: '3','6','7','10' → 4th largest=3 ✓ (largest=10,6,7,3)
# QuickSelect: partition around pivot comparing by numeric value
# WHY custom comparator: '10'>'9' lexicographically but 10>9 numerically.
# Comparator: compare int(a) vs int(b) or compare by length then lexicographically for same length.
# kth largest = kth from end in sorted = quickselect in O(n) expected.
# WHY compare as integers (len then lex): '100' > '99' by length, '9' > '10' lex but not numerically.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log k). Space O(k) heap.
#  Sort approach: O(n log n) — simpler to write for an interview.
#  Follow-up: Kth Largest Element in Array (#215) — integers not strings; use QuickSelect.
#  Follow-up: if strings can have leading zeros, strip them before comparison."

99.title: RECOVER BINARY SEARCH TREE  (BST / Ordered Set)
99.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Exactly two nodes in a BST are swapped. Recover the BST without changing structure. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Modify in-place (swap values)? Yes. O(1) space is the follow-up? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: root=[1,3,null,null,2] (3 and 1 swapped) → [3,1,null,null,2] → recover to [1,3,null,null,2] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Inorder traversal gives sorted values with two out-of-order elements.
#  Find them; swap their values. O(n) time, O(n) space for values.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _99_RecoverBST_Brute:
    def recoverTree(self, root):
        nodes=[]; vals=[]
        def inorder(n):
            if n: inorder(n.left); nodes.append(n); vals.append(n.val); inorder(n.right)
        inorder(root)
        sorted_vals=sorted(vals)
        for node,v in zip(nodes,sorted_vals): node.val=v

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is O(n) extra storage.
#  Morris traversal-like inorder: track prev node.
#  First mistake: prev.val > curr.val → first = prev.
#  Second mistake: again prev.val > curr.val → second = curr.
#  Swap first.val and second.val at the end. O(n) time, O(1) space."
# Key insight: an inorder BST traversal produces a sorted sequence — exactly one descent (prev > curr) marks the first swapped node, another marks the second.
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _99_RecoverBST:
    def recoverTree(self, root):
        first = second = prev = None
        def inorder(node):
            nonlocal first, second, prev
            if not node: return
            inorder(node.left)
            if prev and prev.val > node.val:
                if not first: first = prev
                second = node
            prev = node
            inorder(node.right)
        inorder(root)
        first.val, second.val = second.val, first.val

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the tree recursion on the example, showing the return value at each node."
#
# root=[3,1,null,null,2]: inorder visits 1,2,3 in correct order? Actually root=3,left=1,1.right=2.
# inorder: 1,2,3. prev=1,curr=2: ok. prev=2,curr=3: ok. No swaps — but expected to find issue.
# Actually the swapped tree is root=[1,3,null,null,2] where 1 and 3 are swapped.
# inorder of that: visit 3(left of 1? No—1 is root,3 is left child,3 has right child 2.
# inorder: 3,2,1 — wait that's decreasing? Hmm.
# Actually root=[1,3,null,null,2]: root=1, root.left=3, 3.right=2.
# inorder visits: 3,2,1. prev=3,curr=2: 3>2→first=3,second=2. prev=2,curr=1: 2>1→second=1. swap 3 and 1. ✓
#
# Two-pointer inorder finds first and second swapped nodes correctly

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(h) recursion stack. Morris: O(1).
#  Follow-up: if three nodes are swapped — more complex logic needed.
#  Follow-up: Validate BST (#98) — check validity without recovering."

450.title: DELETE NODE IN A BST  (BST / Ordered Set)
450.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Delete a key from a BST. Handle three cases: leaf, one child, two children. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Key guaranteed to exist? Not necessarily — return unchanged if not found. Right."
#
# "Let me walk: root=[5,3,6,2,4,null,7], key=3 → [5,4,6,2,null,null,7] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Recursive: find key, handle three cases. O(h) time. This IS optimal.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _450_DeleteNodeInBST_Brute:
    def deleteNode(self, root, key):
        if not root: return None
        if key < root.val: root.left=self.deleteNode(root.left,key)
        elif key > root.val: root.right=self.deleteNode(root.right,key)
        else:
            if not root.left: return root.right
            if not root.right: return root.left
            cur=root.right
            while cur.left: cur=cur.left
            root.val=cur.val
            root.right=self.deleteNode(root.right,cur.val)
        return root

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Recursive BST deletion — already O(h). Walk-through of the three cases:
#  delete(node, key):
#    If node is None → return None (key not found).
#    If key < node.val → node.left = delete(node.left, key); return node.
#    If key > node.val → node.right = delete(node.right, key); return node.
#    ← key == node.val: three sub-cases:
#    Case 1: no left child → return node.right (replace node with right subtree).
#    Case 2: no right child → return node.left.
#    Case 3: two children:
#      Find inorder successor = leftmost node of right subtree.
#      Copy successor's value into current node.
#      Delete the successor from the right subtree.
#      return node.
#  WHY inorder successor: it's the smallest value LARGER than node → maintains BST property.
#  Time: O(h). Space: O(h) recursion."
# Time: O(n) — optimal single-pass solution. Linear time is best achievable.

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _450_DeleteNodeInBST:
    def deleteNode(self, root, key):
        if not root:
            return None
        if key < root.val:
            root.left = self.deleteNode(root.left, key)
        elif key > root.val:
            root.right = self.deleteNode(root.right, key)
        else:
            if not root.left:
                return root.right
            if not root.right:
                return root.left
            successor = root.right
            while successor.left:
                successor = successor.left
            root.val = successor.val
            root.right = self.deleteNode(root.right, successor.val)
        return root

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace deleteNode in BST [5,3,6,2,4,null,7], key=3."
# Find key=3. Node 3 has left=2 and right=4.
# Case: has both children. Find in-order successor (leftmost of right subtree)=4.
# Replace 3's val with 4. Delete 4 from right subtree:
#   deleteNode(4-subtree, 4): 4 is leaf → return None. 3(now renamed 4).right=None.
# Tree: 5(4(2,None),6(None,7)) ✓
# Alternatively: in-order predecessor=2. Replace 3 with 2, delete 2 from left subtree.
# WHY successor/predecessor: maintains BST property after deletion.
# Case leaf: return None. Case one child: return that child.
# BST delete: curr=root. Traverse: curr.left if val<curr.val else curr.right. On match: curr.left=None (leaf). Or: curr.right.next→inorder_successor replaces curr. prev.next=successor.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(h): O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed. Space O(h) recursion.
#  Follow-up: Insert into BST (#701) — simpler, just find the right spot.
#  Follow-up: if we also need to balance after deletion, AVL (self-balancing BST)/Red-Black tree operations."

701.title: INSERT INTO A BINARY SEARCH TREE  (BST / Ordered Set)
701.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Insert val into a BST such that it remains a valid BST. Return the root. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  val guaranteed not to exist in the BST? Yes per constraints."
#
# "Let me walk: root=[4,2,7,1,3], val=5 → [4,2,7,1,3,5] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Navigate to the correct leaf position; insert. O(h) time. This IS optimal.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _701_InsertIntoBST_Brute:
    def insertIntoBST(self, root, val):
        if not root: return TreeNode(val)
        if val < root.val: root.left=self.insertIntoBST(root.left,val)
        else: root.right=self.insertIntoBST(root.right,val)
        return root

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "BST insertion — O(h), walk-through:
#  insert(node, val):
#    If node is None → return TreeNode(val)  ← found the insertion point.
#    If val < node.val:
#      node.left = insert(node.left, val)   ← recurse left; attach result as new left
#    else:
#      node.right = insert(node.right, val) ← recurse right; attach result as new right
#    return node  ← return current node unchanged (or with updated child)
#  HOW insertion works: we recurse until we hit a None, create the node there, and return it.
#  The parent gets the new node as its child via 'node.left = insert(node.left, val)'.
#  WHY this maintains BST property: we only go left when val < node.val, ensuring
#  the new node lands in a position consistent with BST ordering.
#  Time: O(h). Space: O(h) recursion."
# Time: O(log n) — binary search on answer space.

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _701_InsertIntoBST:
    def insertIntoBST(self, root, val):
        if not root:
            return TreeNode(val)
        cur = root
        while True:
            if val < cur.val:
                if not cur.left:
                    cur.left = TreeNode(val); break
                cur = cur.left
            else:
                if not cur.right:
                    cur.right = TreeNode(val); break
                cur = cur.right
        return root

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace insertIntoBST on [4,2,7,1,3], val=5."
# node=4: 5>4 → go right. node=7: 5<7 → go left. node=None → return new TreeNode(5).
# 7.left = TreeNode(5). Return 4(2(1,3),7(5,None)) ✓
# val=0:
# node=4: 0<4→left. node=2: 0<2→left. node=1: 0<1→left→None→return TreeNode(0).
# 1.left=TreeNode(0). ✓
# WHY always insert as a leaf: BST insertion never restructures existing nodes — find the
#   correct BST position (always None slot) and place new node there.
# WHY recursive returns node: propagates the new/existing node up to reconnect parent.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(h). Space O(1) iterative vs O(h) recursive.
#  Follow-up: Delete from BST (#450) — more complex due to rebalancing.
#  Follow-up: if BST must stay balanced, use AVL (self-balancing BST) or Red-Black tree rotation."

669.title: TRIM A BINARY SEARCH TREE  (BST / Ordered Set)
669.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Trim a BST so all values lie in [low, high]. Return the trimmed root. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Nodes outside [low, high] are deleted entirely (not just the node, subtree may be kept)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: root=[3,0,4,null,2,null,null,1], low=1, high=3 → [3,2,null,1] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Recursive: if node.val < low, the left subtree is also < low → return trim(right). Vice versa for > high.
#  O(n) time. This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _669_TrimBST_Brute:
    def trimBST(self, root, low, high):
        if not root: return None
        if root.val < low: return self.trimBST(root.right, low, high)
        if root.val > high: return self.trimBST(root.left, low, high)
        root.left=self.trimBST(root.left,low,high)
        root.right=self.trimBST(root.right,low,high)
        return root

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Recursive BST trim — already O(n). Walk-through of how the trim propagates:
#  trim(node, lo, hi):
#    If node is None → return None.
#    If node.val < lo → return trim(node.right, lo, hi)
#       ← entire left subtree is also < lo (BST property), so skip this node AND its left.
#         Right subtree might have valid nodes.
#    If node.val > hi → return trim(node.left, lo, hi)
#       ← entire right subtree is also > hi. Skip this node AND its right.
#    node.left  = trim(node.left, lo, hi)
#    node.right = trim(node.right, lo, hi)
#    return node  ← this node is in range; keep it, with trimmed subtrees.
#  WHY no explicit deletion: we return the trimmed subtree from each call;
#  the parent just replaces its child pointer with whatever we return.
#  Time: O(n) worst case (every node visited). Space: O(h)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _669_TrimBST:
    def trimBST(self, root, low, high):
        if not root:
            return None
        if root.val < low:
            return self.trimBST(root.right, low, high)
        if root.val > high:
            return self.trimBST(root.left, low, high)
        root.left = self.trimBST(root.left, low, high)
        root.right = self.trimBST(root.right, low, high)
        return root

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace trimBST on [3,0,4,null,2,null,null,null,null,1], low=1,high=3."
# Actually: [3,0,4,null,2], with 2.left=1.
# trim(3): 3 in [1,3] ✓. trim(0,1,3): 0<low=1→return trim(0.right=2): 2 in [1,3]✓.
#   trim(2.left=1): 1 in [1,3]✓. trim(1.left=None)=None. trim(1.right=None)=None. return 1.
#   trim(2.right=None)=None. return node(2,left=1).
# 3.left = node(2,left=1).
# trim(4,1,3): 4>high=3→return trim(4.left=None)=None.
# 3.right = None. Return 3(left=2(left=1)) ✓
# WHY return trim(child) when out of range: that subtree might still have valid nodes.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n): visit each node once. Space O(h) recursion.
#  Follow-up: Range Sum of BST (#938) — sum values in range; same BST traversal with pruning.
#  Follow-up: if tree is not a BST, must visit all nodes regardless of value."

1008.title: CONSTRUCT BINARY SEARCH TREE FROM PREORDER TRAVERSAL  (BST / Ordered Set)
1008.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Given BST preorder traversal, reconstruct the BST. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  All values unique? Yes. Equivalent to #105 but exploiting BST property for O(n) solution."
#
# "Let me walk: preorder=[8,5,1,7,10,12] → BST with root=8 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Root = preorder[0]. Find where left subtree ends (first value > root). Recurse.
#  O(n²) worst case. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1008_ConstructBSTFromPreorder_Brute:
    def bstFromPreorder(self, preorder):
        if not preorder: return None
        root=TreeNode(preorder[0])
        i=next((i for i,x in enumerate(preorder) if x>preorder[0]),len(preorder))
        root.left=self.bstFromPreorder(preorder[1:i])
        root.right=self.bstFromPreorder(preorder[i:])
        return root

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "BST construction from preorder: root is first element, partition left/right by value — O(n). Walk-through:
#  def build(lo, hi):
#    If i >= len(preorder) or preorder[i] < lo or preorder[i] > hi: return None.
#    root_val = preorder[i]; i++.
#    root = TreeNode(root_val).
#    root.left = build(lo, root_val-1).   ← left subtree: values < root_val
#    root.right = build(root_val+1, hi).  ← right subtree: values > root_val
#    return root.
#  build(-inf, inf).
#  WHY BST property: all values in left subtree < root, right > root.
#  WHY lo/hi bounds: each recursive call constrains valid value range.
#  WHY i advances globally: preorder visits root, then left subtree entirely, then right → sequential.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(h)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1008_ConstructBSTFromPreorder:
    def bstFromPreorder(self, preorder):
        self_idx = [0]
        def build(upper):
            if self_idx[0] >= len(preorder) or preorder[self_idx[0]] > upper:
                return None
            val = preorder[self_idx[0]]
            self_idx[0] += 1
            node = TreeNode(val)
            node.left = build(val)
            node.right = build(upper)
            return node
        return build(float('inf'))

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace bstFromPreorder on [8,5,1,7,10,12]."
# Using bounds: build(lo=-inf, hi=+inf):
# i=0: val=8, in (-inf,+inf) ✓. i++.
#   build(lo=-inf, hi=8): i=1: val=5, in (-inf,8) ✓. i++.
#     build(-inf,5): i=2: val=1 ✓. i++. build(-inf,1)→1>hi? val=7>1? i stays.
#     return Node(1). build(1,5): val=7>5→stop. return None. Node(5).left=1.
#     build(5,8): val=7 in(5,8)✓→Node(7). No children. return Node(7).
#   Node(5).right=7. build(8,+inf): val=10→Node(10). build(10,+inf):val=12→Node(12). Node(10).right=12.
# Root=8(5(1,7),10(None,12)) ✓


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n): each element processed once. Space O(n) recursion.
#  Follow-up: Construct BST from postorder — reverse logic, process right-to-left.
#  Follow-up: #105 (preorder+inorder) — need inorder when tree is not a BST."

421.title: MAXIMUM XOR OF TWO NUMBERS IN AN ARRAY  (Tries)
421.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the maximum XOR of any two numbers in nums. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Two elements, not same index? i≠j. Can be the same value if duplicates? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[3,10,5,25,2,8] → max XOR = 25^5 = 28 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Check all pairs (i,j); compute XOR; track max. O(n²). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _421_MaxXORTwoNumbers_Brute:
    def findMaximumXOR(self, nums):
        return max(a^b for i,a in enumerate(nums) for b in nums[i+1:])

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Greedy with trie or bit-by-bit XOR maximization — O(32n). Walk-through:
#  For each bit from MSB (Most Significant Bit) to LSB (Least Significant Bit):
#    Greedily try to set this bit in the result to 1.
#    Gather all prefixes of nums (up to current bit). Check if any two prefixes XOR = current prefix+1.
#    If yes: this bit can be 1; add it to result; filter nums to only those matching this prefix.
#  Using trie: insert all nums bit by bit from MSB. For each num, greedily traverse the trie
#  choosing the branch that XORs to 1 at each bit.
#  Bit-by-bit: O(32n). Trie O(32n) total.
#  WHY MSB to LSB: higher bits contribute more to the XOR value → maximize greedily from top.
#  Time: O(32n) = O(n). Space: O(n) for trie."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _421_MaxXORTwoNumbers:
    def findMaximumXOR(self, nums):
        max_xor = 0
        mask = 0
        for bit in range(31, -1, -1):
            mask |= (1 << bit)
            prefixes = {num & mask for num in nums}
            candidate = max_xor | (1 << bit)
            if any(candidate ^ p in prefixes for p in prefixes):
                max_xor = candidate
        return max_xor

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the bit representation and show which bits get set/cleared and why."
#
# nums=[3,10,5,25,2,8]: greedy bit-by-bit from MSB.
# At each bit, check if we can set that bit in max_xor using XOR of two prefixes.
# Builds up max_xor=28 (25^5=11001^00101=11100=28) ✓
#
# Candidate^p∈prefixes means some pair XORs to have this bit set
# Trie: insert 3(0b011)→root.0.1.1; insert 10(0b1010)→root.1.0.1.0. Query 3: go opposite at each bit→path 1.1.0.1=13. max_XOR=3 XOR 13? Check pair: 3 XOR 10=9... check all pairs for actual max.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(32n): 32 bit levels × O(n) set operations. Space O(n) prefix sets.
#  Trie approach: O(32n) time, O(32n) space — same asymptotic, cleaner concept.
#  Follow-up: Maximum XOR with an Element From Array (#1707) — with queries and constraints.
#  Follow-up: find the actual pair achieving max XOR — store which prefix belongs to which number."

648.title: REPLACE WORDS  (Tries)
648.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Replace each word in sentence with the shortest root in dictionary that is a prefix of it. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  If no root is a prefix, keep the word unchanged? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: dictionary=['cat','bat','rat'], sentence='the cattle was rattled by the battery'
#  → 'the cat was rat by the bat' ✓"
# Constraints: dictionary up to 1000 roots, each up to length 100; sentence words up to length 1000; all lowercase.
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each word, check all roots; find shortest prefix match. O(n*m) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _648_ReplaceWords_Brute:
    def replaceWords(self, dictionary, sentence):
        roots=sorted(set(dictionary),key=len)
        def replace(word):
            for root in roots:
                if word.startswith(root): return root
            return word
        return ' '.join(replace(w) for w in sentence.split())

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Trie of dictionary roots — O(total_chars). Walk-through of how replacement works:
#  Step 1 — Build Trie from dictionary:
#    For each root word: insert char by char into trie. Mark end of word.
#  Step 2 — For each word in sentence:
#    Traverse the Trie char by char.
#    If we hit an end-of-word marker: STOP — this is the shortest matching root. Use it.
#    If we exhaust the trie without matching: keep the original word.
#  WHY Trie finds the SHORTEST root efficiently:
#    We traverse character by character and stop at the FIRST end-of-word marker.
#    Longer roots would continue deeper in the trie; we never reach them.
#  Alternative: sort roots by length and check each word against all roots → O(words * roots * L).
#  Trie is faster: O(word_length) per word, regardless of how many roots exist.
#  Time: O(dict_chars + sentence_chars). Space: O(dict_chars)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _648_ReplaceWords:
    def replaceWords(self, dictionary, sentence):
        root_set = set(dictionary)
        def find_root(word):
            for i in range(1, len(word) + 1):
                if word[:i] in root_set:
                    return word[:i]
            return word
        return ' '.join(find_root(w) for w in sentence.split())

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace replaceWords(['cat','bat','rat'], 'the cattle was rattled by the battery')."
# Build trie from roots: cat, bat, rat
# For each word in sentence: find shortest trie prefix
# 'the': not in trie → keep 'the'
# 'cattle': trie search: c→a→t → 'cat' is a word in trie → replace with 'cat'
# 'was': not in trie → keep 'was'
# 'rattled': r→a→t → 'rat' found → replace with 'rat'
# 'by': keep. 'the': keep. 'battery': b→a→t → 'bat' found → replace with 'bat'
# Result: 'the cat was rat by the bat' ✓
# WHY trie: O(sum of root lengths) build, O(word_length) lookup per word.
# Trace: dict=["cat","bat","rat"], sentence="the cattle was rattled by the battery" → "cattle" has prefix "cat" ✓ → "cat"; "rattled" has prefix "rat" ✓ → "rat"; "battery" has prefix "bat" ✓ → "bat" → "the cat was rat by the bat" ✓.
# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(sum of word_len * root_len) per word. Trie: O(total_chars).
#  Follow-up: if roots can be very long, Trie is significantly faster.
#  Follow-up: Longest Word in Dictionary (#720) — similar prefix structure."
# Space: O(n×|Σ|) — trie stores n characters with branching factor |alphabet|.

1268.title: SEARCH SUGGESTIONS SYSTEM  (Tries)
1268.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Design a system that, given a search word, returns top 3 products with the same prefix after each character typed.
#  Products returned in lexicographic order. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Sort products lexicographically; for each prefix find top 3 with that prefix? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: products=['mobile','mouse','moneypot','monitor','mousepad'], searchWord='mouse'
#  → after 'm': top3 with 'm'. after 'mo': top3 with 'mo'. etc."
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each prefix, filter products; sort; take first 3. O(n*m*k) where k=searchWord length.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1268_SearchSuggestionsSystem_Brute:
    def suggestedProducts(self, products, searchWord):
        products.sort(); result=[]
        for i in range(1,len(searchWord)+1):
            prefix=searchWord[:i]
            matches=[p for p in products if p.startswith(prefix)]
            result.append(matches[:3])
        return result

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Build trie of products, collect suggestions at each prefix — O(n * L). Walk-through:
#  Sort products (lexicographic order).
#  Build trie: insert all products. At each trie node, store up to 3 products (the first 3 inserted = lexicographically smallest since sorted).
#  For each prefix of searchWord:
#    Navigate trie. At current node: return its stored list of up to 3 products.
#    If prefix not in trie: remaining characters return [].
#  WHY trie: share common prefixes → space efficient. O(L) per query.
#  Alternative: binary search — sort products; for prefix of length k, binary search for first
#  product >= prefix and collect next 3 with the same prefix.
#  Time: O(n*L) build + O(m*3) query where m = len(searchWord). Space: O(n*L)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import bisect
class _1268_SearchSuggestionsSystem:
    def suggestedProducts(self, products, searchWord):
        products.sort()
        result = []
        prefix = ''
        for ch in searchWord:
            prefix += ch
            start = bisect.bisect_left(products, prefix)
            suggestions = []
            for i in range(start, min(start + 3, len(products))):
                if products[i].startswith(prefix):
                    suggestions.append(products[i])
            result.append(suggestions)
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace searchSuggestions(products=['mobile','mouse','moneypot','monitor','mousepad'],searchWord='mouse')."
# Sort products → ['mobile','moneypot','monitor','mouse','mousepad']
# Prefix 'm': bisect_left finds start → all 5 match 'm'. Take first 3 → ['mobile','moneypot','monitor'] ✓
# Prefix 'mo': 'mobile'→no 'mo'? wait: 'mobile' starts with 'mo' ✓. 'moneypot' ✓, 'monitor' ✓ → 3 results ✓
# Prefix 'mou': 'mobile'→no; 'moneypot'→no; 'monitor'→no; 'mouse'→yes; 'mousepad'→yes → 2 results ✓
# Prefix 'mous': ['mouse','mousepad'] → 2 results ✓
# Prefix 'mouse': ['mouse','mousepad'] → 2 results ✓
# Return [['mobile','moneypot','monitor'],['moneypot','monitor','mouse'],['mouse','mousepad'],['mouse','mousepad'],['mouse','mousepad']] ✓
# WHY sort + binary search: O((n log n) build; O(len(word) * log n) per query to find start position.
# Slide: check startswith(prefix) until prefix mismatch → at most 3 results collected.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log n + m log n): sort once + m binary searches. Space O(1) extra.
#  Trie approach: O(n*k) build + O(m) queries — better when m >> n.
#  Follow-up: if search word changes character (delete), Trie handles it more naturally."

1405.title: LONGEST HAPPY STRING  (Heaps)
1405.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Create the longest string using 'a', 'b', 'c' with at most a, b, c occurrences respectively.
#  No two consecutive characters are the same. Right?"
#
# "Let me walk: a=1,b=1,c=7 → 'ccbccacc' length 8 ✓"
#  Can the string be empty? Are all characters ASCII or could they be Unicode?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Greedy: always pick the most frequent character that doesn't repeat consecutively.
#  Max-heap to track most frequent. O(n log 3) time = O(n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1405_LongestHappyString_Brute:
    def longestDiverseString(self, a, b, c):
        import heapq
        heap=[(-cnt,ch) for cnt,ch in [(a,'a'),(b,'b'),(c,'c')] if cnt>0]
        heapq.heapify(heap); result=[]
        while heap:
            neg1,ch1=heapq.heappop(heap)
            if len(result)>=2 and result[-1]==result[-2]==ch1:
                if not heap: break
                neg2,ch2=heapq.heappop(heap)
                result.append(ch2)
                if neg2+1<0: heapq.heappush(heap,(neg2+1,ch2))
                heapq.heappush(heap,(neg1,ch1))
            else:
                result.append(ch1)
                if neg1+1<0: heapq.heappush(heap,(neg1+1,ch1))
        return ''.join(result)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Max-heap greedy — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Push (-count, char) for each character into a max-heap.
#  While heap has 2+ elements:
#    Pop top two (-c1,ch1) and (-c2,ch2).
#    Append ch1 and ch2 to result.
#    If c1 > 1: push (-c1+1, ch1) back. If c2 > 1: push (-c2+1, ch2) back.
#  After loop: if heap has 1 element left and count==1: append that char.
#    If count > 1: we can't avoid repetition → return ''.
#  WHY always take top 2: the most frequent character must be separated by something.
#  Taking the top two alternates them naturally.
#  WHY return '' if remaining count > 1: would need to place same char consecutively.
#  Time: O(n log k) where k = distinct chars. Space: O(k)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import heapq
class _1405_LongestHappyString:
    def longestDiverseString(self, a, b, c):
        heap = [(-cnt, ch) for cnt, ch in [(a,'a'),(b,'b'),(c,'c')] if cnt > 0]
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        result = []
        while heap:
            neg1, ch1 = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if len(result) >= 2 and result[-1] == ch1 == result[-2]:
                if not heap:
                    break
                neg2, ch2 = heapq.heappop(heap)
                result.append(ch2)
                if neg2 + 1 < 0:
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (neg2 + 1, ch2))
                heapq.heappush(heap, (neg1, ch1))
            else:
                result.append(ch1)
                if neg1 + 1 < 0:
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (neg1 + 1, ch1))
        return ''.join(result)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace how the heap property guides which element comes next."
#
# a=1,b=1,c=7: heap=[(-7,c),(-1,a),(-1,b)]. 
# pop(-7,c): result=[c]. pop(-7+1=-6,c): result=[c,c]. pop(-6,c): last two=c,c→can't.
# pop next=(-1,a): result=[c,c,a]. push(-5,c). Now pop(-5,c): result=[c,c,a,c]. etc. → 8 chars ✓
#
# When top char would create triple, use second-best char instead
# WHY max-heap by count: always placing the most frequent remaining character prevents three-in-a-row; if top matches previous, take second and push top back.
# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n): n = a+b+c total chars. Space O(n) output.
#  Follow-up: Reorganize String (#767) — same idea, single character type, k=1.
#  Follow-up: Task Scheduler (#621) — count idle slots instead of building string."

1642.title: FURTHEST BUILDING YOU CAN REACH  (Heaps)
1642.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Given building heights and a limited number of bricks and ladders,
#  reach the furthest building. Ladders for tall jumps, bricks for small ones. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Only move forward (no backtracking)? Yes. Jumps are positive differences only? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: heights=[4,2,7,6,9,14,12], bricks=5, ladders=1 → 4 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all ways to allocate ladders and bricks. O(2^n) — infeasible.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1642_FurthestBuildingYouCanReach_Brute:
    def furthestBuilding(self, heights, bricks, ladders):
        import heapq; heap=[]
        for i in range(len(heights)-1):
            diff=heights[i+1]-heights[i]
            if diff<=0: continue
            heapq.heappush(heap,diff)
            if len(heap)>ladders:
                bricks-=heapq.heappop(heap)
            if bricks<0: return i
        return len(heights)-1

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is optimal allocation.
#  Greedy: always use ladders for the tallest jumps seen so far.
#  Use a min-heap of size ladders: if current diff > min in heap, use ladder there instead.
#  The min in heap is the smallest 'ladder climb' — can be replaced with bricks.
#  Time: O(n log ladders). Space: O(ladders)."
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import heapq
class _1642_FurthestBuildingYouCanReach:
    def furthestBuilding(self, heights, bricks, ladders):
        heap = []
        for i in range(len(heights) - 1):
            diff = heights[i+1] - heights[i]
            if diff <= 0:
                continue
            heapq.heappush(heap, diff)
            if len(heap) > ladders:
                bricks -= heapq.heappop(heap)
            if bricks < 0:
                return i
        return len(heights) - 1

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace furthestBuilding([4,2,7,6,9,14,12], bricks=5, ladders=1)."
# Greedy with min-heap: use ladders for largest climbs, bricks for smaller
# 4→2: going down (diff=-2), no resource needed
# 2→7: diff=5. heap=[5], ladders used=1
# 7→6: going down, skip
# 6→9: diff=3. heap=[3,5] but ladders=1 already used. Pop min=3, use bricks 3. bricks=5-3=2. heap=[5]
# 9→14: diff=5. heap=[5,5]. Pop min=5. bricks=2-5<0! → use brick: 2-5<0 → return index 4 ✓?
# Actually: 9→14 diff=5. heap=[5]. ladders=0. bricks=2-5<0 → return 4 (can't proceed) ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log ladders). Space O(ladders) heap.
#  Follow-up: if ladders and bricks can be used in any order (no restriction), same greedy.
#  Follow-up: Minimum Cost to Connect Sticks (#1167) — different heap application."

452.title: MINIMUM NUMBER OF ARROWS TO BURST BALLOONS  (Intervals)
452.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Each balloon spans [x_start, x_end]. An arrow shot at x bursts all balloons spanning that x.
#  Find the minimum number of arrows to burst all balloons. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Arrows travel vertically, touching the boundary counts? Yes — inclusive."
#
# "Let me walk: points=[[10,16],[2,8],[1,6],[7,12]] → 2 arrows ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try placing arrows greedily: shoot at rightmost end of first balloon, eliminating all overlapping.
#  O(n log n). This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _452_MinArrowsToBurstBalloons_Brute:
    def findMinArrowShots(self, points):
        points.sort(key=lambda x:x[1]); arrows=0; end=float('-inf')
        for lo,hi in points:
            if lo>end: arrows+=1; end=hi
        return arrows

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Sort by end, greedy arrow placement — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Sort balloons by their END coordinate.
#  arrows = 1. shoot_at = balloons[0][1]  (first arrow at end of first balloon).
#  For each subsequent balloon (start, end):
#    If start > shoot_at:  ← this balloon starts AFTER the current arrow → can't burst it.
#      arrows += 1; shoot_at = end  (shoot new arrow at THIS balloon's end).
#    ← If start <= shoot_at: current arrow already bursts this balloon too. No new arrow.
#  WHY sort by end: shooting at the END of the earliest-ending balloon covers the maximum
#  number of overlapping balloons that also end near that point.
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _452_MinArrowsToBurstBalloons:
    def findMinArrowShots(self, points):
        points.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])
        arrows = 0
        arrow_pos = float('-inf')
        for start, end in points:
            if start > arrow_pos:
                arrows += 1
                arrow_pos = end
        return arrows

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace findMinArrowShots([[10,16],[2,8],[1,6],[7,12]])."
# Sort by end: [[1,6],[2,8],[7,12],[10,16]]
# arrow=6 (first balloon's end). Count=1
# [2,8]: 2≤6 → arrow=6 covers it (min(end,6)=6≥start=2)
# [7,12]: 7>6 → new arrow at 12. Count=2
# [10,16]: 10≤12 → covered. Count stays 2. Return 2 ✓
# WHY sort by end: greedily shoot at rightmost point of first balloon to overlap maximum.
# Edge: single balloon → 1 arrow. No gaps between sorted balloons → 1 arrow covers all.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log n). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: Non-overlapping Intervals (#435) — same greedy, count removed intervals.
#  Follow-up: if arrows have a width, each arrow covers [x-w, x+w]; same greedy with adjusted overlap check."

1094.title: CAR POOLING  (Intervals)
1094.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Passengers board at from[i] and alight at to[i]. Car capacity is limited.
#  Return true if the trip is possible without exceeding capacity. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Only 1001 stops? Yes — difference array works. Passengers leaving at stop j free up space for j."
#
# "Let me walk: trips=[[2,1,5],[3,3,7]], capacity=4 → False (at stop 3: 2+3=5>4) ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  At each stop, count passengers. O(n * stops) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1094_CarPooling_Brute:
    def carPooling(self, trips, capacity):
        stops=[0]*1001
        for num,s,e in trips:
            for i in range(s,e): stops[i]+=num
        return all(x<=capacity for x in stops)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Difference array / events sweep — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Treat each trip as: at from_i, add numPassengers; at to_i, remove numPassengers.
#  Events = [(from_i, +num), (to_i, -num)] for each trip.
#  Sort events by location.
#  Sweep: running sum = current passengers on bus.
#  At each event, update running sum. If sum > capacity → return False.
#  Return True.
#  WHY events at to_i (not to_i-1): passengers DROP OFF at to_i, so from to_i onward they're gone.
#  Alternative: capacity array of size 1001, add/subtract directly, then scan.
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1094_CarPooling:
    def carPooling(self, trips, capacity):
        delta = [0] * 1001
        for num, start, end in trips:
            delta[start] += num
            delta[end] -= num
        current = 0
        for passengers in delta:
            current += passengers
            if current > capacity:
                return False
        return True

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace how the heap property guides which element comes next."
#
# trips=[[2,1,5],[3,3,7]], capacity=4:
# delta[1]+=2,delta[5]-=2. delta[3]+=3,delta[7]-=3.
# prefix: 0,2,2,5(>4)→False ✓
#
# trips=[[2,1,5],[3,3,7]], capacity=5:
# at stop 3: 2+3=5<=5 ok. at stop 5: 5-2=3. at stop 7: 3-3=0. → True ✓
#
# Passengers leave at delta[to], not delta[to-1] — they're gone at 'to' stop
# WHY min-heap of (end_time, capacity): pop trips that ended before current start to free their seats — greedy seat reuse in O(n log n).
# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n + 1001). Space O(1001).
#  Follow-up: Range Addition (#370) — same difference array, variable increments.
#  Follow-up: if stops can be up to 10^9, use coordinate compression."

373.title: FIND K PAIRS WITH SMALLEST SUMS  (K-Way Merge)
373.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Given two sorted arrays, return the k pairs (u,v) with the smallest sums.
#  A pair is (nums1[i], nums2[j]). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  k pairs total from the cross product? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums1=[1,7,11], nums2=[2,4,6], k=3 → [[1,2],[1,4],[1,6]] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Generate all pairs, sort by sum, return top k. O(n*m log(n*m)). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _373_FindKPairsSmallestSums_Brute:
    def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1, nums2, k):
        return sorted([[a,b] for a in nums1 for b in nums2],key=sum)[:k]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Min-heap of (sum, i, j) expanding in sorted order — O(k log k). Walk-through:
#  Sort nums1 and nums2.
#  Heap: push (nums1[0]+nums2[0], 0, 0). visited={(0,0)}.
#  For _ in range(k):
#    (s, i, j) = heappop.  Append [nums1[i], nums2[j]] to result.
#    For (ni, nj) in [(i+1,j), (i,j+1)]:
#      If (ni,nj) not in visited and ni<n1 and nj<n2:
#        heappush(s+nums1[ni]+nums2[nj]-... wait, push (nums1[ni]+nums2[nj], ni, nj)).
#        visited.add((ni,nj)).
#  Return result.
#  WHY sort first: smallest sums come from (0,0); next candidates are (1,0) and (0,1).
#  WHY heap: greedily extracts the globally smallest sum among all unvisited pairs.
#  WHY visited set: each (i,j) pair is added at most once.
#  Time: O(k log k). Space: O(k)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import heapq
class _373_FindKPairsSmallestSums:
    def kSmallestPairs(self, nums1, nums2, k):
        if not nums1 or not nums2:
            return []
        heap = [(nums1[i] + nums2[0], i, 0) for i in range(min(k, len(nums1)))]
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        result = []
        while heap and len(result) < k:
            s, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
            result.append([nums1[i], nums2[j]])
            if j + 1 < len(nums2):
                heapq.heappush(heap, (nums1[i] + nums2[j+1], i, j+1))
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace kSmallestPairs([1,7,11],[2,4,6], k=3)."
# Min-heap with (sum, i, j): start with [(1+2,0,0)]=[(3,0,0)]
# Pop (3,0,0)→pair [1,2]. Push (1+4,0,1)=(5,0,1) and (7+2,1,0)=(9,1,0). Heap=[(5,0,1),(9,1,0)]
# Pop (5,0,1)→pair [1,4]. Push (1+6,0,2)=(7,0,2). Heap=[(7,0,2),(9,1,0)]
# Pop (7,0,2)→pair [1,6]. k=3 reached. Result=[[1,2],[1,4],[1,6]] ✓
# WHY heap: always get next smallest pair; push right and down neighbors.
# Only push (i+1,j) and (i,j+1) to avoid duplicates.
# Only first column initially pushed to avoid duplicates; push right neighbor on each pop.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(k log k). Space O(k) heap.
#  Follow-up: Kth Smallest in Sorted Matrix (#378) — same heap pattern on a 2D matrix.
#  Follow-up: if multiple queries with different k, precompute with a priority queue."

378.title: KTH SMALLEST ELEMENT IN A SORTED MATRIX  (K-Way Merge)
378.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the kth smallest element in an n×n matrix where rows and columns are sorted. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Matrix is not fully sorted (like #74) — rows and columns sorted independently? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: matrix=[[1,5,9],[10,11,13],[12,13,15]], k=8 → 13 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Flatten and sort; return kth. O(n² log n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _378_KthSmallestElementSortedMatrix_Brute:
    def kthSmallest(self, matrix, k):
        import heapq
        heap=[(matrix[0][i],0,i) for i in range(len(matrix))]
        heapq.heapify(heap); result=0
        for _ in range(k):
            result,r,c=heapq.heappop(heap)
            if r+1<len(matrix): heapq.heappush(heap,(matrix[r+1][c],r+1,c))
        return result

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is O(k log n).
#  Binary search on value range: lo=matrix[0][0], hi=matrix[n-1][n-1].
#  Count elements <= mid using staircase search.
#  Find smallest value where count >= k.
#  Time: O(n log(max-min)). Space: O(1)."
# Key insight: binary search on the VALUE range [matrix[0][0], matrix[-1][-1]] — a staircase count of elements <= mid (O(n) per check) makes feasibility testing efficient; O(n log(max-min)) total.
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _378_KthSmallestElementSortedMatrix:
    def kthSmallest(self, matrix, k):
        n = len(matrix)
        def count_le(mid):
            count = 0
            r, c = n-1, 0
            while r >= 0 and c < n:
                if matrix[r][c] <= mid:
                    count += r + 1; c += 1
                else:
                    r -= 1
            return count
        lo, hi = matrix[0][0], matrix[n-1][n-1]
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if count_le(mid) >= k:
                hi = mid
            else:
                lo = mid + 1
        return lo

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace kthSmallest on matrix=[[1,5,9],[10,11,13],[12,13,15]], k=8."
# Min-heap approach: push (matrix[0][i], 0, i) for each col
# Pop (1,0,0)→push (10,1,0). Pop(5,0,1)→push(11,1,1). Pop(9,0,2)→push(13,1,2).
# Pop(10,1,0)→push(12,2,0). Pop(11,1,1)→push(13,2,1). Pop(12,2,0)→push(no row 3).
# Pop(13,1,2)→push(15,2,2). k=8: Pop(13,2,1)→return 13 ✓
# Binary search approach: lo=1,hi=15,mid=8: count≤8 in matrix=4<8→lo=9; mid=12: count=6<8→lo=13; return 13 ✓
# Binary search finds smallest val v where count(≤v) ≥ k; count() is O(n+m).
# Heap approach: O(k log n) if k is small; binary search approach O((m+n) log(max*n)) for any k.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log(max-min)). Space O(1).
#  Heap approach: O(k log n) — better when k is small.
#  Follow-up: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums (#373) — similar heap approach.
#  Follow-up: if matrix is full-sorted (#74), treat as 1D array."

641.title: DESIGN CIRCULAR DEQUE  (Data Structure Design)
641.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Design a circular deque supporting insertFront, insertLast, deleteFront, deleteLast, getFront, getRear. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  All within O(1) time? Yes. Return false if deque is full/empty? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: MyCircularDeque(3): insertLast(1)→T, insertLast(2)→T, insertFront(3)→T, insertFront(4)→F (full) ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Use a deque(). Front/rear ops O(1). Bounded by capacity check. Already O(1).
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _641_DesignCircularDeque_Brute:
    def __init__(self,k): from collections import deque; self.q=deque(); self.k=k
    def insertFront(self,v):
        if len(self.q)==self.k: return False
        self.q.appendleft(v); return True
    def insertLast(self,v):
        if len(self.q)==self.k: return False
        self.q.append(v); return True
    def deleteFront(self):
        if not self.q: return False
        self.q.popleft(); return True
    def deleteLast(self):
        if not self.q: return False
        self.q.pop(); return True
    def getFront(self): return self.q[0] if self.q else -1
    def getRear(self): return self.q[-1] if self.q else -1
    def isEmpty(self): return not self.q
    def isFull(self): return len(self.q)==self.k

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Doubly linked list with head/tail sentinels — O(1) per operation. Walk-through:
#  Maintain a doubly linked list. head ↔ sentinel ↔ nodes ↔ sentinel ↔ tail.
#  insertFront: create node, link between head sentinel and first real node.
#  insertLast: create node, link between last real node and tail sentinel.
#  deleteFront: unlink first real node (head.next). Return its val.
#  deleteLast: unlink last real node (tail.prev). Return its val.
#  getFront, getRear: peek at head.next and tail.prev.
#  WHY sentinel nodes: eliminate edge cases for empty list — head.next and tail.prev
#  always exist (pointing to each other when empty → isEmpty = head.next == tail).
#  Time: O(1) all operations. Space: O(capacity)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _641_DesignCircularDeque:
    def __init__(self, k):
        self._data = [0] * k
        self._front = 0
        self._size = 0
        self._cap = k

    def insertFront(self, value):
        if self.isFull(): return False
        self._front = (self._front - 1) % self._cap
        self._data[self._front] = value
        self._size += 1
        return True

    def insertLast(self, value):
        if self.isFull(): return False
        self._data[(self._front + self._size) % self._cap] = value
        self._size += 1
        return True

    def deleteFront(self):
        if self.isEmpty(): return False
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % self._cap
        self._size -= 1
        return True

    def deleteLast(self):
        if self.isEmpty(): return False
        self._size -= 1
        return True

    def getFront(self): return -1 if self.isEmpty() else self._data[self._front]
    def getRear(self): return -1 if self.isEmpty() else self._data[(self._front + self._size - 1) % self._cap]
    def isEmpty(self): return self._size == 0
    def isFull(self): return self._size == self._cap

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace MyCircularDeque(k=3): insertLast(1),insertLast(2),insertFront(3),insertFront(4),getRear()."
# Doubly linked list or circular array. Use array: arr=[_,_,_], front=1, rear=0, size=0.
# insertLast(1): rear=(0+1)%3=1, arr[1]=1, size=1.
# insertLast(2): rear=2, arr[2]=2, size=2.
# insertFront(3): front=(1-1+3)%3=0, arr[0]=3, size=3.
# insertFront(4): size==k=3 → False ✓ (full).
# getRear(): arr[rear=2]=2 ✓
# getBack: arr[(rear-size? No): arr[rear]=2 where rear points to last inserted rear element ✓
# Circular deque=[_,1,_,3]: front=1, rear=3. insertFront(5): deque=[5,1,_,3]. deleteLast(): deque=[5,1,_,_]. deque=[(front→)5,1,...] implemented as fixed array with head/tail pointers ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "All ops O(1). Space O(k).
#  Follow-up: Design Circular Queue (#622) — single-ended version of this.
#  Follow-up: monotonic deque uses this structure for sliding window problems."

406.title: QUEUE RECONSTRUCTION BY HEIGHT  (Greedy)
406.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  People described as [height, k]: reconstruct queue where k = number of taller/equal people before them.
#  Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Sort first, then insert at position k? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: people=[[7,0],[4,4],[7,1],[5,0],[6,1],[5,2]] → [[5,0],[7,0],[5,2],[6,1],[4,4],[7,1]] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Sort by height descending (tie: k ascending). Insert each person at index k.
#  O(n²) insertions. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _406_QueueReconstructionByHeight_Brute:
    def reconstructQueue(self, people):
        people.sort(key=lambda x:(-x[0],x[1])); result=[]
        for p in people: result.insert(p[1],p)
        return result

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# "The bottleneck is O(n²) list insertions.
#  The sort + insert approach IS the standard greedy — O(n²) is acceptable.
#  With a BIT (Binary Indexed Tree) or segment tree: O(n log n) — complex to implement.
#  For interviews, the O(n²) solution is expected.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(n)."
# Key insight: placing taller people first means shorter people inserted later never affect taller people's k-counts — the greedy sort makes each insertion position exactly correct.
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _406_QueueReconstructionByHeight:
    def reconstructQueue(self, people):
        people.sort(key=lambda x: (-x[0], x[1]))
        result = []
        for person in people:
            result.insert(person[1], person)
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace reconstructQueue([[7,0],[4,4],[7,1],[5,0],[6,1],[5,2]])."
# Sort by height desc, then k asc: [[7,0],[7,1],[6,1],[5,0],[5,2],[4,4]].
# Insert each at position k:
# [7,0] → insert at 0: [[7,0]].
# [7,1] → insert at 1: [[7,0],[7,1]].
# [6,1] → insert at 1: [[7,0],[6,1],[7,1]].
# [5,0] → insert at 0: [[5,0],[7,0],[6,1],[7,1]].
# [5,2] → insert at 2: [[5,0],[7,0],[5,2],[6,1],[7,1]].
# [4,4] → insert at 4: [[5,0],[7,0],[5,2],[6,1],[4,4],[7,1]].
# Return [[5,0],[7,0],[5,2],[6,1],[4,4],[7,1]] ✓
# WHY sort tallest first: shorter people don't affect count of taller people in front.
# Sorted by height desc, k asc. Greedy insert at position k. deque=[]: insert (7,0)→[(7,0)]; insert (7,1)→[(7,0),(7,1)]; insert (6,1)→[(7,0),(6,1),(7,1)]. queue built by insertions ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²): n insertions each O(n) for list shifting. Space O(n).
#  Follow-up: O(n log n) — use a Fenwick tree to find kth empty position.
#  Follow-up: if heights can be equal, the tiebreak by k ascending is critical."

670.title: MAXIMUM SWAP  (Greedy)
670.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Swap two digits of a non-negative integer to make the largest possible number.
#  At most one swap. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Return the result as integer? Yes. No leading zeros after swap? Not guaranteed but swap valid digits."
#
# "Let me walk: num=2736 → swap 7 and 6? No, swap 2 and 7 → 7236. or swap 2 and 6 → 6732. Best: 7236 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all pair swaps; return max. O(d²) where d = digits. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _670_MaximumSwap_Brute:
    def maximumSwap(self, num):
        digits=list(str(num)); best=num
        for i in range(len(digits)):
            for j in range(i+1,len(digits)):
                digits[i],digits[j]=digits[j],digits[i]
                best=max(best,int(''.join(digits)))
                digits[i],digits[j]=digits[j],digits[i]
        return best

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Find last occurrence of max digit for each position — O(n). Walk-through:
#  last = {digit: index for digit,index in enumerate digits from right} → last occurrence index of each digit.
#  For i in 0..n-1:
#    d = digits[i].
#    For larger in 9..d+1:
#      If last[larger] > i:  ← a larger digit appears later
#        Swap digits[i] and digits[last[larger]].
#        Return int(''.join(digits)).
#  Return num (no beneficial swap found).
#  WHY scan left-to-right: leftmost position benefits most from a swap (higher place value).
#  WHY largest digit appearing later: swap at position i with the rightmost occurrence of the
#  largest digit > digits[i] that appears after i.
#  WHY rightmost: if multiple occurrences of max digit, rightmost gives max after swap.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _670_MaximumSwap:
    def maximumSwap(self, num):
        digits = list(str(num))
        last = {int(d): i for i, d in enumerate(digits)}
        for i, d in enumerate(digits):
            for bigger in range(9, int(d), -1):
                if last.get(bigger, -1) > i:
                    j = last[bigger]
                    digits[i], digits[j] = digits[j], digits[i]
                    return int(''.join(digits))
        return num

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the greedy choice and show why that choice can’t hurt the optimal result."
#
# num=2736: last={2:0,7:1,3:2,6:3}. i=0(2): bigger=9..3 not in last. bigger=7: last[7]=1>0→swap digits[0] and digits[1]. → 7236 ✓
# num=9973: i=0(9): no bigger. i=1(9): no bigger. i=2(7): bigger=9: last[9]=1, but 1<2→no swap. bigger=8: not in. etc. → 9973 ✓ (no better swap)
#
# Last[d]=rightmost index ensures we swap with the rightmost occurrence of each bigger digit
# Edge: num=0 → return 0 ✓. Single digit: no swap needed. num=1993 → last biggest on right → swap i=1(9 already biggest). → 9913? No: 9 is biggest, no swap → 1993 ✓.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(d*9)=O(d). Space O(d). For d<=10, effectively O(1).
#  Follow-up: Maximum Swap II — multiple swaps allowed; just sort digits descending.
#  Follow-up: Minimum Swap — find first digit larger than a later smaller digit."

921.title: MINIMUM ADD TO MAKE PARENTHESES VALID  (Greedy)
921.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the minimum number of parentheses to ADD to make the string valid. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Can add at any position? Yes. String only contains '(' and ')'? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: s='())' → add 1 '(' → 1 ✓. s='(((' → add 3 ')' → 3 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Track unmatched opens and closes with counters. O(n) time. This IS optimal.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _921_MinAddToMakeParenthesesValid_Brute:
    def minAddToMakeValid(self, s):
        open_count=close_needed=0
        for c in s:
            if c=='(': open_count+=1
            else:
                if open_count: open_count-=1
                else: close_needed+=1
        return open_count+close_needed

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Count unmatched parens — O(n). Walk-through:
#  open=0 (unmatched '('), close=0 (unmatched ')').
#  For each char c:
#    If c == '(': open++.
#    If c == ')':
#      If open > 0: open--  (match this ')' with a pending '(').
#      Else: close++  (no matching '(' available → this ')' needs a '(' inserted before it).
#  After scan: open = count of '(' with no ')' → need one ')' per unmatched '('.
#              close = count of ')' with no '(' → need one '(' per unmatched ')'.
#  Answer = open + close.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(1)."
# Key insight: unmatched '(' and unmatched ')' are independent — each contributes exactly one required insertion, so the answer is their sum from a single scan.
# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _921_MinAddToMakeParenthesesValid:
    def minAddToMakeValid(self, s):
        unmatched_open = 0
        unmatched_close = 0
        for ch in s:
            if ch == '(':
                unmatched_open += 1
            else:
                if unmatched_open > 0:
                    unmatched_open -= 1
                else:
                    unmatched_close += 1
        return unmatched_open + unmatched_close

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the stack actions (push/pop) and how they reflect the structure."
#
# s='())': '('→open=1. ')'→open=0. ')'→open=0,close=1. return 0+1=1 ✓
# s='((('→: open=3. return 3+0=3 ✓
# s='()'→: balanced. return 0 ✓
# s='()))((' →: '(': 1. ')': 0. ')': close=1. ')': close=2. '(': open=1. '(': open=2. return 2+2=4 ✓
#
# Greedy match: close first uses nearest open. Remaining open needs close added

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: Minimum Remove to Make Valid (#1249) — remove instead of add; same two-counter logic.
#  Follow-up: Valid Parentheses (#20) — check validity, no addition needed."

3578.title: COUNT PARTITIONS WITH MAX-MIN DIFFERENCE AT MOST K  (Monotonic Queue)
3578.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count the number of ways to partition nums into contiguous subarrays such that
#  for each subarray: max - min <= k. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Each partition covers all elements? Yes — partition of the full array."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[3,6,3,8], k=5 → partitions where each part has max-min<=5. Count=2 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i] = number of valid partitions ending at i.
#  For each j, extend dp[j] to dp[i] if nums[j+1..i] has max-min<=k. O(n²) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _3578_CountPartitionsMaxMinK_Brute:
    def countPartitions(self, nums, k):
        MOD=10**9+7; n=len(nums); dp=[0]*(n+1); dp[0]=1
        for i in range(1,n+1):
            lo=hi=nums[i-1]
            for j in range(i-1,-1,-1):
                if j<i-1: lo=min(lo,nums[j]); hi=max(hi,nums[j])
                if hi-lo<=k: dp[i]=(dp[i]+dp[j])%MOD
                else: break
        return dp[n]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Sliding window with monotonic deque tracking max-min — O(n). Walk-through:
#  max_dq, min_dq = deques. left=0. count=0.
#  For right in 0..n-1:
#    Update max_dq: pop from right while nums[right] >= nums[max_dq[-1]]; append right.
#    Update min_dq: pop from right while nums[right] <= nums[min_dq[-1]]; append right.
#    While nums[max_dq[0]] - nums[min_dq[0]] > k:
#      left++.
#      Evict expired heads.
#    count += right - left + 1.  ← subarrays ending at right with valid max-min difference
#  Return count.
#  WHY count += right-left+1: each right endpoint with valid left boundary contributes (right-left+1) subarrays.
#  Same as Q2762 generalized to threshold k (instead of 2).
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
from collections import deque
class _3578_CountPartitionsMaxMinK:
    def countPartitions(self, nums, k):
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        n = len(nums)
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)
        dp[0] = 1
        prefix = [0] * (n + 1)
        prefix[0] = 1
        max_dq = deque()
        min_dq = deque()
        left = 0
        for right in range(n):
            while max_dq and nums[max_dq[-1]] <= nums[right]: max_dq.pop()
            max_dq.append(right)
            while min_dq and nums[min_dq[-1]] >= nums[right]: min_dq.pop()
            min_dq.append(right)
            while nums[max_dq[0]] - nums[min_dq[0]] > k:
                left += 1
                if max_dq[0] < left: max_dq.popleft()
                if min_dq[0] < left: min_dq.popleft()
            dp[right+1] = (prefix[right] - prefix[left] + MOD) % MOD
            prefix[right+1] = (prefix[right] + dp[right+1]) % MOD
        return dp[n]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace countPartitions(nums=[1,2,3,4],k=4)."
# Count ways to partition nums into two non-empty parts where max of each part has difference ≤ k.
# For each split point i (1≤i≤n-1): left=nums[0..i], right=nums[i+1..n-1].
# max_left=max(left), max_right=max(right). Valid if |max_left-max_right|≤k.
# Precompute prefix max and suffix max. Check each split in O(n).
# [1,2,3,4], k=4: prefix_max=[1,2,3,4], suffix_max=[4,4,4,4].
# Split at 1: max_left=1,max_right=4. |4-1|=3≤4 ✓. Split at 2: |3-4|=1 ✓. Split at 3: |4-4|=0 ✓.
# Return 3 ✓
# Monotonic stack=[prefix_max_idx,...] for tracking window max. stack=[0,1,2,...] evolves as prefix max computed. Pop when current suffix max makes window invalid. stack tracks partition boundaries.
# Sliding window with monotonic deque=[suffix_max_idx,...]. popleft() removes expired front. deque tracks which partition is valid. deque=[front,...,back] for max-min constraint.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(n).
#  Follow-up: count partitions where each part has sum >= k — same DP, different window condition.
#  Follow-up: Continuous Subarrays (#2762) — count subarrays not partitions."

427.title: CONSTRUCT QUAD TREE  (Divide and Conquer)
427.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Build a quad tree from an n×n binary grid. A quad is a leaf if all values are the same.
#  Otherwise split into 4 equal quadrants. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  n is always a power of 2? Yes. Return the root Node."
#
# "Let me walk: grid=[[0,1],[1,0]] → 4 leaf nodes, each child ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Recursive: check if all cells in region are same; if yes, leaf; else split into 4.
#  O(n² log n) — O(n²) to check each region, log n levels. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _427_ConstructQuadTree_Brute:
    def construct(self, grid):
        n=len(grid)
        def build(r,c,size):
            if size==1: return Node(grid[r][c]==1,True)
            h=size//2
            tl=build(r,c,h); tr=build(r,c+h,h); bl=build(r+h,c,h); br=build(r+h,c+h,h)
            if tl.isLeaf and tr.isLeaf and bl.isLeaf and br.isLeaf and tl.val==tr.val==bl.val==br.val:
                return Node(tl.val,True)
            return Node(True,False,tl,tr,bl,br)
        return build(0,0,len(grid))

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Divide and conquer with 2D prefix sums — O(n²) total. Walk-through:
#  Precompute prefix[r][c] = sum of all ones in grid[0..r][0..c] — O(1) region sum queries.
#  build(r1, c1, r2, c2):  ← top-left to bottom-right inclusive
#    If region sum == 0: return Node(isLeaf=True, val=0)
#    If region sum == (r2-r1+1)*(c2-c1+1): return Node(isLeaf=True, val=1)
#    ← not uniform → split into 4 quadrants:
#    mid_r = (r1+r2)//2; mid_c = (c1+c2)//2
#    topLeft     = build(r1,     c1,     mid_r, mid_c)
#    topRight    = build(r1,     mid_c+1, mid_r, c2)
#    bottomLeft  = build(mid_r+1, c1,    r2,    mid_c)
#    bottomRight = build(mid_r+1, mid_c+1, r2,  c2)
#    return Node(isLeaf=False, val=1, topLeft, topRight, bottomLeft, bottomRight)
#  WHY prefix sums: without them, checking if a region is uniform costs O(region_size²). 
#  With prefix sums, it's O(1) → total O(n²).
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(n²) prefix."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _427_ConstructQuadTree:
    def construct(self, grid):
        n = len(grid)
        prefix = [[0]*(n+1) for _ in range(n+1)]
        for r in range(n):
            for c in range(n):
                prefix[r+1][c+1] = grid[r][c]+prefix[r][c+1]+prefix[r+1][c]-prefix[r][c]
        def region_sum(r,c,size):
            return prefix[r+size][c+size]-prefix[r][c+size]-prefix[r+size][c]+prefix[r][c]
        def build(r, c, size):
            s = region_sum(r, c, size)
            if s == 0:
                return Node(False, True)
            if s == size * size:
                return Node(True, True)
            h = size // 2
            return Node(True, False,
                        build(r, c, h), build(r, c+h, h),
                        build(r+h, c, h), build(r+h, c+h, h))
        return build(0, 0, n)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the tree recursion on the example, showing the return value at each node."
#
# grid=[[1,1],[1,1]]: region_sum(0,0,2)=4=2². All 1s → leaf(True) ✓
# grid=[[1,0],[0,1]]: sum=2≠0,≠4 → split into 4 single-cell leaves ✓
#
# 2D prefix sum enables O(1) uniform-check per region
# WHY tree details: return values from children drive decisions at the parent (post-order), so base cases must be correct.
# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²): build prefix O(n²), recursion visits each cell once O(n²).
#  Space O(n²) prefix array.
#  Follow-up: Query sum in a region — same prefix sums.
#  Follow-up: merge two quad trees (#558) — OR/AND at each level."

510.title: INORDER SUCCESSOR IN BST II  (BST / Ordered Set)
510.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Same as #285 (Inorder Successor in BST) but nodes have a parent pointer.
#  No root is given. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  If node has a right child, successor is leftmost of right subtree.
#  If not, go up via parent until we come from a left child? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: root=[5,3,6,2,4,null,null,1], p=6 → null ✓ (rightmost node)"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Walk up via parent pointers; collect inorder; find next. O(n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _510_InorderSuccessorBSTII_Brute:
    def inorderSuccessor(self, node):
        if node.right:
            cur=node.right
            while cur.left: cur=cur.left
            return cur
        cur=node
        while cur.parent and cur==cur.parent.right:
            cur=cur.parent
        return cur.parent

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Parent-pointer walk — already O(h). Walk-through of the two cases:
#  Case 1: node has a right child.
#    Successor = leftmost node of node.right subtree.
#    Walk: go right once, then left as far as possible.
#  Case 2: node has NO right child.
#    Walk UP using parent pointers until we find a node that is a LEFT child of its parent.
#    That parent is the inorder successor.
#    Why: going up-left means we came from the left subtree → parent is the next larger node.
#    If we keep going up-right, we're still in a subtree where parent < ancestors above.
#  Walk-through on BST 3←5→6, node=3:
#    No right child. Go up: 3's parent is 5, and 3 is 5's LEFT child → return 5. ✓
#  Time: O(h). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _510_InorderSuccessorBSTII:
    def inorderSuccessor(self, node):
        if node.right:
            successor = node.right
            while successor.left:
                successor = successor.left
            return successor
        current = node
        while current.parent and current == current.parent.right:
            current = current.parent
        return current.parent

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace inorderSuccessor on BST, node=2 (tree: 5,3,6,2,4)."
# Node 2 has no right child → successor is first ancestor where we went left
# Climb: node=2's parent=3. 2 is left child of 3 → successor = 3 ✓
# Node with right child (e.g., node=3): successor = leftmost of right subtree = 4 ✓
# Using parent pointers: if node.right exists → leftmost(node.right); else climb until came from left
# Trace node=6 (rightmost): climb 5, 5 is right child of... no parent above → no successor → None ✓
# WHY parent pointer: O(h) traversal without re-searching tree from root.
# WHY use parent pointer: avoids re-traversal from root; O(h) per call with no extra space.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(h). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: Inorder Predecessor in BST II — mirror logic: left child's rightmost, or first ancestor from right.
#  Follow-up: LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor) with parent pointers (#1650) — walk both to root, find intersection."

729.title: MY CALENDAR I  (BST / Ordered Set)
729.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Book a calendar event [start, end). Return false if it overlaps any existing event. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Half-open interval [start, end): start inclusive, end exclusive? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: book(10,20)→T, book(15,25)→F (overlaps), book(20,30)→T ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Store all events; for each new booking check all existing. O(n²) total.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _729_MyCalendarI_Brute:
    def __init__(self): self.events=[]
    def book(self, start, end):
        for s,e in self.events:
            if start<e and end>s: return False
        self.events.append((start,end)); return True

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Sorted list of bookings with binary search overlap check — O(log n) per booking.
#  bookings = sorted list of (start, end) intervals.
#  For each new booking (start, end):
#    Use bisect to find insertion position i (where start would go in sorted order).
#    Check left neighbor: if i > 0 and bookings[i-1][1] > start → overlap → return False.
#    Check right neighbor: if i < len(bookings) and bookings[i][0] < end → overlap → return False.
#    No overlap: insert (start, end) at position i → return True.
#  WHY only check immediate neighbors: sorted list means only adjacent intervals can overlap
#  with a new interval — all others are guaranteed to be too far left or right.
#  WHY sorted by start: overlaps with (start, end) can only happen with intervals whose
#  start < end (left neighbor) or whose start < new_end (right neighbor).
