        dp=[float('inf')]*(n+1); dp[0]=0
        squares=[i*i for i in range(1,int(n**0.5)+1)]
        for i in range(1,n+1):
            for sq in squares:
                if sq>i: break
                dp[i]=min(dp[i],dp[i-sq]+1)
        return dp[n]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "BFS on numbers, treating perfect squares as edges — O(n * sqrt(n)). Walk-through:
#  Pre-compute squares: squares = [i² for i ≤ sqrt(n)].
#  BFS from n: each step subtracts a square → finds minimum steps (=min squares) to reach 0.
#  queue = deque([n]). visited = {n}. steps = 0.
#  While queue:
#    steps++. For _ in range(len(queue)):
#      curr = queue.popleft().
#      For sq in squares:
#        nxt = curr - sq.
#        If nxt == 0: return steps.
#        If nxt > 0 and nxt not in visited: visited.add(nxt); queue.append(nxt).
#  WHY BFS: guarantees minimum number of steps (= minimum squares summing to n).
#  Alternative: DP dp[i] = min(dp[i-j²]+1 for j² ≤ i). dp[0]=0. Return dp[n].
#  Time: O(n * sqrt(n)). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _279_PerfectSquares:
    def numSquares(self, n):
        dp = [float('inf')] * (n + 1)
        dp[0] = 0
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            j = 1
            while j * j <= i:
                dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - j*j] + 1)
                j += 1
        return dp[n]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace numSquares on n=12."
# squares=[1,4,9]. dp[0]=0.
# dp[1]=min(dp[1-1]+1)=1. dp[2]=min(dp[1]+1)=2. dp[3]=3. 
# dp[4]=min(dp[4-1]+1,dp[4-4]+1)=min(4,1)=1. (use 4=2²)
# dp[5]=min(dp[4]+1,dp[1]+1)=min(2,2)=2. dp[8]=min(dp[7]+1,dp[4]+1)=min(3,2)=2.
# dp[9]=min(dp[8]+1,dp[5]+1,dp[0]+1)=min(3,3,1)=1. (9=3²)
# dp[10]=2. dp[11]=3. dp[12]=min(dp[11]+1,dp[8]+1,dp[3]+1)=min(4,3,4)=3.
# Return 3 ✓ (12=4+4+4).

# WHY BFS: the queue processes nodes in increasing distance/level, so the first time we reach a node gives the shortest path for that level.
# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n*sqrt(n)). Space O(n).
#  BFS also works: O(n*sqrt(n)) but same complexity.
#  Follow-up: Coin Change (#322) — coins instead of squares; same DP.
#  Follow-up: verify answer using Lagrange's theorem for O(sqrt(n)) check."

983.title: MINIMUM COST FOR TICKETS  (Unbounded Knapsack)
983.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Travel plan on days[i]. Buy tickets for 1-day, 7-day, or 30-day at costs[0,1,2].
#  Find minimum cost to cover all travel days. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  days is sorted? Yes. Maximum day value? 365."
#
# "Let me walk: days=[1,4,6,7,8,20], costs=[2,7,15] → 11 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i] = min cost to cover all travel days from day i onward.
#  O(n * 3) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _983_MinCostForTickets_Brute:
    def mincostTickets(self, days, costs):
        day_set=set(days); dp=[0]*367
        for d in range(365,-1,-1):
            if d not in day_set: dp[d]=dp[d+1]
            else: dp[d]=min(costs[0]+dp[min(366,d+1)],costs[1]+dp[min(366,d+7)],costs[2]+dp[min(366,d+30)])
        return dp[days[0]]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "1-D DP over days 1..365 — O(W * 3) = O(1). Walk-through:
#  dp[i] = minimum cost to travel from day i to day 365.
#  travel_days = set of travel days for O(1) lookup.
#  For i from 365 down to 1:
#    If i not in travel_days: dp[i] = dp[i+1] (no travel on day i → same cost as tomorrow).
#    Else: dp[i] = min(
#      costs[0] + dp[i+1],    ← 1-day pass covers day i only
#      costs[1] + dp[i+7],    ← 7-day pass covers days i..i+6
#      costs[2] + dp[i+30])   ← 30-day pass covers days i..i+29
#  Return dp[1].
#  WHY dp[i+7] and dp[i+30]: these passes cover the next 7 or 30 days for free.
#  Time: O(W) where W=365 = O(1). Space: O(W) = O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
from collections import deque
class _983_MinCostForTickets:
    def mincostTickets(self, days, costs):
        travel_days = set(days)
        dp = [0] * 366
        for day in range(1, 366):
            if day not in travel_days:
                dp[day] = dp[day - 1]
            else:
                dp[day] = min(
                    dp[day - 1] + costs[0],
                    dp[max(0, day - 7)] + costs[1],
                    dp[max(0, day - 30)] + costs[2]
                )
        return dp[365]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace mincostTickets([1,4,6,7,8,20], costs=[2,7,15])."
# dp[i]=min cost to cover days 1..i. days=set([1,4,6,7,8,20]).
# dp[0]=0. For i=1..20:
# i=1 (travel day): dp[1]=min(dp[0]+2, dp[max(0,1-7)]+7, dp[max(0,1-30)]+15)=min(2,7,15)=2.
# i=2..3 (no travel): dp[2]=dp[1]=2. dp[3]=2.
# i=4 (travel): dp[4]=min(dp[3]+2,dp[0]+7,dp[0]+15)=min(4,7,15)=4.
# i=5: dp[5]=dp[4]=4. i=6 (travel): dp[6]=min(dp[5]+2,dp[0]+7,dp[0]+15)=min(6,7,15)=6.
# i=7 (travel): dp[7]=min(dp[6]+2,dp[1]+7,dp[0]+15)=min(8,9,15)=8.
# i=8 (travel): dp[8]=min(dp[7]+2,dp[2]+7,dp[0]+15)=min(10,9,15)=9.
# i=9..19: no travel. dp stays=9. i=20: dp[20]=min(dp[19]+2,dp[13]+7,dp[0]+15)=min(11,16,15)=11.
# Return 11 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(365). Space O(365).
#  Follow-up: if days can be > 365, switch to n-day DP on travel days only.
#  Follow-up: if ticket prices change per week, extend the DP transitions."

673.title: NUMBER OF LONGEST INCREASING SUBSEQUENCE  (Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS))
673.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the number of longest increasing subsequences. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Not the actual subsequences, just the count? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[1,3,5,4,7] → LIS length=4. Count: [1,3,5,7],[1,3,4,7] → 2 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i]=(length,count) of LIS ending at i. O(n²) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _673_NumberOfLongestIncreasingSubsequence_Brute:
    def findNumberOfLIS(self, nums):
        n=len(nums); lengths=[1]*n; counts=[1]*n
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i):
                if nums[j]<nums[i]:
                    if lengths[j]+1>lengths[i]: lengths[i]=lengths[j]+1; counts[i]=counts[j]
                    elif lengths[j]+1==lengths[i]: counts[i]+=counts[j]
        max_len=max(lengths); return sum(c for l,c in zip(lengths,counts) if l==max_len)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DP tracking (LIS_length, count) per position — O(n²). Walk-through:
#  dp[i] = (length of LIS ending at i, number of such LIS).
#  For each i: for each j < i where nums[j] < nums[i]:
#    If dp[j][0]+1 > dp[i][0]: dp[i] = (dp[j][0]+1, dp[j][1]).  ← new longer LIS
#    Elif dp[j][0]+1 == dp[i][0]: dp[i] = (dp[i][0], dp[i][1]+dp[j][1]).  ← same length, add counts
#  max_len = max(dp[i][0]). return sum(dp[i][1] for i where dp[i][0]==max_len).
#  WHY track count alongside length: when multiple ways achieve same LIS length, accumulate counts.
#  WHY sum at end: total LIS count = sum of counts at all positions that achieve max_len.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _673_NumberOfLongestIncreasingSubsequence:
    def findNumberOfLIS(self, nums):
        n = len(nums)
        lengths = [1] * n
        counts = [1] * n
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i):
                if nums[j] < nums[i]:
                    if lengths[j] + 1 > lengths[i]:
                        lengths[i] = lengths[j] + 1
                        counts[i] = counts[j]
                    elif lengths[j] + 1 == lengths[i]:
                        counts[i] += counts[j]
        max_len = max(lengths)
        return sum(c for l, c in zip(lengths, counts) if l == max_len)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the DP state transition on the given example(s)."
#
# nums=[1,3,5,4,7]: lengths=[1,2,3,3,4], counts=[1,1,1,1,2].
# lengths[4]=4(via 5 or 4 as penultimate). counts[4]=counts[2]+counts[3]=1+1=2. → 2 ✓
#
# Two cases: strictly longer (reset count) or same length (accumulate count)
# dp[i]=LIS length ending at i. cnt[i]=number of such LIS. dp[j]=dp[i]+1 when nums[j]>nums[i]. cnt[j]+=cnt[i] when dp[j]==dp[i]+1. Final: cnt[i] where dp[i]==max_length.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²). Space O(n).
#  Follow-up: Longest Increasing Subsequence (#300) — just the length; O(n log n) via patience sort.
#  Follow-up: Length of LIS in O(n log n) with BIT (Binary Indexed Tree)+count — more complex."

1027.title: LONGEST ARITHMETIC SUBSEQUENCE  (Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS))
1027.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the longest arithmetic subsequence: elements equally spaced (constant difference). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Return the length, not the subsequence itself? Yes. At least length 2? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[3,6,9,12] → diff=3, length=4 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i][diff] = longest arithmetic subsequence ending at i with difference diff.
#  O(n²) time and space. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1027_LongestArithmeticSubsequence_Brute:
    def longestArithSeqLength(self, nums):
        n=len(nums); dp=[{} for _ in range(n)]; best=2
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(i):
                diff=nums[i]-nums[j]
                dp[i][diff]=dp[j].get(diff,1)+1
                best=max(best,dp[i][diff])
        return best

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DP with per-node difference tracking — O(n²). Walk-through:
#  dp[i][diff] = length of longest arithmetic subsequence ending at index i with common diff 'diff'.
#  For each j < i:
#    d = nums[i] - nums[j].
#    dp[i][d] = dp[j].get(d, 1) + 1
#      ← extend subsequence ending at j with difference d, or start a new one of length 2.
#    best = max(best, dp[i][d]).
#  WHY hash map per index: differences can be negative or large — dict is more flexible than array.
#  WHY initialize to 1: a single element is always an AP (Arithmetic Progression) of length 1; two elements is length 2.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(n²) worst case."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1027_LongestArithmeticSubsequence:
    def longestArithSeqLength(self, nums):
        n = len(nums)
        dp = [dict() for _ in range(n)]
        best = 2
        for i in range(1, n):
            for j in range(i):
                diff = nums[i] - nums[j]
                dp[i][diff] = dp[j].get(diff, 1) + 1
                best = max(best, dp[i][diff])
        return best

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the monotonic condition and show how each mid update narrows the search."
#
# nums=[3,6,9,12]: diff=3 at each step. dp[1]={3:2}, dp[2]={3:3}, dp[3]={3:4}. best=4 ✓
# nums=[9,4,7,2,10]: various diffs. best=3([4,7,10] or [9,4,-1]?) → 3 ✓
#
# Dp[i][diff] = length of AP ending at nums[i] with common difference diff
# Edge: nums=[0,0] → diff=0, dp[1]={0:2}, answer=2 ✓. Single element → 1. Negative diffs handled: diff can be any integer (stored in dict).

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²). Space O(n²) for dicts.
#  Follow-up: Arithmetic Slices (#413) — contiguous arithmetic subsequences.
#  Follow-up: Longest Arithmetic Subsequence of Given Difference (#1218) — fixed diff, O(n)."

1048.title: LONGEST STRING CHAIN  (Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS))
1048.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  A word chain: each word can be extended by inserting one letter to get the next word.
#  Find the longest such chain. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Words don't need to be in order in the input? Correct — we choose the ordering."
#
# "Let me walk: words=['a','b','ba','bca','bda','bdca'] → longest chain = 4: 'a'->'ba'->'bda'->'bdca' ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Sort by length. DP: dp[word] = longest chain ending at word.
#  For each word, try removing each character to get predecessor.
#  O(n * L²) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1048_LongestStringChain_Brute:
    def longestStrChain(self, words):
        words.sort(key=len); dp={}; best=1
        for w in words:
            dp[w]=1
            for i in range(len(w)):
                prev=w[:i]+w[i+1:]
                if prev in dp: dp[w]=max(dp[w],dp[prev]+1)
            best=max(best,dp[w])
        return best

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DP: longest chain where each word is predecessor of next — O(n * L). Walk-through:
#  Sort words by length. dp[word] = longest chain ending at word.
#  For each word (sorted by length):
#    For each predecessor (word with one char removed):
#      dp[word] = max(dp[word], dp.get(predecessor, 0) + 1).
#  Return max(dp.values()).
#  HOW generate predecessors: for each position i, remove word[i] → get a candidate predecessor.
#  If candidate in word set: it's a valid predecessor.
#  WHY sort by length: when processing word, all shorter predecessors are already computed.
#  WHY all deletions: 'predecessor' is defined as removing one letter from the current word.
#  Time: O(n * L²) where L = max length. Space: O(n * L)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1048_LongestStringChain:
    def longestStrChain(self, words):
        words.sort(key=len)
        dp = {}
        best = 1
        for word in words:
            dp[word] = 1
            for i in range(len(word)):
                predecessor = word[:i] + word[i+1:]
                if predecessor in dp:
                    dp[word] = max(dp[word], dp[predecessor] + 1)
            best = max(best, dp[word])
        return best

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace longestStrChain(['a','b','ba','bca','bda','bdca'])."
# Sort by length. For each word, try removing each char and look up in dp
# 'a': dp={'a':1}. 'b': dp['b']=1
# 'ba': remove 'b'→'a'(dp=1)+1=2; remove 'a'→'b'(dp=1)+1=2 → dp['ba']=2
# 'bca': remove 'b'→'ca'(0+1=1); remove 'c'→'ba'(2+1=3); remove 'a'→'bc'(0+1=1) → dp['bca']=3
# 'bda': remove 'b'→'da'(1); remove 'd'→'ba'(2+1=3); remove 'a'→'bd'(1) → dp['bda']=3
# 'bdca': remove 'b'→'dca'(1); remove 'd'→'bca'(3+1=4); remove 'c'→'bda'(3+1=4); remove 'a'→'bdc'(1) → dp['bdca']=4
# Return 4 ✓ (chain: 'a'→'ba'→'bda'→'bdca')
# dp[i]=dp[word]=chain length ending at word. dp[j]=dp.get(word[:k]+word[k+1:],0)+1 for each removal. dp[i] accumulated. dp[j]=max chain ending at current word. Return max(dp.values()) ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n * L²): n words × L chars removed × L to slice. Space O(n * L).
#  Follow-up: if words can only be extended (not any insertion), different DP.
#  Follow-up: return the actual longest chain — track parent pointers in dp."

63.title: UNIQUE PATHS II  (2D Grid DP)
63.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  m×n grid with obstacles (1) and free cells (0). Count paths from top-left to bottom-right.
#  Can only move right or down. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  If start or end is blocked, return 0? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: obstacleGrid=[[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]] → 2 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i][j] = number of paths to (i,j). If obstacle, dp=0.
#  O(mn) time. This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _63_UniquePathsII_Brute:
    def uniquePathsWithObstacles(self, obstacleGrid):
        m,n=len(obstacleGrid),len(obstacleGrid[0])
        dp=[[0]*n for _ in range(m)]
        for i in range(m):
            if obstacleGrid[i][0]==1: break
            dp[i][0]=1
        for j in range(n):
            if obstacleGrid[0][j]==1: break
            dp[0][j]=1
        for i in range(1,m):
            for j in range(1,n):
                if obstacleGrid[i][j]==0: dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j]+dp[i][j-1]
        return dp[m-1][n-1]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Standard grid DP with obstacle handling — O(mn). Walk-through:
#  dp[i][j] = number of unique paths to cell (i,j).
#  If obstacleGrid[i][j] == 1: dp[i][j] = 0 (blocked, no paths through here).
#  Else:
#    dp[0][0] = 1 (start). First row: dp[0][j] = dp[0][j-1] if no obstacle (else 0).
#    First col: dp[i][0] = dp[i-1][0] if no obstacle (else 0).
#    Interior: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1].
#  WHY 0 propagates: once a cell in the first row/col is blocked, all cells to its right/below
#  are also unreachable (only one direction to come from).
#  Answer = dp[m-1][n-1]. Time: O(mn). Space: O(mn) or O(n) rolling."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _63_UniquePathsII:
    def uniquePathsWithObstacles(self, obstacleGrid):
        m, n = len(obstacleGrid), len(obstacleGrid[0])
        dp = [0] * n
        dp[0] = 1 if obstacleGrid[0][0] == 0 else 0
        for i in range(m):
            for j in range(n):
                if obstacleGrid[i][j] == 1:
                    dp[j] = 0
                elif j > 0:
                    dp[j] += dp[j-1]
        return dp[n-1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace uniquePathsWithObstacles([[0,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,0]])."
# Obstacle at (1,1). dp[i][j]=paths to (i,j). dp[0][0]=1.
# Row 0: dp[0][1]=1, dp[0][2]=1 (no obstacles).
# dp[1][0]=1 (from above). dp[1][1]=0 (obstacle!). dp[1][2]=dp[0][2]+dp[1][1]=1+0=1.
# dp[2][0]=dp[1][0]=1. dp[2][1]=dp[1][1]+dp[2][0]=0+1=1. dp[2][2]=dp[1][2]+dp[2][1]=1+1=2.
# Return 2 ✓ (paths: right→right→down→down and down→down→right→right).
# dp[0][0]: if grid[0][0]=1 (obstacle at start) → dp[0][0]=0 → all paths blocked → return 0 ✓
# WHY in-place DP: dp[i][j] only needs dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1] → can reuse grid.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(mn). Space O(n).
#  Follow-up: Unique Paths I (#62) — no obstacles; math formula C(m+n-2,m-1).
#  Follow-up: minimum path sum — same DP structure, different objective."

120.title: TRIANGLE  (2D Grid DP)
120.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Triangle grid: find minimum path sum from top to bottom. Each step moves to adjacent number on row below. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Adjacent means index i or i+1 in next row? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: triangle=[[2],[3,4],[6,5,7],[4,1,8,3]] → 2+3+5+1=11 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Bottom-up DP: start from bottom row, accumulate min path sum upward.
#  O(n²) time, O(n) space. This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _120_Triangle_Brute:
    def minimumTotal(self, triangle):
        dp=triangle[-1][:]
        for row in reversed(triangle[:-1]):
            dp=[row[i]+min(dp[i],dp[i+1]) for i in range(len(row))]
        return dp[0]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Bottom-up DP on triangle — O(n²). Walk-through:
#  Start from the BOTTOM row of the triangle (avoids handling variable-length rows when going top-down).
#  dp = triangle[-1] (copy bottom row — these are the base costs).
#  For i from second-to-last row up to row 0:
#    For j in 0..len(row)-1:
#      dp[j] = triangle[i][j] + min(dp[j], dp[j+1])
#        ← at position (i,j), choose to go to (i+1,j) or (i+1,j+1) — take minimum.
#  Return dp[0].
#  WHY bottom-up: at each position, dp[j] already contains the minimum path sum
#  from that position to the bottom → naturally builds the answer.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(n) — modify dp in-place."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _120_Triangle:
    def minimumTotal(self, triangle):
        dp = triangle[-1][:]
        for row in reversed(triangle[:-1]):
            dp = [row[i] + min(dp[i], dp[i+1]) for i in range(len(row))]
        return dp[0]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minimumTotal on triangle=[[2],[3,4],[6,5,7],[4,1,8,3]]."
# DP from bottom up: dp = last row = [4,1,8,3].
# Row 2 (index 2): [6,5,7].
#   dp[0]=6+min(4,1)=7. dp[1]=5+min(1,8)=6. dp[2]=7+min(8,3)=10. dp=[7,6,10].
# Row 1 (index 1): [3,4].
#   dp[0]=3+min(7,6)=9. dp[1]=4+min(6,10)=10. dp=[9,10].
# Row 0: [2]. dp[0]=2+min(9,10)=11. return 11 ✓
# Path: 2→3→5→1=11 ✓
# WHY bottom-up: at each step, each position takes the min cost of the two adjacent positions below.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²): n rows, each row i has i+1 elements. Space O(n) rolling array.
#  Follow-up: return the actual path — track choices with parent pointers.
#  Follow-up: Minimum Path Sum in a Matrix (#64) — rectangular grid, same DP."

931.title: MINIMUM FALLING PATH SUM  (2D Grid DP)
931.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the minimum sum falling path through the matrix. Each step can go to the cell directly below or diagonally adjacent. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  n×n matrix? Yes. Start from any cell in row 0, end at any cell in row n-1?"
#
# "Let me walk: matrix=[[2,1,3],[6,5,4],[7,8,9]] → paths: 1+5+8=14? 1+4+7=12? 1+4+8=13. min=13? Actually 2+5+7=14, 1+4+7=12, or 3+4+7=14. → 12 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP in-place or with copy: for each cell, take min of three cells above.
#  O(n²) time. This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _931_MinFallingPathSum_Brute:
    def minFallingPathSum(self, matrix):
        n=len(matrix); dp=[row[:] for row in matrix]
        for r in range(1,n):
            for c in range(n):
                best=dp[r-1][c]
                if c>0: best=min(best,dp[r-1][c-1])
                if c<n-1: best=min(best,dp[r-1][c+1])
                dp[r][c]+=best
        return min(dp[-1])

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Top-down DP modifying matrix in-place — O(n²). Walk-through:
#  dp[i][j] = minimum path sum to reach cell (i,j) from the top row.
#  First row: base case, dp[0][j] = matrix[0][j].
#  For i in 1..n-1:
#    For j in 0..n-1:
#      best_above = min of dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i-1][j+1] (within bounds).
#      dp[i][j] = matrix[i][j] + best_above.
#  Answer = min(dp[n-1]).
#  WHY 3 predecessors: can come from directly above or diagonally (one step left/right).
#  In-place modification: overwrite matrix[i][j] with the dp value → O(1) extra space.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _931_MinFallingPathSum:
    def minFallingPathSum(self, matrix):
        n = len(matrix)
        for r in range(1, n):
            for c in range(n):
                best = matrix[r-1][c]
                if c > 0: best = min(best, matrix[r-1][c-1])
                if c < n-1: best = min(best, matrix[r-1][c+1])
                matrix[r][c] += best
        return min(matrix[-1])

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minFallingPathSum([[2,1,3],[6,5,4],[7,8,9]])."
# dp[i][j] = min falling path sum ending at (i,j)
# Row 0: dp[0]=[2,1,3]
# Row 1: dp[1][0]=min(2,1)+6=7; dp[1][1]=min(2,1,3)+5=6; dp[1][2]=min(1,3)+4=5
# Row 2: dp[2][0]=min(7,6)+7=13; dp[2][1]=min(7,6,5)+8=13; dp[2][2]=min(6,5)+9=14
# Return min(13,13,14)=13 ✓
# Edge: single row → return min of that row.
# DP row-by-row (no DFS needed): visited cells in row order. dp[i][j]=min(dp[i-1][j-1],dp[i-1][j],dp[i-1][j+1])+grid[i][j]. All cells visited exactly once per row.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²). Space O(1) (in-place).
#  Follow-up: Minimum Falling Path Sum II (#1289) — can't pick same column twice; O(n²).
#  Follow-up: Triangle (#120) — triangular falling path, same bottom-up DP."

1277.title: COUNT SQUARE SUBMATRICES WITH ALL ONES  (2D Grid DP)
1277.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count the number of square submatrices (of any size) that consist entirely of 1s. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  A 1×1 square of 1 counts? Yes. We count all squares, not just the largest."
#
# "Let me walk: matrix=[[0,1,1,1],[1,1,1,1],[0,1,1,1]] → answer=15 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i][j] = side length of largest square with bottom-right at (i,j).
#  That value also = number of squares with bottom-right at (i,j).
#  O(mn) time. This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1277_CountSquareSubmatricesWithAllOnes_Brute:
    def countSquares(self, matrix):
        total=0
        for i in range(len(matrix)):
            for j in range(len(matrix[0])):
                if matrix[i][j] and i and j:
                    matrix[i][j]=min(matrix[i-1][j],matrix[i][j-1],matrix[i-1][j-1])+1
                total+=matrix[i][j]
        return total

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "2-D DP — dp[i][j] = side length of largest all-1 square with (i,j) as bottom-right. O(mn).
#  Base: dp[i][0] = matrix[i][0]. dp[0][j] = matrix[0][j].
#  For i≥1, j≥1:
#    If matrix[i][j] == 0: dp[i][j] = 0.
#    Else: dp[i][j] = min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1], dp[i-1][j-1]) + 1.
#  Count: for each (i,j), there are dp[i][j] squares with bottom-right at (i,j)
#  (sizes 1×1, 2×2, ..., dp[i][j]×dp[i][j]).
#  Total = sum of all dp[i][j].
#  WHY min of 3 neighbors: the 3 neighbors constrain how large a square fits here.
#  The bottleneck is the smallest of the three adjacent squares.
#  Time: O(mn). Space: O(mn) or O(n) rolling."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1277_CountSquareSubmatricesWithAllOnes:
    def countSquares(self, matrix):
        total = 0
        for i in range(len(matrix)):
            for j in range(len(matrix[0])):
                if matrix[i][j] == 1 and i > 0 and j > 0:
                    matrix[i][j] = min(matrix[i-1][j], matrix[i][j-1], matrix[i-1][j-1]) + 1
                total += matrix[i][j]
        return total

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace countSquares([[0,1,1,1],[1,1,1,1],[0,1,1,1]])."
# dp[i][j] = largest square with bottom-right at (i,j). Also = count of squares ending here.
# dp[0][1..3]=1 each (1×1 squares). dp[1][0]=1.
# dp[1][1]=min(dp[0][0],dp[0][1],dp[1][0])+1=min(0,1,1)+1=1. (top-left is 0)
# dp[1][2]=min(dp[0][1],dp[0][2],dp[1][1])+1=min(1,1,1)+1=2. (2×2 square possible)
# dp[1][3]=min(dp[0][2],dp[0][3],dp[1][2])+1=min(1,1,2)+1=2.
# dp[2][1..2]: dp[2][1]=1. dp[2][2]=min(dp[1][1],dp[1][2],dp[2][1])+1=min(1,2,1)+1=2. dp[2][3]=min(dp[1][2],dp[1][3],dp[2][2])+1=min(2,2,2)+1=3.
# Sum all dp values = 0+1+1+1+1+1+2+2+0+1+2+3=15 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(mn). Space O(1) in-place.
#  Follow-up: Maximal Square (#221) — find the largest square; take max instead of sum.
#  Follow-up: Count Rectangle Submatrices With All Ones (#1504) — harder, needs histogram."

1937.title: MAXIMUM NUMBER OF POINTS WITH COST  (2D Grid DP)
1937.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Pick one element from each row to maximise sum. Moving from row i to i+1:
#  bonus points[i][j] - |j_next - j_current|. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  This is DP where at each row, we take the best from previous row minus absolute column difference?"
#
# "Let me walk: points=[[1,2,3],[1,5,1],[3,1,1]] → path (0,2)→(1,1)→(2,0): 3+5-1+3-1=9 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[j] = max points when picking column j in current row. O(mn²) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1937_MaxPointsWithCost_Brute:
    def maxPoints(self, points):
        m,n=len(points),len(points[0]); dp=points[0][:]
        for i in range(1,m):
            new_dp=[0]*n
            for j in range(n):
                new_dp[j]=points[i][j]+max(dp[k]-abs(k-j) for k in range(n))
            dp=new_dp
        return max(dp)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DP with column-wise max propagation — O(mn). Walk-through:
#  dp[i][j] = max points up to row i ending at column j.
#  For row 0: dp[0][j] = points[0][j].
#  For each subsequent row i:
#    left[j] = max of dp[i-1][j'], j'≤j, minus |j-j'| = max(left[j-1]-1, dp[i-1][j]).
#    right[j] = max of dp[i-1][j'], j'>=j, minus |j-j'| (scan from right).
#    dp[i][j] = max(left[j], right[j]) + points[i][j].
#  WHY two passes per row: direct O(m²) for each row is too slow.
#  Left pass: dp[j] carries the max 'credit' coming from the left, decreasing by 1 per column moved.
#  Right pass: same from the right. Both together give the optimal previous row value.
#  Time: O(mn). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1937_MaxPointsWithCost:
    def maxPoints(self, points):
        m, n = len(points), len(points[0])
        dp = list(points[0])
        for i in range(1, m):
            left = [0] * n
            right = [0] * n
            left[0] = dp[0]
            for j in range(1, n):
                left[j] = max(left[j-1], dp[j] + j) - 1
            right[n-1] = dp[n-1] - (n-1)
            for j in range(n-2, -1, -1):
                right[j] = max(right[j+1], dp[j] - j) + 1
            dp = [points[i][j] + max(left[j] + j, right[j] - j) for j in range(n)]
        return max(dp)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace maxPoints([[1,2,3],[1,5,1],[3,1,1]])."
# points[i][j] for row i, col j. Moving from row i to i+1 col c costs |c-prev_c|.
# dp[i][j] = max points ending at (i,j)
# Row 0: dp[0]=[1,2,3]
# Row 1: dp[1][j]=max over c: dp[0][c]+points[1][j]-|j-c|
# WHY optimize with left/right sweeps: |j-c| = j-c or c-j
# Left sweep: left[j]=max(dp[0][c]+c) for c≤j → dp[1][j]≥left[j]+points[1][j]-j
# Right sweep: right[j]=max(dp[0][c]-c) for c≥j → dp[1][j]≥right[j]+points[1][j]+j
# dp[1]=[4,7,3] ← wait: dp[1][1]=max(1+2-1,2+5,3+5-1... 2+5+... )=7? 7 ✓
# Return max(dp[2])=9 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(mn). Space O(n).
#  Follow-up: if the cost is different from |i-j|, adjust the pass computation.
#  Follow-up: Minimum Falling Path Sum (#931) — adjacent only, no absolute difference needed."

1653.title: MINIMUM DELETIONS TO MAKE STRING BALANCED  (String DP)
1653.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Delete minimum characters to make all 'a's come before all 'b's. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  The string only contains 'a' and 'b'? Yes. Result must have all a's before all b's (can be empty)."
#
# "Let me walk: s='aababbab' → 'aabab': delete 1 'b' and 1 'a' or... min deletions=2? Expected 2 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each split point i: delete all 'b's in s[:i] + all 'a's in s[i:].
#  O(n²) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1653_MinDeletionsToMakeStringBalanced_Brute:
    def minimumDeletions(self, s):
        n=len(s); best=n
        for i in range(n+1):
            cost=s[:i].count('b')+s[i:].count('a')
            best=min(best,cost)
        return best

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Greedy: scan left-to-right, count b-deletions; scan right-to-left, count a-deletions — O(n). Walk-through:
#  b_count = 0. deletions = 0.
#  For c in s:
#    If c == 'b': b_count++.   ← one more 'b' seen so far
#    Elif c == 'a':
#      If b_count > 0: deletions++; b_count--.  ← this 'a' comes after some 'b' → must remove one
#      (Either remove this 'a' or the previous 'b' — greedy: remove the 'a' since it appeared last)
#  Return deletions.
#  WHY greedy: once we see an 'a' after a 'b', one deletion is needed. We model removing the 'a'
#  (decrement b_count as if we'd removed a 'b' that was already used — equivalent accounting).
#  Alternative two-pass: count a→b swaps needed from both sides.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1653_MinDeletionsToMakeStringBalanced:
    def minimumDeletions(self, s):
        b_count = 0
        deletions = 0
        for ch in s:
            if ch == 'b':
                b_count += 1
            else:
                deletions = min(deletions + 1, b_count)
        return deletions

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minimumDeletions('aababbab')."
# DP: dp[i] = min deletions to balance string s[0..i]
# Two choices at each 'b': delete this 'b' (dp[i-1]+1) or accept 'b' and delete all 'a's after
# Actually: count b_count (b's seen so far) and a_del (a's to delete for current state)
# Scan: track count_b and dp
# s='aababbab': a,a,b,a,b,b,a,b
# a: dp=min(dp+1,dp)? Let a_count be a's after current b's...
# Simpler: ans=min over split point (delete all a's right of split + all b's left) - use prefix/suffix counts
# prefix_b[i] = #b in s[0..i]; suffix_a[i] = #a in s[i..n-1]
# min(prefix_b[i]+suffix_a[i]) over all i = 2 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: if string has more than 2 characters, DP with states for each character.
#  Follow-up: Minimum Swaps to Make String Balanced (#1963) — swap-based variant."

95.title: UNIQUE BINARY SEARCH TREES II  (Tree / Graph DP)
95.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Generate all structurally unique BSTs that contain values 1..n. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Return list of root nodes. n=0 → [None]? Per constraints n>=1."
#
# "Let me walk: n=3 → 5 unique BSTs ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each possible root r in [1..n]: left subtree uses [1..r-1], right uses [r+1..n].
#  Combine all left-right pairs with root r. Memoize on (lo,hi).
#  O(4^n / n^(3/2)) (Catalan number) unique trees. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _95_UniqueBinarySearchTreesII_Brute:
    def generateTrees(self, n):
        def generate(lo,hi):
            if lo>hi: return [None]
            result=[]
            for r in range(lo,hi+1):
                for left in generate(lo,r-1):
                    for right in generate(r+1,hi):
                        node=TreeNode(r); node.left=left; node.right=right; result.append(node)
            return result
        return generate(1,n)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Memoized DFS generating all valid BST structures — O(Catalan(n)*n).
#  Walk-through of how each unique BST is generated:
#  generate(lo, hi):
#    If lo > hi: return [None]  ← empty subtree (valid, 1 structure).
#    If (lo,hi) in memo: return memo[(lo,hi)].
#    results = []
#    For each value r from lo to hi:  ← pick root
#      for left in generate(lo, r-1):    ← all possible left subtrees
#        for right in generate(r+1, hi): ← all possible right subtrees
#          node = TreeNode(r)
#          node.left = left; node.right = right
#          results.append(node)
#    memo[(lo,hi)] = results; return results
#  WHY each r gives a valid BST: values lo..r-1 (all < r) go left, values r+1..hi (all > r) go right.
#  Cartesian product of left×right gives all distinct shapes.
#  Time: O(Catalan(n)*n). Space: O(same) to store all trees."
# Time: O(log n) — binary search on answer space.

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
from functools import lru_cache
class _95_UniqueBinarySearchTreesII:
    def generateTrees(self, n):
        @lru_cache(None)
        def generate(lo, hi):
            if lo > hi:
                return (None,)
            result = []
            for root_val in range(lo, hi + 1):
                for left in generate(lo, root_val - 1):
                    for right in generate(root_val + 1, hi):
                        node = TreeNode(root_val)
                        node.left = left
                        node.right = right
                        result.append(node)
            return tuple(result)
        return list(generate(1, n))

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace generateTrees on n=3."
# For root=1: left=generateTrees(1,0)=[None]. right=generateTrees(2,3)=[2(None,3),3(2,None)].
#   Trees: 1(None,2(None,3)), 1(None,3(2,None)).
# For root=2: left=generateTrees(1,1)=[1]. right=generateTrees(3,3)=[3].
#   Tree: 2(1,3).
# For root=3: left=generateTrees(1,2)=[1(None,2),2(1,None)]. right=[None].
#   Trees: 3(1(None,2),None), 3(2(1,None),None).
# Total 5 trees ✓ (Catalan number C(3)=5).
# WHY all roots from 1 to n: root splits remaining nodes into left/right subtrees.
# Each combination of left/right subtree choices gives one unique BST.
# Graph: dp[1..n] trees = all unique BST structures. component: each subtree is sub-component. find(root_value)→left/right subtrees. Cost=O(n^3) memoization.
# dp[i..j]=all unique BSTs using nodes i..j. dp[i]=1 for single nodes. dp[1..3]=5 trees. Recurrence: dp[i..j]=sum over r of dp[i..r-1]*dp[r+1..j].

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(Catalan(n) * n). Space O(Catalan(n) * n).
#  Follow-up: Unique Binary Search Trees I (#96) — count only, not generate; DP O(n²).
#  Follow-up: if we need trees with values from an arbitrary sorted array, same approach."

337.title: HOUSE ROBBER III  (Tree / Graph DP)
337.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Rob houses in a binary tree; no two adjacent (parent-child) houses can be robbed.
#  Maximise total amount. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Adjacent means direct parent-child only? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: root=[3,2,3,null,3,null,1] → rob 3,3,3,1=10? No: can't rob adjacent. rob(root=3)=3+1+3=7? Or rob(root=2,3)=2+3+1+3=... → 7 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each node: max(rob this node + rob grandchildren, don't rob + max rob children).
#  Without caching, exponential. With lru_cache, O(n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _337_HouseRobberIII_Brute:
    def rob(self, root):
        def dfs(node):
            if not node: return (0,0)
            left_skip,left_rob=dfs(node.left)
            right_skip,right_rob=dfs(node.right)
            rob_this=node.val+left_skip+right_skip
            skip_this=max(left_rob,left_skip)+max(right_rob,right_skip)
            return skip_this,rob_this
        skip,rob=dfs(root)
        return max(skip,rob)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Post-order returning (skip, take) pair — already O(n). Walk-through:
#  rob(node) returns (max_if_not_robbed, max_if_robbed):
#    null node: return (0, 0).
#    (l_skip, l_take) = rob(left)    ← left child's pair
#    (r_skip, r_take) = rob(right)   ← right child's pair
#    skip = max(l_skip, l_take) + max(r_skip, r_take)
#      ← if we SKIP this node, children can be robbed or skipped — pick max of each.
#    take = node.val + l_skip + r_skip
#      ← if we TAKE this node, MUST skip both children (no adjacent).
#    return (skip, take)
#  WHY return PAIR instead of one value: whether to rob THIS node depends on whether
#  the parent will be robbed. Returning both options lets the parent pick.
#  Answer = max(rob(root)). Time: O(n). Space: O(h)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _337_HouseRobberIII:
    def rob(self, root):
        def dfs(node):
            if not node:
                return 0, 0
            left_no_rob, left_rob = dfs(node.left)
            right_no_rob, right_rob = dfs(node.right)
            rob_this = node.val + left_no_rob + right_no_rob
            no_rob_this = max(left_rob, left_no_rob) + max(right_rob, right_no_rob)
            return no_rob_this, rob_this
        no_rob, rob = dfs(root)
        return max(no_rob, rob)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace rob on tree [3,4,5,1,3,null,1]."
# For each node, return (rob_this, skip_this)
# Leaves: node(1)=(1,0), node(3)=(3,0), node(1)=(1,0)
# node(4): rob=4+0+0=4, skip=max(1,0)+max(3,0)=1+3=4 → (4,4)
# node(5): rob=5+0+0=5, skip=max(1,0)=1 → (5,1)
# root(3): rob=3+skip(4)+skip(5)=3+4+1=8, skip=max(4,4)+max(5,1)=4+5=9
# Return max(8,9)=9 ✓
# WHY pair return: each node reports both options so parent can choose optimally.
# DFS postorder: visit left subtree → visit right subtree → compute. visited: each node once. call stack: dfs(root)→dfs(root.left)→dfs(root.right)→return (rob,skip) tuple.
# Tree DP graph: component = each subtree. find(node)→(rob,skip) pair. cost=node.val when robbing. dp[left],dp[right] subtree results combined at parent.
# dp[i]=(rob_val,skip_val) for node i. dp[leaf]=(leaf.val,0). dp[node]=(node.val+dp[left].skip+dp[right].skip, max(dp[left])+max(dp[right])). dp[root] final answer ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(h) recursion.
#  Follow-up: House Robber I/II (#198/#213) — 1D arrays; same rob/not-rob DP.
#  Follow-up: if the tree is very deep (n=10^4), consider iterative post-order DFS."

1976.title: NUMBER OF WAYS TO ARRIVE AT DESTINATION  (Tree / Graph DP)
1976.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the number of shortest paths from 0 to n-1 in a weighted directed graph. Return mod 10^9+7. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  'Shortest' means minimum total time (sum of edge weights)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: n=7, roads=[[0,6,7],[0,1,2],[1,2,3],[1,3,3],[6,3,3],[3,5,1],[6,5,1],[2,5,1],[0,4,5],[4,6,2]] → 4 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Dijkstra + count: dist[v] = shortest distance, ways[v] = count of shortest paths.
#  O((V+E) log V). This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1976_NumberOfWaysToArriveAtDestination_Brute:
    def countPaths(self, n, roads):
        import heapq; from collections import defaultdict
        MOD=10**9+7; graph=defaultdict(list)
        for u,v,t in roads: graph[u].append((v,t)); graph[v].append((u,t))
        dist=[float('inf')]*n; ways=[0]*n; dist[0]=0; ways[0]=1
        heap=[(0,0)]
        while heap:
            d,u=heapq.heappop(heap)
            if d>dist[u]: continue
            for v,t in graph[u]:
                if dist[u]+t<dist[v]: dist[v]=dist[u]+t; ways[v]=ways[u]; heapq.heappush(heap,(dist[v],v))
                elif dist[u]+t==dist[v]: ways[v]=(ways[v]+ways[u])%MOD
        return ways[n-1]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Dijkstra + path count — already O((V+E) log V). Walk-through:
#  Dual-purpose Dijkstra: track both shortest distance AND number of shortest paths.
#  dist[node] = shortest time to reach node. count[node] = how many shortest paths.
#  Initialize dist[0]=0, count[0]=1.
#  Min-heap: [(0, 0)].
#  Pop (d, u). If d > dist[u]: skip.
#  For each neighbor v with edge w:
#    new_d = d + w
#    If new_d < dist[v]:    ← found strictly shorter path
#      dist[v] = new_d; count[v] = count[u]; push.
#    elif new_d == dist[v]: ← another path of SAME length
#      count[v] = (count[v] + count[u]) % MOD  ← add these paths to count
#  WHY this counts correctly: when we find a path of the same length, it's an alternative
#  route → all paths from u add to the count at v.
#  Return count[n-1]. Time: O((V+E) log V). Space: O(V+E)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict
class _1976_NumberOfWaysToArriveAtDestination:
    def countPaths(self, n, roads):
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        graph = defaultdict(list)
        for u, v, t in roads:
            graph[u].append((v, t))
            graph[v].append((u, t))
        dist = [float('inf')] * n
        ways = [0] * n
        dist[0] = 0
        ways[0] = 1
        heap = [(0, 0)]
        while heap:
            d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
            if d > dist[u]:
                continue
            for v, t in graph[u]:
                new_dist = dist[u] + t
                if new_dist < dist[v]:
                    dist[v] = new_dist
                    ways[v] = ways[u]
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (new_dist, v))
                elif new_dist == dist[v]:
                    ways[v] = (ways[v] + ways[u]) % MOD
        return ways[n-1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace countPaths(n=7, roads=[[0,6,7],[0,1,2],[1,2,3],[1,3,3],[6,3,3],[3,5,1],[6,5,2],[0,4,5],[4,6,4],[5,2,3]])."
# Dijkstra for shortest distances from node 0
# count[v] = number of shortest paths to v
# dist[0]=0, count[0]=1. Process node 0 (dist=0): update neighbors
# ... eventually dist[6]=7 (direct edge 0→6), dist[5]=3 (0→1→3→5 or 0→6→5)
# count[6]=1 (via direct edge), count[5]=multiple paths
# Return count[n-1] % MOD ✓
# WHY Dijkstra + count: for each neighbor, if shorter path found → reset count; if equal → add count.
# Standard SSSP extended with path count tracking.
# dp[v]=count[v]=number of shortest paths to v. dp[v]=sum(dp[u] for all u where dist[u]+edge(u,v)==dist[v]). dp[0]=1. dp[j]+=dp[i] when shortest path through i reaches j ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O((V+E) log V). Space O(V+E).
#  Follow-up: Network Delay Time (#743) — just shortest distance.
#  Follow-up: if directed vs undirected matters, check the graph construction."

1066.title: CAMPUS BIKES II  (Bitmask DP)
1066.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  n workers, m bikes. Assign each worker exactly one bike minimising TOTAL Manhattan distance.
#  (This is different from #1057 which is greedy.) Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Minimum sum assignment → bitmask DP over workers/bikes?"
#
# "Let me walk: workers=[[0,0],[2,1]], bikes=[[1,2],[3,3]] → cost matrix; optimal=6 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all permutations of bike assignments. O(m! / (m-n)! * n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1066_CampusBikesII_Brute:
    def assignBikes(self, workers, bikes):
        from itertools import permutations
        n=len(workers); m=len(bikes)
        best=float('inf')
        for perm in permutations(range(m),n):
            cost=sum(abs(workers[i][0]-bikes[j][0])+abs(workers[i][1]-bikes[j][1]) for i,j in enumerate(perm))
            best=min(best,cost)
        return best

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Bitmask DP — minimum total distance assignment. O(n² * 2^n). Walk-through:
#  n workers, n bikes. dp[mask] = min total distance when workers assigned to bikes in 'mask'.
#  worker_idx = popcount(mask) = which worker we're assigning next (0-indexed).
#  dp[0] = 0 (no assignments yet).
#  For mask in 1..2^n-1:
#    worker = bin(mask).count('1') - 1  (0-indexed worker for this step).
#    For each bike b where bit b is set in mask:
#      prev_mask = mask ^ (1 << b)  (state without this bike assigned).
#      dp[mask] = min(dp[mask], dp[prev_mask] + dist(workers[worker], bikes[b])).
#  Answer = min dp over masks with n bits set.
#  WHY bitmask: represents which bikes are used → O(2^n) states × n bikes = O(n * 2^n).
#  Time: O(n² * 2^n). Space: O(2^n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1066_CampusBikesII:
    def assignBikes(self, workers, bikes):
        n, m = len(workers), len(bikes)
        INF = float('inf')
        dp = [INF] * (1 << m)
        dp[0] = 0
        for mask in range(1 << m):
            worker_idx = bin(mask).count('1')
            if worker_idx >= n:
                continue
            if dp[mask] == INF:
                continue
            for bike_idx in range(m):
                if not (mask >> bike_idx & 1):
                    wr, wc = workers[worker_idx]
                    br, bc = bikes[bike_idx]
                    cost = abs(wr - br) + abs(wc - bc)
                    new_mask = mask | (1 << bike_idx)
                    dp[new_mask] = min(dp[new_mask], dp[mask] + cost)
        return min(dp[mask] for mask in range(1 << m) if bin(mask).count('1') == n)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace the bit representation and show which bits get set/cleared and why."
#
# workers=[[0,0],[2,1]], bikes=[[1,2],[3,3]]: n=2, m=2. 2^2=4 states.
# dp[0]=0. dp[01]→worker0+bike0=|0-1|+|0-2|=3. dp[10]→worker0+bike1=|0-3|+|0-3|=6.
# dp[11]→dp[01]+worker1+bike1=3+3=6. or dp[10]+worker1+bike0=6+|2-1|+|1-2|=6+2=8.
# min of all masks with 2 bits set = min(dp[11])=6 ✓
#
# Worker_idx = popcount(mask) tells us which worker to assign next

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n * m * 2^m). Space O(2^m).
#  Practical for m<=20 with n<=m.
#  Follow-up: Campus Bikes I (#1057) — greedy minimum; doesn't minimise total.
#  Follow-up: if n>m, impossible — each worker needs a unique bike."

1986.title: MINIMUM NUMBER OF WORK SESSIONS TO FINISH THE TASKS  (Bitmask DP)
1986.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Divide tasks into sessions; each session can hold tasks with total time <= sessionTime.
#  Minimise number of sessions. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Tasks can be assigned in any order to any session? Yes. n<=14 → bitmask DP."
#
# "Let me walk: tasks=[1,2,3], sessionTime=3 → 2 sessions: [1,2],[3] ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Backtracking: assign each task to an existing session or a new one. O(n^n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1986_MinWorkSessionsToFinishTasks_Brute:
    def minSessions(self, tasks, sessionTime):
        n=len(tasks); dp=[float('inf')]*(1<<n); dp[0]=0
        session_time=[0]*(1<<n)
        for mask in range(1,1<<n):
            for i in range(n):
                if mask>>i&1:
                    prev=mask^(1<<i)
                    if session_time[prev]+tasks[i]<=sessionTime:
                        if dp[prev]+1<dp[mask] or (dp[prev]+1==dp[mask] and session_time[prev]+tasks[i]<session_time[mask]):
                            dp[mask]=dp[prev]; session_time[mask]=session_time[prev]+tasks[i]
                    else:
                        if dp[prev]+1<dp[mask]:
                            dp[mask]=dp[prev]+1; session_time[mask]=tasks[i]
        return dp[(1<<n)-1]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Bitmask DP — O(n * 2^n). Walk-through:
#  mask = bitmask of completed tasks. dp[mask] = minimum sessions to complete tasks in mask.
#  For each mask from 0 to 2^n-1:
#    For each subset of mask that fits in one session (sum ≤ sessionTime):
#      dp[mask] = min(dp[mask], dp[mask ^ submask] + 1)
#        ← use submask tasks in one new session; remaining = mask ^ submask.
#  Precompute valid submasks (sum ≤ sessionTime) for efficiency.
#  Answer = dp[(1<<n)-1] (all tasks done).
#  WHY bitmask: tasks can be assigned to sessions in any order → need to track which tasks done.
#  Time: O(n * 2^n). Space: O(2^n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1986_MinWorkSessionsToFinishTasks:
    def minSessions(self, tasks, sessionTime):
        n = len(tasks)
        full = (1 << n) - 1
        dp = [float('inf')] * (1 << n)
        remaining = [0] * (1 << n)
        dp[0] = 0
        remaining[0] = sessionTime
        for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
            for i in range(n):
                if not (mask >> i & 1):
                    continue
                prev = mask ^ (1 << i)
                if remaining[prev] >= tasks[i]:
                    new_sessions = dp[prev]
                    new_remaining = remaining[prev] - tasks[i]
                else:
                    new_sessions = dp[prev] + 1
                    new_remaining = sessionTime - tasks[i]
                if new_sessions < dp[mask] or (new_sessions == dp[mask] and new_remaining > remaining[mask]):
                    dp[mask] = new_sessions
                    remaining[mask] = new_remaining
        return dp[full]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minSessions([1,2,3], sessionTime=3)."
# Bitmask DP: dp[mask] = min sessions to complete tasks in mask
# dp[0]=1 (start first session). For each mask, try adding each task to current session.
# OR try opening new session when current overflows.
# dp[0b001]=1 (task 0 in session 1, time 1, remaining 2)
# dp[0b010]=1 (task 1 in session 1, time 2, remaining 1)
# dp[0b011]=1 (tasks 0+1 in session 1, time 3, remaining 0)
# dp[0b100]=1 (task 2 in session 1, time 3 exactly)
# dp[0b101]: task 0+2 = time 4 > 3 → new session needed. dp[0b101]=2
# dp[0b111]=2 (session1: task1+task2=2+3>3? → session1:task0+task1=3, session2:task2=3) ✓ Return 2 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n * 2^n). Space O(2^n).
#  Follow-up: if sessionTime is very large, use bin-packing approximation.
#  Follow-up: Fair Distribution of Cookies (#2305) — same bitmask DP structure."

2305.title: FAIR DISTRIBUTION OF COOKIES  (Bitmask DP)
2305.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Distribute all cookies to k children minimising the maximum cookies any child receives.
#  All cookies must be distributed. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Each bag of cookies goes to exactly one child? Yes. Minimise the maximum bag sum per child."
#
# "Let me walk: cookies=[8,15,10,20,8], k=2 → bags to 2 children: min max = 31 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Backtracking: assign each cookie bag to one of k children. Track max. O(k^n).
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _2305_FairDistributionOfCookies_Brute:
    def distributeCookies(self, cookies, k):
        totals=[0]*k; self_best=[float('inf')]
        def bt(i):
            if i==len(cookies):
                self_best[0]=min(self_best[0],max(totals)); return
            seen=set()
            for j in range(k):
                if totals[j] not in seen:
                    seen.add(totals[j]); totals[j]+=cookies[i]
                    bt(i+1); totals[j]-=cookies[i]
        bt(0); return self_best[0]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Bitmask DP: distribute cookies among k children — O(k * 2^n). Walk-through:
#  dp[mask] = minimum unfairness (max child's total) when cookies in mask are distributed.
#  Process child by child:
#    For each child 1..k: for each mask subset: assign some submask to this child.
#    dp_new[mask] = min over submasks of mask: max(dp_prev[mask^submask], sum(submask)).
#  Precompute sum for each submask.
#  WHY bitmask: n ≤ 8 cookies → 2^8 = 256 states feasible.
#  WHY k passes (per child): distribute one child's allocation per pass.
#  WHY min of max: minimize the maximum (most unfair) distribution.
#  Time: O(k * 3^n) subset enumeration. Space: O(2^n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _2305_FairDistributionOfCookies:
    def distributeCookies(self, cookies, k):
        n = len(cookies)
        subset_sum = [0] * (1 << n)
        for mask in range(1, 1 << n):
            lsb = mask & (-mask)
            bit = lsb.bit_length() - 1
            subset_sum[mask] = subset_sum[mask ^ lsb] + cookies[bit]
        INF = float('inf')
        dp = [[INF] * (1 << n) for _ in range(k + 1)]
        dp[0][0] = 0
        for j in range(1, k + 1):
            for mask in range(1 << n):
                sub = mask
                while sub:
                    if dp[j-1][mask ^ sub] != INF:
                        dp[j][mask] = min(dp[j][mask], max(dp[j-1][mask ^ sub], subset_sum[sub]))
                    sub = (sub - 1) & mask
        return dp[k][(1 << n) - 1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace distributeCookies([8,15,10,20,8], k=2)."
# Bitmask DP: dp[mask] = minimum maximum cookies any child gets for subset 'mask'
# Enumerate all 2^5=32 subsets. For each subset, try assigning to each child.
# dp[0b11111] = min over all k-partitions of cookies → 31 total, split: one child gets 20+15=35, other 8+10+8=26 → max=35?
# Or: 20+8+8=36, 15+10=25 → max=36. Or: 20+10=30, 15+8+8=31 → max=31.
# Best split: 20+15=35 vs 26, or 20+8+8=36 vs 25, or min max=31 (20+10 and 15+8+8)
# Return 31 ✓
# WHY bitmask DP: n≤8 so 2^n feasible; iterate subsets assigning cookies to children.
# dp[mask]=max cookies any child gets for this assignment mask. dp[0]=0. Enumerate sub-subsets: dp[i]=min(dp[i^j]+cookie_sum(j)) over all valid sub-assignments j of i. dp[(1<<n)-1]=answer ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(3^n * k): for each child, iterate over all submasks. Space O(2^n * k).
#  Follow-up: Min Work Sessions (#1986) — same bitmask DP, different cost function.
#  Follow-up: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets (#698) — checks feasibility, not min-max."

3600.title: MAXIMIZE SPANNING TREE STABILITY WITH UPGRADES  (Minimum Spanning Tree)
3600.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  We have edges that can be upgraded. Maximise the stability of the MST, where stability = minimum edge weight in MST after optimal upgrades. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  We can upgrade some edges (improve their weight). MST stability = minimum edge weight in the MST?"
#
# "Let me walk: binary search on target stability; check if MST can be formed with min edge >= target."
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Binary search on the answer (target stability). For each target: can we form a spanning tree using only edges >= target (after upgrades)? Use Kruskal with upgrades counted.
#  O(E log E * α(V)) per binary search step. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _3600_MaximizeSpanningTreeStabilityWithUpgrades_Brute:
    def maxStability(self, n, edges, k):
        # Binary search on minimum edge weight in MST
        weights = sorted(set(e[2] for e in edges))
        def can_achieve(target):
            parent = list(range(n))
            def find(x):
                while parent[x] != x: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]
                return x
            upgrades_needed = 0; edges_used = 0
            for u, v, w, can_upgrade in sorted(edges, key=lambda x: -x[2]):
                if w >= target or (can_upgrade and upgrades_needed < k):
                    pu, pv = find(u), find(v)
                    if pu != pv:
                        parent[pu] = pv; edges_used += 1
                        if w < target: upgrades_needed += 1
            return edges_used == n - 1
        lo, hi = min(e[2] for e in edges), max(e[2] for e in edges)
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2
            if can_achieve(mid): lo = mid
            else: hi = mid - 1
        return lo

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Binary search on answer + Kruskal's feasibility check — O(E log E log W). Walk-through:
#  We want to maximize the minimum edge weight in the spanning tree (max-min-stability).
#  Binary search on the answer 'mid':
#    can_achieve(mid): run Kruskal's using only edges with weight >= mid (after optional upgrades).
#    If MST spans all nodes → feasible. Else → not feasible.
#  Kruskal's: sort edges by weight descending (we want heaviest edges). Union-Find to build MST.
#    Upgraded edges: can use k edges from the upgrade pool to boost weight to allow spanning.
#  Binary search converges to the maximum feasible mid.
#  WHY binary search works: if stability mid is achievable, stability mid-1 is also achievable
#  (monotone property). Binary search finds the boundary.
#  Time: O(E log E log W). Space: O(V)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _3600_MaximizeSpanningTreeStabilityWithUpgrades:
    def maxStability(self, n, edges, k):
        def can_achieve(target):
            parent = list(range(n))
            def find(x):
                while parent[x] != x: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]; x = parent[x]
                return x
            used = upgrades = 0
            for u, v, w, upgradeable in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: -e[2]):
                effective = w >= target or (upgradeable and upgrades < k)
                if effective:
                    pu, pv = find(u), find(v)
                    if pu != pv:
                        parent[pu] = pv; used += 1
                        if w < target: upgrades += 1
            return used == n - 1
        lo = min(e[2] for e in edges); hi = max(e[2] for e in edges)
        while lo < hi:
            mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2
            if can_achieve(mid): lo = mid
            else: hi = mid - 1
        return lo

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace maxStability(n=3, edges=[[0,1,3],[1,2,5],[0,2,2]], upgrades=[[0,1,7]], k=1)."
# Step 1 — base MST via Kruskal (sort by weight):
# edges sorted: [0,2,2],[0,1,3],[1,2,5]. Union-Find: all separate.
# Add [0,2,2]: union(0,2) → MST edges: {[0,2,2]}. cost=2.
# Add [0,1,3]: union(0,1) → MST edges: {[0,2,2],[0,1,3]}. MST complete (n-1=2 edges). min_edge=2.
# Step 2 — try upgrade [0,1]: weight 3→7. New MST: {[0,2,2],[0,1,7]}. min_edge=2 (unchanged).
# Without upgrade: min=2. With upgrade: min=2. Stability=2 ✓.
# If upgrade made [0,2] go from 2→6: new MST min_edge=min(6,3)=3 > 2 → upgrade helps! Return 3.
# WHY bottleneck MST: stability = weakest link; upgrading an MST edge can raise the bottleneck.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(E log E log W). Space O(V).
#  Follow-up: Minimum Spanning Tree (#1135) — standard Kruskal.
#  Follow-up: Find Critical and Pseudo-Critical Edges (#1489) — edge classification in MST."

357.title: COUNT NUMBERS WITH UNIQUE DIGITS  (Digit DP)
357.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count n-digit numbers (including 0) where all digits are unique. n=0 → 1 (just '0'). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  0 counts as a 1-digit number with unique digits? Yes. Numbers <= 10^n."
#
# "Let me walk: n=2 → 91 (0-9: 10, then 2-digit: 9*9=81) ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Count k-digit unique numbers for k=1..n, sum them. O(n) time. This IS optimal.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _357_CountNumbersWithUniqueDigits_Brute:
    def countNumbersWithUniqueDigits(self, n):
        if n==0: return 1
        result=10; unique=9; available=9
        for k in range(2,min(n,10)+1):
            unique*=available; result+=unique; available-=1
        return result

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Digit DP counting unique-digit numbers — O(10). Walk-through:
#  dp[k] = count of k-digit numbers with all unique digits.
#  dp[1] = 9 (1-9, no leading zeros).
#  dp[k] = dp[k-1] * (10 - (k-1))  ← each new digit: 10-(k-1) remaining choices (not used yet).
#  Example: dp[2] = 9*9 = 81 (9 choices first digit × 9 choices second = 9*9).
#  dp[3] = 9*9*8. dp[4] = 9*9*8*7. ... dp[10] = 9*9*8*7*...*1.
#  Total = 1 (number 0) + sum(dp[1..min(n,10)]).
#  WHY stop at 10: more than 10 digits would require repeating a digit (pigeonhole).
#  Time: O(10) = O(1). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _357_CountNumbersWithUniqueDigits:
    def countNumbersWithUniqueDigits(self, n):
        if n == 0:
            return 1
        result = 10
        unique_product = 9
        available = 9
        for _ in range(2, min(n, 10) + 1):
            unique_product *= available
            result += unique_product
            available -= 1
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace countNumbersWithUniqueDigits(n=2)."
# n=0: 1 (just 0). n=1: 10 (digits 0-9). n=2: 10 + 9*9 = 91 ✓
# dp[k]=count of k-digit numbers with all unique digits.
# dp[1]=9 (1-9). dp[2]=9*9=81. dp[3]=9*9*8=648. Multiply available*prev.
# Total for n=2: dp[0]+dp[1]+dp[2]=1+9+81=91 ✓
# dp[i]=dp[i-1]*(10-(i-1)). For i=1: 9*1=9. For i=2: 9*9=81. dp[i] decreasing factor each step.
# Edge: n=0→1. n=1→10. dp[k]=0 for k>10 (only 10 distinct digits exist).
# WHY digit-by-digit DP: first digit has 9 choices (no 0); each subsequent has 10-i choices.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1).
#  For n>=10, no more unique digit numbers exist (only 10 possible digits).
#  Follow-up: Numbers at Most N Given Digit Set (#902) — digit DP variant.
#  Follow-up: Digit DP (#233) — count numbers satisfying digit constraints up to N."

688.title: KNIGHT PROBABILITY IN CHESSBOARD  (Probability DP)
688.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Knight on r×c board at (row,column). After k moves, what's the probability of staying on board? Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Knight moves uniformly at random to any of 8 L-shaped positions? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: n=3, k=2, row=0, column=0 → 0.0625 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[r][c] = probability of being at (r,c). Update for each move.
#  O(k * n²) time. This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _688_KnightProbabilityInChessboard_Brute:
    def knightProbability(self, n, k, row, column):
        dp=[[0]*n for _ in range(n)]; dp[row][column]=1.0
        for _ in range(k):
            new_dp=[[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
            for r in range(n):
                for c in range(n):
                    if not dp[r][c]: continue
                    for dr,dc in [(2,1),(2,-1),(-2,1),(-2,-1),(1,2),(1,-2),(-1,2),(-1,-2)]:
                        nr,nc=r+dr,c+dc
                        if 0<=nr<n and 0<=nc<n:
                            new_dp[nr][nc]+=dp[r][c]/8
            dp=new_dp
        return sum(dp[r][c] for r in range(n) for c in range(n))

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Probability DP over turns — O(k * n²). Walk-through:
#  dp[r][c] = probability knight is at (r,c) at current turn.
#  Initialize dp[row][column] = 1.0.
#  For each of k turns:
#    new_dp = zero matrix of same size.
#    For each (r,c) with dp[r][c] > 0:
#      For each of 8 knight moves (nr,nc):
#        If in bounds: new_dp[nr][nc] += dp[r][c] / 8.
#           ← probability spreads equally among 8 possible moves.
#    dp = new_dp.
#  Return sum of all dp values (total probability still on board).
#  WHY divide by 8: knight chooses uniformly at random among 8 moves.
#  Moves landing off-board are simply not added → probability 'leaks out'.
#  Time: O(k * n²). Space: O(n²)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _688_KnightProbabilityInChessboard:
    def knightProbability(self, n, k, row, column):
        MOVES = [(2,1),(2,-1),(-2,1),(-2,-1),(1,2),(1,-2),(-1,2),(-1,-2)]
        dp = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
        dp[row][column] = 1.0
        for _ in range(k):
            new_dp = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]
            for r in range(n):
                for c in range(n):
                    if dp[r][c] == 0: continue
                    for dr, dc in MOVES:
                        nr, nc = r+dr, c+dc
                        if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n:
                            new_dp[nr][nc] += dp[r][c] / 8.0
            dp = new_dp
        return sum(dp[r][c] for r in range(n) for c in range(n))

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace knightProbability(n=3, k=2, row=0, col=0)."
# dp[r][c] = probability of being on (r,c) after current moves. Initially dp[0][0]=1.0
# After move 1: from (0,0), valid moves: (1,2),(2,1). Each with prob 1/8.
# dp1[1][2]=1/8=0.125, dp1[2][1]=1/8=0.125. All other cells=0.
# After move 2: from (1,2), valid moves: (0,0),(2,0),(3,...)→off-board. On-board: (0,0),(2,0).
# dp2[0][0] += dp1[1][2]/8 = 0.125/8 ≈ 0.0156
# From (2,1), valid moves: (0,0),(0,2). dp2[0][0] += 0.125/8 ≈ 0.0156
# Total prob remaining on board = sum(dp2) ≈ 0.0625 ✓
# WHY DP forward propagation: distribute current probability to reachable next cells.
# Cells going off-board are lost; sum all remaining = answer.
# dp[i][j] probability accumulates: dp_next[i][j]+=dp_cur[r][c]/8 for each valid knight move (r,c)→(i,j). dp[i][j] after k moves = prob of being at (i,j). Sum all dp[i][j] = answer ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(k*n²). Space O(n²).
#  Follow-up: if k is very large, matrix exponentiation achieves O(n² log k).
#  Follow-up: Out of Boundary Paths (#576) — count paths not probabilities."

714.title: BEST TIME TO BUY AND SELL STOCK WITH TRANSACTION FEE  (State Machine DP)
714.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Buy and sell stocks with a transaction fee. Unlimited transactions. Maximise profit. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Pay fee on each sell? Yes. Can hold only one stock at a time? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: prices=[1,3,2,8,4,9], fee=2 → profit=8 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP with two states: cash (not holding) and hold (holding stock).
#  O(n) time. This IS optimal. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _714_BestTimeToBuyAndSellStockWithTransactionFee_Brute:
    def maxProfit(self, prices, fee):
        cash=0; hold=-prices[0]
        for p in prices[1:]:
            cash=max(cash,hold+p-fee)
            hold=max(hold,cash-p)
        return cash

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "State machine DP — O(n). Walk-through:
#  Two states: hold = max profit while holding a stock; cash = max profit while not holding.
#  Initialize: hold = -prices[0], cash = 0.
#  For each price p:
#    hold = max(hold, cash - p)    ← keep holding OR buy today (pay p, deduct from cash).
#    cash = max(cash, hold + p - fee) ← keep cash OR sell today (gain p, pay fee).
#  WHY simultaneous update: we use the PREVIOUS hold/cash values for both transitions
#  (selling and buying on the same day isn't allowed — but in this formulation it's OK
#  because the fee ensures it's never profitable to do so).
#  Answer = cash. Time: O(n). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _714_BestTimeToBuyAndSellStockWithTransactionFee:
    def maxProfit(self, prices, fee):
        cash = 0
        hold = -prices[0]
        for price in prices[1:]:
            cash = max(cash, hold + price - fee)
            hold = max(hold, cash - price)
        return cash

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace bestTimeToBuyAndSellStockWithFee([1,3,2,8,4,9], fee=2)."
# dp[i][0]=max profit NOT holding stock on day i. dp[i][1]=max profit HOLDING stock on day i.
# dp[0][0]=0, dp[0][1]=-1 (bought on day 0).
# Day 1(price=3): dp[1][0]=max(0,-1+3-2)=0, dp[1][1]=max(-1,0-3)=-1.
# Day 3(price=8): dp[3][0]=max(0,-1+8-2)=5, dp[3][1]=max(-1,5-8)=-1.
# Day 5(price=9): dp[5][0]=max(5,1+9-2)=8, dp[5][1]=max(1,8-9)=1. → return dp[5][0]=8 ✓
# dp[i][0]=max(dp[i-1][0], dp[i-1][1]+prices[i]-fee). dp[i][1]=max(dp[i-1][1], dp[i-1][0]-prices[i]).
# WHY two states: holding vs not-holding captures all possible transaction states in O(n).

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: Best Time with Cooldown (#309) — 1-day rest after selling; add cooldown state.
#  Follow-up: At most k transactions (#188) — DP with k states."

172.title: FACTORIAL TRAILING ZEROES  (Maths / Geometry)
172.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count trailing zeros in n!. Each zero comes from a factor of 10 = 2×5. 5s are the bottleneck. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Count how many times 5 divides n! ? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: n=25 → 25//5=5, 25//25=1 → 6 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Compute n! then count trailing zeros by dividing by 10 repeatedly. O(n!) time — impractical for large n.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _172_FactorialTrailingZeroes_Brute:
    def trailingZeroes(self, n):
        count=0
        while n>=5: n//=5; count+=n
        return count

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Count factors of 5 — O(log n). Walk-through:
#  Trailing zeros = min(factors of 2, factors of 5) in n!.
#  Factors of 2 always > factors of 5 → count only factors of 5.
#  Multiples of 5 contribute 1 factor of 5. Multiples of 25 contribute 2 (one extra). Etc.
#  count = n//5 + n//25 + n//125 + ...  until 5^k > n.
#  WHY this sum: n//5 counts all multiples of 5. n//25 counts those that contribute an EXTRA
#  factor (already counted once in n//5). n//125 for triple factors, etc.
#  Example: n=30 → 30//5=6 + 30//25=1 = 7. (5,10,15,20,25,30 → but 25=5² gives extra) ✓
#  Time: O(log n). Space: O(1)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _172_FactorialTrailingZeroes:
    def trailingZeroes(self, n):
        count = 0
        while n >= 5:
            n //= 5
            count += n
        return count

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace trailingZeroes(25)."
# Count factors of 5 in 25!. Every 5th number contributes one 5. Every 25th contributes two.
# 25//5=5 (numbers 5,10,15,20,25). 25//25=1 (number 25 contributes extra 5). 25//125=0.
# Total=5+1=6 ✓ (25!=...×10×15×20×25×...→six trailing zeros).
# trailingZeroes(100): 100//5=20, 100//25=4, 100//125=0. Total=24 ✓
# WHY divide by powers of 5: 2s always outnumber 5s, so only 5s matter for trailing zeros.
# trailingZeroes(0)=0 ✓ (0!=1, no zeros).
# WHY not count 2s: factors of 2 are far more abundant (every even number) → always more 2s than 5s. Only 5s limit trailing zeros.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(log₅ n). Space O(1).
#  Follow-up: count trailing zeros in base b: count factors of smallest prime in b.
#  Follow-up: count factors of 2 — same algorithm; but factors of 5 are always fewer."

204.title: COUNT PRIMES  (Maths / Geometry)
204.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count prime numbers less than n (strictly less). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  n=0 or n=1 → 0? Yes. n=2 → 0 (no prime < 2)? Yes."
#
# "Let me walk: n=10 → primes 2,3,5,7 → 4 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each number, check if prime. O(n√n) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _204_CountPrimes_Brute:
    def countPrimes(self, n):
        if n<2: return 0
        sieve=[True]*n; sieve[0]=sieve[1]=False
        for i in range(2,int(n**0.5)+1):
            if sieve[i]:
                for j in range(i*i,n,i): sieve[j]=False
        return sum(sieve)

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Sieve of Eratosthenes — O(n log log n). Walk-through:
#  is_prime = [True] * n. Mark 0 and 1 as not prime.
#  For p from 2 to sqrt(n):
#    If is_prime[p]: mark all multiples p², p²+p, p²+2p, ... as not prime.
#    (Start from p² because smaller multiples of p were already marked by smaller primes.)
#  Count remaining True values.
#  WHY start marking from p²: p*2, p*3, ..., p*(p-1) were already marked by 2, 3, ..., (p-1).
#  WHY O(n log log n): each prime p marks n/p numbers → sum over primes ≈ n * sum(1/p) ≈ n log log n.
#  Time: O(n log log n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _204_CountPrimes:
    def countPrimes(self, n):
        if n < 2:
            return 0
        is_prime = [True] * n
        is_prime[0] = is_prime[1] = False
        for i in range(2, int(n**0.5) + 1):
            if is_prime[i]:
                for j in range(i*i, n, i):
                    is_prime[j] = False
        return sum(is_prime)

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace countPrimes(10) using Sieve of Eratosthenes."
# sieve = [True]*10; mark sieve[0]=sieve[1]=False
# p=2: mark 4,6,8 → False; sieve=[F,F,T,T,F,T,F,T,F,F]
# p=3: mark 6(done),9 → sieve[9]=False; sieve=[F,F,T,T,F,T,F,T,F,F]
# p=4: already False, skip; p=5: 5²=25≥10, stop outer loop
# Count True: indices 2,3,5,7 → 4 primes ✓
# WHY start inner loop at p²: smaller multiples already marked by earlier primes.
# Edge: n≤2 → return 0 (no primes less than 2).
# Time O(n log log n); space O(n) for sieve array.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log log n). Space O(n).
#  Follow-up: Count Primes in range [l,r] — segmented sieve for large ranges.
#  Follow-up: find nth prime — sieve of appropriate size."

264.title: UGLY NUMBER II  (Maths / Geometry)
264.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the nth ugly number (positive integer with only prime factors 2, 3, 5).
#  1 is the first ugly number. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Generate them in order? Yes. n=1 → 1?"
#
# "Let me walk: first 10 ugly numbers: 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12. n=10 → 12 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  For each number check if ugly; count until nth. O(n * log n) time — very slow for large n.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _264_UglyNumberII_Brute:
    def nthUglyNumber(self, n):
        ugly=[1]; i2=i3=i5=0
        while len(ugly)<n:
            next2,next3,next5=ugly[i2]*2,ugly[i3]*3,ugly[i5]*5
            nxt=min(next2,next3,next5); ugly.append(nxt)
            if nxt==next2: i2+=1
            if nxt==next3: i3+=1
            if nxt==next5: i5+=1
        return ugly[-1]

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Min-heap or three-pointer DP — O(n log n) or O(n). Walk-through (three-pointer):
#  ugly = [1]. i2=i3=i5=0 (pointers into ugly array for ×2, ×3, ×5 candidates).
#  For k in 1..n:
#    next2 = ugly[i2]*2. next3 = ugly[i3]*3. next5 = ugly[i5]*5.
#    nxt = min(next2, next3, next5).
#    ugly.append(nxt).
#    If nxt == next2: i2++.
#    If nxt == next3: i3++.
#    If nxt == next5: i5++.
#  Return ugly[n-1].
#  WHY advance all equal pointers: 6=2×3=3×2 would appear as next2 AND next3 → advance both
#  to avoid duplicates.
#  WHY three pointers: each pointer tracks which ugly number to multiply by 2/3/5 next.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _264_UglyNumberII:
    def nthUglyNumber(self, n):
        ugly = [1]
        i2 = i3 = i5 = 0
        while len(ugly) < n:
            next2, next3, next5 = ugly[i2]*2, ugly[i3]*3, ugly[i5]*5
            nxt = min(next2, next3, next5)
            ugly.append(nxt)
            if nxt == next2: i2 += 1
            if nxt == next3: i3 += 1
            if nxt == next5: i5 += 1
        return ugly[-1]

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace nthUglyNumber(10)."
# Pointers p2=p3=p5=0. ugly=[1].
# Next ugly = min(ugly[p2]*2, ugly[p3]*3, ugly[p5]*5)=min(2,3,5)=2. Advance p2. ugly=[1,2].
# min(4,3,5)=3. Advance p3. ugly=[1,2,3].
# min(4,6,5)=4. Advance p2. ugly=[1,2,3,4].
# min(6,6,5)=5. Advance p5. ugly=[1,2,3,4,5].
# min(6,6,10)=6. Both p2 and p3 give 6 → advance both. ugly=[1,2,3,4,5,6].
# min(8,9,10)=8. ugly=[1,2,3,4,5,6,8]... Continue to 10th: [1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9,10,12]. Return 12 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(n) for the sequence.
#  Follow-up: Super Ugly Number (#313) — arbitrary prime set; k pointers instead of 3.
#  Follow-up: Ugly Number I (#263) — check if a single number is ugly."

611.title: VALID TRIANGLE NUMBER  (Maths / Geometry)
611.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count the number of triplets that can form a valid triangle from nums.
#  Triangle inequality: sum of two sides > third side. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  Values can include 0? Yes — triangles with 0 are invalid. Count ordered? No — triplet indices."
#
# "Let me walk: nums=[2,2,3,4] → [2,2,3],[2,2,4],[2,3,4] → 3 ✓"
# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Sort. For each pair (i,j), binary search for how many k>j satisfy nums[k] < nums[i]+nums[j].
#  O(n² log n). Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _611_ValidTriangleNumber_Brute:
    def triangleNumber(self, nums):
        nums.sort(); count=0
        for k in range(len(nums)-1,1,-1):
            left,right=0,k-1
            while left<right:
                if nums[left]+nums[right]>nums[k]: count+=right-left; right-=1
                else: left+=1
        return count

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
