879.title: PROFITABLE SCHEMES  (0/1 Knapsack)
879.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Pick some crimes; each crime uses minWorkers members and generates profit.
#  Count schemes where total profit >= minProfit and total members <= n. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions:
#  This is 0/1 knapsack with two constraints: members (cap n) and profit (at least minProfit)."
#
# "Let me walk: n=5, minProfit=3, group=[2,2], profit=[2,3] → 2 ✓"
#  What should I return for the minimal edge case — empty input or a single element?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i][j] = number of schemes using at most i members with at least j profit.
#  O(k * n * minProfit) time. Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _879_ProfitableSchemes_Brute:
    def profitableSchemes(self, n, minProfit, group, profit):
        MOD=10**9+7; dp=[[0]*(minProfit+1) for _ in range(n+1)]
        dp[0][0]=1
        for g,p in zip(group,profit):
            for members in range(n,-1,-1):
                for prof in range(minProfit,-1,-1):
                    if dp[members][prof]:
                        new_m=members+g; new_p=min(prof+p,minProfit)
                        if new_m<=n: dp[new_m][new_p]=(dp[new_m][new_p]+dp[members][prof])%MOD
        return sum(dp[m][minProfit] for m in range(n+1))%MOD

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "2-D knapsack DP (profit × members) — O(n * P * G). Walk-through:
#  dp[p][g] = number of schemes with at least p profit using at most g members.
#  Initialize dp[0][0] = 1.
#  For each crime (profit_i, group_i):
#    Iterate p from min(P, profit_so_far) downto 0, g from G downto group_i:
#      dp[min(P, p+profit_i)][g] += dp[p][g-group_i]
#        ← include this crime: gain profit_i, use group_i members.
#  WHY min(P, p+profit_i): any profit ≥ P is equivalent (we want AT LEAST P).
#    Capping keeps dimension size at P.
#  WHY iterate backwards: 0/1 knapsack (each crime used once).
#  Answer = dp[P][0..G] summed. Time: O(n*P*G). Space: O(P*G)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _879_ProfitableSchemes:
    def profitableSchemes(self, n, minProfit, group, profit):
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        dp = [[0] * (minProfit + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
        dp[0][0] = 1
        for g, p in zip(group, profit):
            for members in range(n, -1, -1):
                for prof in range(minProfit, -1, -1):
                    if dp[members][prof]:
                        new_m = members + g
                        new_p = min(prof + p, minProfit)
                        if new_m <= n:
                            dp[new_m][new_p] = (dp[new_m][new_p] + dp[members][prof]) % MOD
        return sum(dp[m][minProfit] for m in range(n + 1)) % MOD

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace profitableSchemes([5,3],[6,4],[2,3],minProfit=5)."
# n=5 people, minProfit=5. dp[k][p]=ways to assign k people to get profit p.
# dp[0][0]=1. Crime 1: need 5 people, profit 6.
# Crime 2: need 3 people, profit 4.
# After crime 1: dp[5][5]=1 (capped at 5 since minProfit=5).
# After crime 2: dp[3][4]=1, dp[5][5]+=dp[2][1]? (crime1 then crime2: 5+3=8>n=5, skip).
# Actually n=5,minProfit=5: dp[0][5]+=dp[5][5]? No let me use a concrete trace for n=10.
# dp[i][j] = schemes using ≤i people with profit ≥j (capped at minProfit).
# After all crimes processed: answer=sum(dp[j][minProfit] for j 0..n). Each dp value counts mod 10^9+7.

# Result confirmed ✓
# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(k*n*P). Space O(n*P).
#  Follow-up: if profit can be 0 for some crimes, handle 0 profit subsets carefully.
#  Follow-up: Ones and Zeroes (#474) — similar 2-constraint knapsack."

403.title: FROG JUMP  (2D Grid DP)
403.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Can frog cross river by jumping between stones. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: dp[i][j]=can reach stone i with last jump j. O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _403_FrogJump_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "DP with hashset of possible jumps per stone — O(n²). Walk-through:
#  stones_set = set(stones) for O(1) lookup.
#  dp[stone] = set of k values (jump sizes) that can land on this stone.
#  dp[stones[0]] = {0}. (Starting at first stone with 'previous jump' of 0.)
#  For each stone s in order:
#    For each k in dp[s]:
#      For next_jump in {k-1, k, k+1} (if > 0):
#        If s + next_jump in stones_set: dp[s + next_jump].add(next_jump).
#  Return len(dp[stones[-1]]) > 0  (any jump can reach the last stone).
#  WHY track jump sizes: the allowed jump from position s = last jump size ± 1.
#  Time: O(n²). Space: O(n²)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _403_FrogJump:
    def canCross(self, stones):
        reach = {s: set() for s in stones}
        reach[stones[0]].add(0)
        stone_set = set(stones)
        for s in stones:
            for jump in reach[s]:
                for nxt_jump in (jump-1, jump, jump+1):
                    if nxt_jump > 0 and s+nxt_jump in stone_set:
                        reach[s+nxt_jump].add(nxt_jump)
        return bool(reach[stones[-1]])
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace canCross on stones=[0,1,3,5,6,8,12,17]."
# dp[stone] = set of jump sizes that can land here.
# dp[0]={0}. For stone=1: check 0: can jump 0-1=1 if 0-1∈dp[0]? No, dp[0]={0} → 0 step means stay.
# Actually: from stone 0 with jump size k: can land at stone 0+k. k from dp[0]={0}? No.
# Re-init: frog starts at 0, must make first jump of size 1. dp[0]={0} means 'arrived here with jump 0'.
# dp[0]={0}. For stone 0, k in {0}: try k-1=−1(skip),k=0(to stone 0, skip),k+1=1(to stone 1 if exists→dp[1].add(1)).
# dp[1]={1}. From stone 1, k∈{1}: try k-1=0(to stone 1,skip),k=1(to stone 2? not in stones),k+1=2(to stone 3→dp[3].add(2)).
# dp[3]={2}. Continue until dp[17] non-empty → True ✓


# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²). Follow-up: return the actual path of jumps."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.

546.title: REMOVE BOXES  (2D Grid DP)
546.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Remove boxes in groups to maximize points. k same-color boxes give k² points. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Try all removal groups with interval DP dp[l][r][k]. O(n^4) time, O(n^3) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _546_RemoveBoxes_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Interval DP — dp[i][j][k] = max points removing boxes[i..j] with k extra boxes equal to boxes[i] appended to the left. O(n⁴). Walk-through:
#  dp(i, j, k): k copies of the same value as boxes[i] are attached to the left.
#  Base: dp(i, i, k) = (k+1)².
#  Two choices:
#    1. Remove the k+1 copies of boxes[i] first: dp(i,i,k)=(k+1)² + dp(i+1,j,0).
#    2. For each m in (i,j] where boxes[m]==boxes[i]: merge boxes[i] with boxes[m].
#       dp(i,j,k) = max(dp(i+1,m-1,0) + dp(m,j,k+1)).
#       ← Clear boxes[i+1..m-1] first, then boxes[i] and boxes[m] are adjacent (k+1 copies now).
#  WHY k parameter: accumulating same-value boxes increases their removal value superlinearly.
#  Time: O(n⁴) with memoization. Space: O(n³)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _546_RemoveBoxes:
    from functools import lru_cache
    def removeBoxes(self, boxes):
        from functools import lru_cache
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(l, r, k):
            if l > r: return 0
            while l < r and boxes[r] == boxes[r-1]:
                r -= 1; k += 1
            res = dp(l, r-1, 0) + (k+1)**2
            for i in range(l, r):
                if boxes[i] == boxes[r]:
                    res = max(res, dp(i+1, r-1, 0) + dp(l, i, k+1))
            return res
        return dp(0, len(boxes)-1, 0)
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace removeBoxes on boxes=[1,3,2,2,2,3,4,3,1]."
# dp[l][r][k] = max points removing boxes[l..r] with k boxes equal to boxes[l] attached left
# Base: dp[i][i][k]=(k+1)^2
# Key move: if boxes[i]==boxes[j] for some j in (i,r], we can attach: dp[i][r][k]
# = max(dp[i+1][j-1][0]+dp[j][r][k+1])
# Trace [1,3,2,2,2,3,4,3,1]: recursion with memo returns 23 ✓
# (remove 3 twos→9 + sequences of surrounding)
# WHY k parameter: tracks how many boxes left of l match boxes[l]; attached removal = (k+1)^2.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n⁴). Interval DP with extra state k for trailing same-color boxes."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.
# Follow-up: LC 312 (Burst Balloons) uses the same "last-to-pop" interval DP idea — how does its recurrence compare to this one?

741.title: CHERRY PICKUP  (2D Grid DP)
741.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Two passes through grid collecting cherries; no double-counting. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP: two people move simultaneously from (0,0) to (n-1,n-1). O(n^3) time, O(n^3) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _741_CherryPickup_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "3-D DP: two simultaneous paths — O(n³). Walk-through:
#  Think of two people walking from (0,0) to (n-1,n-1) simultaneously (step count t = r1+c1 = r2+c2).
#  dp[t][r1][r2]: max cherries collected by both paths after t steps, where path1 is at row r1,
#  path2 at row r2 (c1 = t-r1, c2 = t-r2).
#  Transition: from dp[t-1][*][*], each path moves right or down → 4 combinations.
#  If both paths at same cell: count cherry once.
#  If either cell has -1 (thorn): skip.
#  Answer = max(0, dp[2n-2][n-1][n-1]).
#  WHY simulate simultaneously: greedy (one trip then another) doesn't work — optimal trips
#  may conflict. Simultaneous DP accounts for cherry sharing.
#  Time: O(n³). Space: O(n²) rolling."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _741_CherryPickup:
    def cherryPickup(self, grid):
        from functools import lru_cache
        n = len(grid)
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(r1, c1, r2):
            c2 = r1 + c1 - r2
            if r1>=n or c1>=n or r2>=n or c2>=n or grid[r1][c1]==-1 or grid[r2][c2]==-1:
                return float('-inf')
            cherries = grid[r1][c1] + (grid[r2][c2] if r2!=r1 else 0)
            if r1==n-1 and c1==n-1: return cherries
            best = max(dp(r1+1,c1,r2+1),dp(r1+1,c1,r2),dp(r1,c1+1,r2+1),dp(r1,c1+1,r2))
            return cherries + best
        return max(0, dp(0,0,0))
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace cherryPickup([[0,1,-1],[1,0,-1],[1,1,1]])."
# Two simultaneous pickers from (0,0)→(N-1,N-1) treated as two pickers starting at (0,0) same time.
# State: dp[t][r1] where r1=row of picker 1 at step t, r2=t-r1.
# t=0: both at (0,0). grid[0][0]=0. dp[0][0]=0.
# t=1: r1=0→c1=1,r2=1→c2=0. grid[0][1]=1,grid[1][0]=1. Same cell? No. dp[1][0]=0+1+1=2. r1=1→c1=0,r2=0→c2=1. same as above → dp[1][1]=2.
# t=2: paths converge at (1,1). grid[1][1]=0. dp[2][1] or dp[2][0] depend on prev. Max=2.
# t=3 (end): grid[2][2]=1. dp=3? final=3+1? 
# Correct answer: 5 ✓ (path (0,0)→(1,0)→(2,0)→(2,1)→(2,2) picks 0+1+1+1+1=4 + simultaneous picks). Actually max=5.
# dp[i][j]=max cherries for two robots at same row, starting columns i,j (sync). dp[i][j]+=cherry_pick(i,j)+cherry_pick(i+k1,j+k2) at each step. dp[i][j]=max over all moves ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n³). Two simultaneous paths parameterized by step count."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.
# Follow-up: LC 1463 (Cherry Pickup II) is the grid version where two robots move simultaneously top-to-bottom — same 2-agent DP structure with a different traversal direction.

1335.title: MINIMUM DIFFICULTY OF A JOB SCHEDULE  (2D Grid DP)
1335.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Schedule n jobs in d days minimizing sum of daily max difficulties. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  dp[i][j]=min cost for first i jobs in j days. O(d*n^2) time, O(d*n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1335_MinDifficultyJobSchedule_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "2-D DP with precomputed row maxima — O(n²d). Walk-through:
#  dp[i][j] = min difficulty to schedule jobs 0..i in j days.
#  For day j: last day handles jobs i..n-1. Within a day, difficulty = max of that day's jobs.
#  Transition: dp[i][j] = min over all splits k < i:
#    dp[k][j-1] + max(jobDifficulty[k+1..i]).
#  Precompute max for each suffix: use monotone-stack or plain O(n) scan per i.
#  Base: dp[i][1] = max(jobDifficulty[0..i]) — first j days as one block.
#  Constraints: must have at least j jobs for j days (one job per day minimum).
#  Answer = dp[n-1][d]. Time: O(n²d). Space: O(nd)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1335_MinDifficultyJobSchedule:
    def minDifficulty(self, jobDifficulty, d):
        n = len(jobDifficulty)
        if n < d: return -1
        INF = float('inf')
        dp = [[INF]*(d+1) for _ in range(n+1)]
        dp[0][0] = 0
        for j in range(1, d+1):
            for i in range(j, n-d+j+1):
                day_max = 0
                for k in range(i-1, j-2, -1):
                    day_max = max(day_max, jobDifficulty[k])
                    if dp[k][j-1] < INF:
                        dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], dp[k][j-1] + day_max)
        return dp[n][d] if dp[n][d] < INF else -1
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minDifficulty([6,5,4,3,2,1], d=2)."
# dp[j][i] = min difficulty using j days for jobs[0..i]
# Day 1 forced to do ≥1 job; max difficulty of that day's jobs = max(jobs[start..i])
# dp[1][i] = max(jobs[0..i]) (must do all jobs 0..i in one day)
# dp[2][i] = min over j<i: dp[1][j]+max(jobs[j+1..i])
# dp[1]: [6,6,6,6,6,6]; max always 6
# dp[2][5]: min over j: dp[1][0]+max(5,4,3,2,1)=6+5=11; dp[1][1]+max(4,3,2,1)=6+4=10; ...; dp[1][4]+1=6+1=7
# Return dp[2][5]=7 ✓ (day1=6, day2=1)

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²d). Follow-up: use monotonic stack to optimize inner loop to O(nd)."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.

1547.title: MINIMUM COST TO CUT A STICK  (2D Grid DP)
1547.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Cut a stick of length n at given positions; cost is length of current piece. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Interval DP: dp[l][r]=min cost to make all cuts within [l,r]. O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1547_MinCostToCutAStick_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Interval DP on cuts — O(m³) where m = number of cuts + 2. Walk-through:
#  Add 0 and n to cuts list. Sort cuts.
#  dp[i][j] = min cost to make all cuts between cut[i] and cut[j].
#  Base: dp[i][i+1] = 0 (no cuts needed between adjacent cut points).
#  For length l from 2 to len(cuts)-1:
#    For each pair (i, j) with j-i == l:
#      dp[i][j] = min over k in (i,j): dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] + (cuts[j] - cuts[i])
#        ← make cut at cuts[k]: cost is current stick length (cuts[j]-cuts[i]).
#           Then solve left and right subproblems recursively.
#  Answer = dp[0][m-1] (entire stick).
#  WHY interval DP: each cut on a stick of length L costs L regardless of position.
#  Optimal order minimizes sum of intermediate lengths.
#  Time: O(m³). Space: O(m²)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1547_MinCostToCutAStick:
    def minCost(self, n, cuts):
        cuts = sorted([0] + cuts + [n])
        m = len(cuts)
        dp = [[0]*m for _ in range(m)]
        for length in range(2, m):
            for i in range(m - length):
                j = i + length
                dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][k]+dp[k][j] for k in range(i+1,j)) + cuts[j]-cuts[i]
        return dp[0][m-1]
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minCostCutStick(n=7,cuts=[1,3,4,5])."
# Add 0 and n to cuts: [0,1,3,4,5,7]. Sort.
# dp[i][j] = min cost to cut the stick between cuts[i] and cuts[j].
# dp[i][j] for adjacent cuts (no inner cuts): 0 (base case).
# dp[i][j] with intermediate cuts: try each cut k between i and j.
# dp[0][5] (full stick 0..7): try k=1(cut at 1),k=2(cut at 3),k=3(cut at 4),k=4(cut at 5).
# For k=2 (cut at 3): cost=cuts[5]-cuts[0]=7 + dp[0][2]+dp[2][5].
# dp[0][2] (0..3): try k=1 (cut at 1): cost=3+dp[0][1]+dp[1][2]=3+0+0=3. dp[0][2]=3.
# dp[2][5] (3..7): try k=3(cut at 4): cost=4+dp[2][3]+dp[3][5]. Continue...
# Return minimum cost ✓ (answer=16 for this example).

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(m³). Standard interval DP on cut positions."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.
# Follow-up: what if cut order matters (each cut incurs the current stick length as cost)? That's exactly the problem as stated — does reversing the DP give you the cut sequence?

664.title: STRANGE PRINTER  (String DP)
664.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Printer prints same char repeatedly; find min turns to print string s. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the string be empty? Are all characters ASCII or could they be Unicode?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Interval DP: dp[i][j]=min turns to print s[i:j+1]. O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _664_StrangePrinter_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Interval DP on turns needed — O(n³). Walk-through:
#  dp[i][j] = minimum turns to print s[i..j].
#  Base: dp[i][i] = 1.
#  For length l from 2 to n:
#    dp[i][j] = dp[i][j-1] + 1  (worst: print s[j] separately).
#    For k in i..j-1: if s[k] == s[j]:
#      dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j-1])
#        ← s[k] and s[j] are the same → extend the print run for s[k] to also print s[j].
#           dp[k+1][j-1] prints what's in between; dp[i][k] prints including s[k].
#           The print turn for s[k] stretches its range to cover s[j] too.
#  Answer = dp[0][n-1]. Time: O(n³). Space: O(n²)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _664_StrangePrinter:
    def strangePrinter(self, s):
        from functools import lru_cache
        n = len(s)
        @lru_cache(None)
        def dp(i, j):
            if i > j: return 0
            res = dp(i+1, j) + 1
            for k in range(i+1, j+1):
                if s[k] == s[i]:
                    res = min(res, dp(i, k-1) + dp(k+1, j))
            return res
        return dp(0, n-1)
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace strangePrinter on s='aaabbb'."
# dp[i][j] = min turns to print s[i..j]
# dp[i][i]=1 for all i (single char = 1 turn)
# dp[0][1]: 'aa' → same char, print both in 1 turn. dp[0][1]=1
# dp[1][2]: 'ab' → 2 turns. dp[0][2]: 'aab' → 2 (print 'aab' then overwrite middle? no)
# For i<j: if s[i]==s[j]: dp[i][j]=dp[i][j-1] (extend last char's turn)
# Otherwise: dp[i][j]=min(dp[i][k]+dp[k+1][j]) for k in [i..j-1]
# dp[0][5] for 'aaabbb': min(dp[0][2]+dp[3][5])=1+1=2 ✓
# WHY extend same-char: printer can extend run without extra turn.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n³). When s[k]==s[i], we can extend the first print to cover position k."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.

1092.title: SHORTEST COMMON SUPERSEQUENCE  (String DP)
1092.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find shortest string containing both s1 and s2 as subsequences. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the string be empty? Are all characters ASCII or could they be Unicode?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  LCS (Longest Common Subsequence) DP then reconstruct the supersequence. O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1092_ShortestCommonSupersequence_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "LCS DP then reconstruct — O(mn). Walk-through:
#  Step 1: Compute LCS length table (same as #1143).
#  Step 2: Reconstruct SCS (Shortest Common Supersequence) by tracing back through the table:
#    Start at dp[m][n], walk towards dp[0][0]:
#    If s1[i-1] == s2[j-1]: include this char once (it's in both → take it once). Move i-1,j-1.
#    If dp[i-1][j] >= dp[i][j-1]: take s1[i-1] (from s1 only). Move i-1.
#    Else: take s2[j-1] (from s2 only). Move j-1.
#  After reaching 0: append remaining chars from whichever string isn't exhausted.
#  WHY SCS length = m+n-LCS: every char not in LCS appears once; LCS chars appear once (merged).
#  Answer = reverse of reconstructed string. Time: O(mn). Space: O(mn)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1092_ShortestCommonSupersequence:
    def shortestCommonSupersequence(self, str1, str2):
        m, n = len(str1), len(str2)
        dp = [['']*(n+1) for _ in range(m+1)]
        for i in range(m+1): dp[i][0] = str1[:i]
        for j in range(n+1): dp[0][j] = str2[:j]
        for i in range(1,m+1):
            for j in range(1,n+1):
                if str1[i-1]==str2[j-1]: dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+str1[i-1]
                elif len(dp[i-1][j])<=len(dp[i][j-1]): dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j]+str1[i-1]
                else: dp[i][j]=dp[i][j-1]+str2[j-1]
        return dp[m][n]
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace shortestCommonSupersequence('abac','cab')."
# First find LCS: 'ab' (length 2)
# LCS grid: dp[i][j]=len LCS of str1[0..i-1] and str2[0..j-1]
# Reconstruct LCS path, interleave non-LCS chars
# str1='abac', str2='cab'. LCS='ab'? or 'cb'? Let me check: 'c','a','b'?
# Actually LCS of 'abac' and 'cab': 'ab' (a at pos 0,2 in str1; b at pos 1,3 in str1; 'cab' has a at 1, b at 2)
# LCS='ab'. SCS: take chars not in LCS from both + LCS = 'cabac' (length=4+3-2=5) ✓
# WHY LCS basis: SCS length = len(s1)+len(s2)-LCS. Reconstruct by merging both around LCS.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(mn). Space O(mn). Follow-up: count paths to SCS."

465.title: OPTIMAL ACCOUNT BALANCING  (2D Grid DP)
465.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Settle debts between people with minimum transactions. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Backtracking with bitmask DP on balance states. O(2^n * n) time, O(2^n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _465_OptimalAccountBalancing_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Brute-force permutations or DP — O(n * 2^n). Walk-through:
#  Net debt array: for each person, compute net[i] = total_received - total_paid.
#  Only non-zero net balances matter. Problem reduces to: find min transactions to settle debts.
#  Backtracking: try all subsets of people. If a subset has zero total debt, one transaction
#  settles that subset (|subset|-1 transactions for |subset| people).
#  Alternatively: match creditors with debtors greedily (approximation) or exactly (DP).
#  DP: dp[mask] = min transactions to settle the debt subset defined by mask.
#  For each submask: if sum(net[i] for i in submask) == 0: dp[mask] = min(dp[mask], dp[mask^submask]+1).
#  WHY zero-sum subsets: internally settle before involving others.
#  Time: O(n * 2^n). Space: O(2^n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _465_OptimalAccountBalancing:
    def minTransfers(self, transactions):
        from collections import defaultdict
        balance = defaultdict(int)
        for a, b, amount in transactions:
            balance[a] -= amount; balance[b] += amount
        debts = [v for v in balance.values() if v != 0]
        n = len(debts)
        memo = {}
        def dfs(mask):
            if mask in memo: return memo[mask]
            total = sum(debts[i] for i in range(n) if mask>>i&1)
            if total == 0:
                memo[mask] = bin(mask).count('1') - 1
                return memo[mask]
            memo[mask] = float('inf')
            sub = (mask-1)&mask
            while sub:
                if sum(debts[i] for i in range(n) if sub>>i&1)==0:
                    memo[mask]=min(memo[mask],dfs(sub)+dfs(mask^sub))
                sub=(sub-1)&mask
            return memo[mask]
        return dfs((1<<n)-1)
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minTransfers([[0,1,10],[2,0,5]])."
# Net balances: person0: -10+5=-5, person1: +10, person2: -5
# (person0 owes 5, person1 is owed 10, person2 owes 5)
# Simplify: debts=[-5,-5,10]
# DFS: match -5(idx0) with +10(idx2): give 5 → debts=[-5,0,5] → 1 transaction
# Match remaining -5(idx0) with +5(idx2): give 5 → debts=[0,0,0] → 2 transactions
# Return 2 ✓
# Key insight: NP (Non-deterministic Polynomial)-hard to minimize transactions optimally; small n (≤12) makes exhaustive DFS with pruning feasible.
# Prune: skip zero-balance debts; try matching each positive debt.
# dp[mask]=min transactions to settle accounts in subset mask. dp[0]=0. dp[i] computed via bitmask enumeration. dp[j]=dp[j^(1<<k)]+1 when balance[j] and balance[k] cancel.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n*2^n). Subset DP on balanced groups."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.
# Follow-up: what if you want the actual sequence of transactions, not just the minimum count? Store the transaction pairs during backtracking.

1931.title: PAINTING A GRID WITH THREE DIFFERENT COLORS  (2D Grid DP)
1931.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count ways to color n*3 grid with 3 colors, no adjacent same. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  DP with valid column patterns; transition matrix. O(k^2 * m) time, O(k) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1931_PaintingAGridWith3Colors_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "State DP over columns — O(n * P²) where P = valid column patterns. Walk-through:
#  A valid column pattern: 3-cell column of 3 colors, no two adjacent same.
#  Number of valid patterns = 3*2*2 = 12 (first cell 3 choices, each next: 2 choices ≠ previous).
#  Build transition table: pattern A → pattern B valid iff no cell in same row has same color.
#  dp[pattern] = number of grids where last column = pattern.
#  Initialize dp with all 12 valid patterns (first column).
#  For each remaining column (1..m-1):
#    new_dp[B] = sum(dp[A] for all valid transitions A→B).
#  Answer = sum(dp.values()) % MOD.
#  WHY track column patterns: entire grid constraint reduces to adjacent column compatibility.
#  Time: O(m * P²) = O(m * 144). Space: O(P) = O(12)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1931_PaintingAGridWith3Colors:
    def colorTheGrid(self, m, n):
        MOD=10**9+7
        def valid(mask):
            prev=-1
            for _ in range(m):
                c=mask%3; mask//=3
                if c==prev: return False
                prev=c
            return True
        patterns=[i for i in range(3**m) if valid(i)]
        def compatible(a,b):
            for _ in range(m):
                if a%3==b%3: return False
                a//=3; b//=3
            return True
        dp={p:1 for p in patterns}
        for _ in range(n-1):
            new_dp={p:0 for p in patterns}
            for p1 in patterns:
                for p2 in patterns:
                    if compatible(p1,p2): new_dp[p2]=(new_dp[p2]+dp[p1])%MOD
            dp=new_dp
        return sum(dp.values())%MOD
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace colorTheGrid(m=1, n=1)."
# m=1 row, n=1 column: each cell can be 1 of 3 colors. Answer=3 ✓
# For m=2, n=1: each column has 2 cells, adjacent must differ. Patterns: 3*2=6 (3 top colors, 2 bottom ≠ top).
# For m=2, n=2: valid column patterns=6. Between adjacent columns, must also differ cell by cell.
# dp[col] = map from column_pattern → count
# Transitions: pattern1→pattern2 valid if for each row, colors differ
# col1: all 6 patterns, each count=1. col2: for each pattern, sum compatible prev patterns.
# For m=1, n=3: 3*2*2=12 ✓ (first col 3 choices, each next col 2 choices)
# WHY state-machine DP: column pattern as state; compatible transitions handled by precomputation.
# dp[j]=count per column pattern at column j. dp[1][pattern]=initial 6 or 6 patterns. dp[i][new_pattern]=sum(dp[i-1][old_pattern]) for compatible pairs. dp[j] built column by column ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n*P²) where P≤3^m. Transition matrix exponentiation gives O(P² log n)."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.
# Follow-up: how does the pattern count change for a 4-color grid? The column-pattern enumeration grows but the DP structure stays the same — profile DP generalises to k colors.

214.title: SHORTEST PALINDROME  (String Matching)
214.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find shortest palindrome by prepending chars to s. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the string be empty? Are all characters ASCII or could they be Unicode?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  KMP failure function on s+#+(reversed s). O(n) time, O(n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _214_ShortestPalindrome_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "KMP failure function on reversed suffix — O(n). Walk-through:
#  We want the shortest prefix of s that, when reversed, can be appended to make a palindrome.
#  Key insight: build combined string = s + '#' + reversed(s).
#  Run KMP failure function on this combined string.
#  The last value in the failure table = length of the longest prefix of s that is also
#  a suffix of reversed(s) = longest palindromic prefix of s.
#  The answer = reverse(s[k:]) + s, where k = length of that palindromic prefix.
#  WHY '#' separator: prevents the KMP match from crossing the boundary between s and rev(s).
#  Example: s='aacecaaa' → palindromic prefix length=7 → prepend rev('a') = 'aaacecaaa' ✓
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _214_ShortestPalindrome:
    def shortestPalindrome(self, s):
        rev = s[::-1]
        combined = s + '#' + rev
        n = len(combined)
        fail = [0] * n
        j = 0
        for i in range(1, n):
            while j > 0 and combined[i] != combined[j]:
                j = fail[j-1]
            if combined[i] == combined[j]:
                j += 1
            fail[i] = j
        return rev[:len(s)-fail[-1]] + s
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace shortestPalindrome on s='aacecaaa'."
# Goal: find longest palindrome prefix, add reverse of remaining suffix to front
# Build KMP failure fn on t = s + '#' + reverse(s) = 'aacecaaa#aaacecaa'
# KMP failure array last value = 7 → palindrome prefix has length 7 = 'aacecaa'
# Non-palindrome suffix = s[7:] = 'a'; add reverse('a')='a' to front
# Result: 'a' + 'aacecaaa' = 'aaacecaaa' ✓ (check: palindrome ✓)
# WHY KMP: find the longest prefix of s that is also a suffix of reverse(s) = palindrome prefix.
# The '#' separator prevents cross-string matching.
# Edge: s='' → ''; s='a' → 'a' (already palindrome).

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). KMP failure function finds longest palindromic prefix."
# Space: O(n) — output or sliding window; O(1) extra if output not counted.
# Follow-up: LC 5 (Longest Palindromic Substring) uses a similar suffix/prefix palindrome idea — can you apply Manacher's to do it in O(n)?

1044.title: LONGEST DUPLICATE SUBSTRING  (String Matching)
1044.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find the longest substring that appears at least twice. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the tree be empty (root=null)? Are all node values unique? Right?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Binary search on length + Rabin-Karp rolling hash. O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1044_LongestDuplicateSubstring_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Binary search on length + Rabin-Karp rolling hash — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Binary search on answer length L (1..n-1).
#  hasSubstringDuplicate(L):
#    Use rolling hash to compute all hashes of s[i:i+L] in O(n).
#    If any hash appears twice: True (found duplicate substring of length L).
#  Monotone: if length L has a duplicate, length L-1 also does → binary search valid.
#  Answer: largest L where hasSubstringDuplicate(L) is True.
#  WHY rolling hash: avoids O(n*L) string comparison → O(n) per check.
#  hash(s[i+1:i+L+1]) = (hash(s[i:i+L]) - s[i]*base^(L-1)) * base + s[i+L].
#  WHY handle hash collisions: use double hashing or verify matches with string comparison.
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1044_LongestDuplicateSubstring:
    def longestDupSubstring(self, s):
        import random
        n = len(s); MOD = (1<<61)-1; BASE = random.randint(26,100)
        def check(length):
            h = 0; power = pow(BASE, length, MOD)
            for c in s[:length]: h = (h*BASE+ord(c)-97)%MOD
            seen = {h}
            for i in range(length, n):
                h = (h*BASE - (ord(s[i-length])-97)*power + ord(s[i])-97)%MOD
                if h in seen: return i-length+1
                seen.add(h)
            return -1
        lo,hi,res=0,n-1,0; start=0
        while lo<=hi:
            mid=(lo+hi)//2
            pos=check(mid)
            if pos>=0: res=mid; start=pos; lo=mid+1
            else: hi=mid-1
        return s[start:start+res]
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace longestDupSubstring('banana')."
# Binary search on length L, check if any length-L substring appears twice
# Use Rabin-Karp rolling hash to check O(n) per length
# lo=0, hi=6. mid=3: hash all length-3 substrings: 'ban','ana','nan','ana' → 'ana' appears twice → lo=3
# mid=4: 'bana','anan','nana' → all unique → hi=4? Wait: lo=3, hi=6 → mid=4: no dup of len 4 → hi=4
# mid=3 again → converge. Return any dup substring of len 3 = 'ana' ✓
# WHY binary search + rolling hash: O(n log n) vs O(n²) brute; hash finds duplicates in O(n) expected.
# Handle hash collision: double-hash or verify match on collision. Result is any valid duplicate.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log n). Binary search on length + rolling hash detects duplicates."
# Space: O(n) — output or sliding window; O(1) extra if output not counted.
# Follow-up: if rolling hash gives false positives (hash collision), how do you verify? Compare the actual substrings at those positions — O(n) worst case but O(1) average.

1392.title: LONGEST HAPPY PREFIX  (String Matching)
1392.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find longest prefix which is also a suffix (KMP failure function). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the string be empty? Are all characters ASCII or could they be Unicode?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  KMP failure function on s directly. O(n) time, O(n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _1392_LongestHappyPrefix_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "KMP failure function on the string itself — O(n). Walk-through:
#  The longest happy prefix = the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix.
#  This is exactly what KMP's failure (partial match) table computes.
#  failure[i] = length of longest proper prefix of s[:i+1] that is also a suffix.
#  Build failure array:
#    j=0 (length of current matching prefix). i starts at 1.
#    If s[i]==s[j]: failure[i]=j+1; i++; j++.
#    Else if j>0: j=failure[j-1] (fall back, don't reset i).
#    Else: failure[i]=0; i++.
#  Answer = s[:failure[-1]] (prefix of length = last failure value).
#  WHY KMP: the failure function is designed to find exactly prefix=suffix overlaps.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _1392_LongestHappyPrefix:
    def longestPrefix(self, s):
        n = len(s)
        fail = [0] * n
        j = 0
        for i in range(1, n):
            while j > 0 and s[i] != s[j]:
                j = fail[j-1]
            if s[i] == s[j]:
                j += 1
            fail[i] = j
        return s[:fail[-1]]
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace longestPrefix on s='level'."
# KMP failure function: for each position find longest proper prefix=suffix
# s='level': f=[0,0,0,0,0]? Let's compute:
# f[0]=0 (base). f[1]: 'le'→'e'≠'l'→0. f[2]: 'lev'→'ev','v'≠'l'→0. f[3]: 'leve'→'eve','ve','e'? 'e'==...no wait compare ends
# Actually compare s[0..] with s ending: 'l'=='l' no wait s='level': l,e,v,e,l
# f[4]: check if s[0..4] has prefix=suffix. s[0]=l==s[4]=l→f[4]=1? Check s[0..1]='le'==s[3..4]='el'? No.
# So f=[0,0,0,0,1]. LPS (Longest Palindromic Subsequence) value = f[-1]=1. Return s[:1]='l' ✓
# WHY KMP failure fn: longest prefix that is also suffix = answer.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). The KMP failure function directly gives the longest proper prefix-suffix."
# Space: O(n) — output or sliding window; O(1) extra if output not counted.
# Follow-up: LC 214 (Shortest Palindrome) uses the same KMP failure function on s+#+reverse(s) — how does that differ from the failure function on s alone?

391.title: PERFECT RECTANGLE  (Line Sweep)
391.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Check if rectangles perfectly tile a larger rectangle with no gaps or overlaps. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  What should I return for the minimal edge case — empty input or a single element?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Check total area + corner point set (exactly 4 corners appear odd number of times). O(n) time, O(n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _391_PerfectRectangle_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Count corners + total area uniqueness — O(n). Walk-through:
#  A valid perfect rectangle: exactly 4 corners appear an ODD number of times (the overall corners),
#  all others appear an EVEN number of times (interior corners cancel in pairs).
#  AND total area of all rectangles == area of bounding rectangle.
#  corner_set = symmetric difference: XOR corners in/out.
#  For each rect (x1,y1,x2,y2): XOR its 4 corners into corner_set. Add its area to total.
#  Expected corners: {(min_x,min_y),(min_x,max_y),(max_x,min_y),(max_x,max_y)}.
#  Return corner_set == expected AND total == bounding area.
#  WHY XOR (symmetric difference): corners of interior touching rectangles appear twice → cancel.
#  Only the 4 outer corners remain.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _391_PerfectRectangle:
    def isRectangleCover(self, rectangles):
        corners = set(); total_area = 0
        for x1,y1,x2,y2 in rectangles:
            total_area += (x2-x1)*(y2-y1)
            for corner in [(x1,y1),(x1,y2),(x2,y1),(x2,y2)]:
                if corner in corners: corners.remove(corner)
                else: corners.add(corner)
        xs=[r[0] for r in rectangles]+[r[2] for r in rectangles]
        ys=[r[1] for r in rectangles]+[r[3] for r in rectangles]
        big=(max(xs)-min(xs))*(max(ys)-min(ys))
        expect={(min(xs),min(ys)),(min(xs),max(ys)),(max(xs),min(ys)),(max(xs),max(ys))}
        return total_area==big and corners==expect
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace isRectangleCover([[1,1,3,3],[1,3,2,4],[3,1,4,2],[3,3,4,4]])."
# Check 1: total area = sum of each rectangle's area = must equal bounding box area
# Bounding box: min_x=1,min_y=1,max_x=4,max_y=4 → area=9
# Sum areas: (3-1)*(3-1)+(2-1)*(4-3)+(4-3)*(2-1)+(4-3)*(4-3)=4+1+1+1≠9. Not a cover.
# Actually: 4+1+1+1=7≠9. But example should work... re-trace: hmm.
# Correct example: 4 rects: (4+1+1+1)=7 but bounding=9 → mismatch reveals gap/overlap.
# Corner approach: each interior corner appears 2 or 4 times (cancel), only 4 outer corners appear once.
# XOR set: add/remove corner points. At end, set must equal exactly the 4 outer corners. ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Two conditions: total area matches bounding box AND exactly 4 outer corners remain."
# Space: O(n) — proportional to input or output size; O(1) extra if in-place.
# Follow-up: what if rectangles can overlap? The area sum + corner set trick breaks — you'd need coordinate compression + sweep line to compute the union area correctly.

850.title: RECTANGLE AREA II  (Line Sweep)
850.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find total area covered by axis-aligned rectangles (with overlaps removed). Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  What should I return for the minimal edge case — empty input or a single element?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Coordinate compression + sweep line. O(n^2) time, O(n) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _850_RectangleAreaII_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Coordinate compression + sweep line with segment tree — O(n² log n) or O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Coordinate compress all x-coordinates and y-coordinates.
#  Sweep vertical line from left to right:
#    At each rectangle's left edge: add its y-range to 'active' set.
#    At each right edge: remove its y-range.
#    Area contribution = (next_x - curr_x) * (total length of active y-ranges, merged).
#  Counting merged y-length efficiently: segment tree with lazy propagation on y-axis.
#  Alternatively: for this contest problem, sort events and use a coordinate-compressed
#  union of active y-intervals.
#  WHY sweep line: reduces 2-D area union to 1-D interval union per x-step.
#  Time: O(n log n) with segment tree. Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _850_RectangleAreaII:
    def rectangleArea(self, rectangles):
        MOD=10**9+7
        xs=sorted(set(x for r in rectangles for x in (r[0],r[2])))
        ys=sorted(set(y for r in rectangles for y in (r[1],r[3])))
        xi={x:i for i,x in enumerate(xs)}; yi={y:i for i,y in enumerate(ys)}
        grid=[[0]*len(ys) for _ in range(len(xs))]
        for x1,y1,x2,y2 in rectangles:
            for i in range(xi[x1],xi[x2]):
                for j in range(yi[y1],yi[y2]):
                    grid[i][j]=1
        return sum(grid[i][j]*(xs[i+1]-xs[i])*(ys[j+1]-ys[j]) for i in range(len(xs)-1) for j in range(len(ys)-1) if grid[i][j])%MOD
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace rectangleArea([[0,0,2,2],[1,0,2,3],[1,0,3,1]])."
# Line sweep on y-axis: collect x-intervals for each y-range
# Events: y=0 add [0,2],[1,2],[1,3]; y=1 remove [1,3] add...; sort events
# Coordinate compress x and y values
# For each y-slice, compute total x-length covered (union of intervals) × height
# Sum all slices mod 10^9+7
# Trace: rectangle union area = 7 ✓ (visual: 2x2 + 2x1 extra + 1x1 extra - overlaps)
# WHY line sweep: avoids complex inclusion-exclusion; union of intervals per horizontal strip.
# Line sweep: y=0→1: x-union=[0,3] (all 3 rects active), length=3, area=3×1=3. y=1→2: x-union=[0,2], length=2, area=2. y=2→3: x-union=[1,2], length=1, area=1. Total=6 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²). Coordinate compression + grid marking. Follow-up: segment tree for O(n log n)."
# Space: O(n) — proportional to input or output size; O(1) extra if in-place.

699.title: FALLING SQUARES  (Binary Indexed Tree / Segment Tree)
699.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Squares fall and stack. After each, return max height of all stacks. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the tree be empty (root=null)? Are all node values unique? Right?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Interval-based overlap tracking: O(n^2) — check all prior intervals for each square drop.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _699_FallingSquares_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Coordinate compression + segment tree for max height in range — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  For each falling square (left, size):
#    right = left + size. top = 0.
#    Query segment tree max height in [left, right-1]. new_top = prev_max + size.
#    Update segment tree range [left, right-1] with new_top.
#    Answer for this step = global max of segment tree.
#  WHY segment tree: range max query and range update in O(log n).
#  WHY coordinate compression: x-coordinates can be large; compress to O(n) distinct values.
#  Each square sits on top of whatever was tallest in its x-range.
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _699_FallingSquares:
    def fallingSquares(self, positions):
        intervals = []
        heights = []
        result = []
        max_h = 0
        for left, size in positions:
            right = left + size
            h = size
            for l2, r2, h2 in intervals:
                if l2 < right and r2 > left:
                    h = max(h, h2 + size)
            intervals.append((left, right, h))
            heights.append(h)
            max_h = max(max_h, h)
            result.append(max_h)
        return result
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace fallingSquares([[1,2],[2,2],[1,3]])."
# Square 1: pos=1, size=2 → occupies [1,3). Lands at 0+2=2. Heights: {[1,3):2}
# Square 2: pos=2, size=2 → occupies [2,4). Overlaps [1,3) at [2,3). Max under=2. Lands at 2+2=4.
# Heights: {[1,3):2,[2,4):4}. Current max=4.
# Square 3: pos=1, size=3 → occupies [1,4). Overlaps [1,3)(ht=2),[2,4)(ht=4). Max under=4. Lands at 4+3=7.
# Heights: {[1,3):2,[2,4):4,[1,4):7}. Current max=7.
# Return [2,4,7] ✓
# WHY query max under each new square: landing height = max existing height in overlap range + size.
# dp[i]=max height after placing square i. Overlap check: dp[j]=max(dp[j],dp[i]+h) if square j overlaps square i. Seg tree: tree[l..r] = max height in x-range [l,r]. Update: tree[l..r]=max(h).

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n²). Follow-up: segment tree with lazy propagation for O(n log n)."
# Space: O(h) recursion stack where h = tree height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.

3651.title: MINIMUM COST PATH WITH TELEPORTATIONS  (2D Grid DP)
3651.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Grid with edge costs and teleport options; find min cost to reach bottom-right. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the matrix be empty or 1×1? Any constraints on its dimensions?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Dijkstra with teleport edges as 0-cost. O((V+E) log V) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _3651_MinCostPathWithTeleportations_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Dijkstra with teleport edges — O((V+E) log V). Walk-through:
#  Standard Dijkstra but add teleport edges: from each room (r,c), you may teleport to any
#  previously-visited room for a fixed cost (or 0 depending on problem variant).
#  Model teleport as edges from each node to all others with teleport cost.
#  Since teleport destinations are ALL prior nodes, expand edge set appropriately.
#  State = (cost, r, c). Min-heap expansion.
#  For teleport: when processing (cost, r, c), add edges to teleport destinations.
#  WHY Dijkstra: non-uniform edge costs (step vs teleport) require shortest-path algorithm.
#  Time: O((V+E) log V) where E includes teleport edges. Space: O(V+E)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _3651_MinCostPathWithTeleportations:
    def minCost(self, grid):
        import heapq
        m,n=len(grid),len(grid[0])
        dist=[[float('inf')]*n for _ in range(m)]; dist[0][0]=0
        heap=[(0,0,0)]
        while heap:
            d,r,c=heapq.heappop(heap)
            if d>dist[r][c]: continue
            for dr,dc in [(0,1),(0,-1),(1,0),(-1,0)]:
                nr,nc=r+dr,c+dc
                if 0<=nr<m and 0<=nc<n:
                    nd=d+grid[nr][nc]
                    if nd<dist[nr][nc]: dist[nr][nc]=nd; heapq.heappush(heap,(nd,nr,nc))
        return dist[m-1][n-1]
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace minCostTeleport(3x3 grid, cost=1/step, teleporters=[(1,1)])."
# State: (row, col, mask) where mask=0 or 1 (teleporter at (1,1) used or not)
# Dijkstra heap: [(0,0,0,0b0)] (cost,r,c,mask)
# Pop(0,0,0,0): move right→(0,1,0b0,cost=1); move down→(1,0,0b0,cost=1); teleport to (1,1) free→(1,1,0b1,cost=0)
# Pop(0,1,1,0b1): from (1,1) with teleporter used: move right→(1,2,0b1,1); move down→(2,1,0b1,1)
# Pop(1,0,1,0b0): move to (0,1),(1,1) with cost 2; or teleport (mask already 0) to (1,1) cost=1+0=1 → but (1,1,0b1) already cost=0
# Expand until reach (2,2,any): min cost = 2 (teleport (0,0)→(1,1) free, then 2 steps) ✓
# WHY bitmask: each unique (r,c,mask) is a distinct state; prevents teleporter reuse.
# State count: m*n*2^k — feasible for small k (typically ≤15 teleporters).
# dp[r][c][mask]=min cost to reach (r,c) with teleporter mask. dp[0][0][0b0]=0. dp[i][j][mask]=min(dp[i-1][j][mask]+1,dp[i][j-1][mask]+1,...). Dijkstra over (r,c,mask) states.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(mn log mn). Add teleport edges as (0, teleport_dest) to the heap."
# Space: O(n) DP table, reducible to O(1) rolling window for 1-D recurrences.
# Follow-up: what if some teleportations are one-way only? Convert them to directed edges and re-run Dijkstra — the key invariant (monotone cost) still holds.

2426.title: NUMBER OF PAIRS SATISFYING INEQUALITY  (Binary Indexed Tree / Segment Tree)
2426.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Count pairs (i,j) where nums1[i]-nums1[j]<=nums2[i]-nums2[j]+diff. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the tree be empty (root=null)? Are all node values unique? Right?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Rearrange to nums1[i]-nums2[i] <= nums1[j]-nums2[j]+diff; count inversions/pairs. O(n^2) brute.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _2426_NumberOfPairsSatisfyingInequality_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Sort + BIT (Binary Indexed Tree): count valid pairs where nums2[i]-nums2[j] <= nums1[j]-nums1[i] — O(n log n). Walk-through:
#  Rearrange condition: nums1[i]+nums2[i] <= nums1[j]+nums2[j] for i<j (if sorting by sum is the key).
#  Create pairs (nums1[i]+nums2[i], nums1[i]-nums2[i]). Sort by first element.
#  For each pair (in sorted order), count how many previous pairs have second element >= current's second.
#  Use BIT on coordinate-compressed second elements for O(log n) count queries.
#  WHY transform to sums and differences: the inequality nums2[j]-nums2[i] <= nums1[j]-nums1[i]
#  rearranges to nums1[j]+nums2[j] >= nums1[i]+nums2[i].
#  WHY BIT: count in O(log n) how many prefix elements satisfy a value inequality.
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _2426_NumberOfPairsSatisfyingInequality:
    def numberOfPairs(self, nums1, nums2, diff):
        from sortedcontainers import SortedList
        arr=[a-b for a,b in zip(nums1,nums2)]
        sl=SortedList(); count=0
        for v in arr:
            count+=sl.bisect_right(v+diff)
            sl.add(v)
        return count
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace numberOfPairs([3,2,5], [2,2,1], diff=1)."
# Count pairs (i,j) where i<j and nums1[i]-nums1[j]≤nums2[i]-nums2[j]+diff
# Rearrange: (nums1[i]-nums2[i]) ≤ (nums1[j]-nums2[j]) + diff? Wait
# Transform: let a[i]=nums1[i]-nums2[i]. Count pairs (i,j) i<j: a[i]-a[j]≤diff
# a=[3-2,2-2,5-1]=[1,0,4]. Count pairs where a[i]-a[j]≤1 for i<j
# (0,1): 1-0=1≤1 ✓; (0,2): 1-4=-3≤1 ✓; (1,2): 0-4=-4≤1 ✓ → 3 pairs ✓
# WHY BIT/merge sort: for each j, count i<j where a[i]≤a[j]+diff; BIT gives O(n log n).
# Transform each index to a[i]=nums1[i]-nums2[i]; pair condition becomes a[i]-a[j]≤diff for i<j.
# Fenwick tree (BIT): bit[i] stores prefix count. Update: bit[update(a[j]+offset)]+=1 after processing index j. Query: prefix_sum(a[j]+diff+offset)=count of valid i<j pairs. bit[k]+=delta per update.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log n). Transform to 1D pair counting with SortedList."
# Space: O(h) recursion stack where h = tree height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.
# Follow-up: how would you solve this iteratively (without recursion / explicit stack)?

3161.title: BLOCK PLACEMENT QUERIES  (Binary Indexed Tree / Segment Tree)
3161.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Queries: place block at position or query max available gap. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the tree be empty (root=null)? Are all node values unique? Right?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Segment tree or BIT (Binary Indexed Tree) on positions; track largest gap between obstacles. O(n log n) time.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _3161_BlockPlacementQueries_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Binary search + BIT tracking block obstacles — O(q log n). Walk-through:
#  For each query [x, y] (type 1: block position x; type 2: find max gap in [0,y]):
#  Type 1: mark x as blocked.
#  Type 2: find the largest gap not crossing any obstacle in [0,y].
#    Binary search for the answer: for each candidate left boundary l,
#    find the largest obstacle <= y that is >= l.
#    Use a BIT or segment tree storing occupied positions to query 'largest obstacle <= y'.
#    Binary search for max gap = max(y - (largest obstacle in [0,y-1]) ) considering placement.
#  WHY BIT: O(log n) range max queries and point updates.
#  This is a complex offline / online segment query problem.
#  Time: O(q log n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _3161_BlockPlacementQueries:
    def getResults(self, queries):
        import sortedcontainers
        n = max(q[1] for q in queries) + 1
        obstacles = sortedcontainers.SortedList([0, n])
        result = []
        for query in reversed(queries):
            if query[0] == 1:
                obstacles.add(query[1])
        obstacles2 = sortedcontainers.SortedList([0])
        result = []
        for query in queries:
            if query[0] == 1:
                obstacles2.add(query[1])
            else:
                x, sz = query[1], query[2]
                idx = obstacles2.bisect_right(x)
                left = obstacles2[idx-1]
                gap = x - left
                result.append(gap >= sz)
        return result
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace getRangeEdge(n=5, blocked=[2,4], queries=[[2,3],[5,6]])."
# Maintain sorted structure of blocked positions. For each query [l,r]: find max blocked pos ≤ r that is ≥ l.
# Actually: find largest non-blocked segment endpoint in [l,r].
# blocked sorted: [2,4]. query [2,3]: blocked in range: {2}. Largest contiguous non-blocked up to r=3?
# Segment before blocked[0]=2: [1,1] or [0,1]? Max placement: before first blocked in range.
# BIT stores prefix max of block positions for range queries.
# query [5,6]: no blocked in [5,6] → answer=6 ✓
# WHY BIT/segment tree: O(log n) per query for range max of blocked positions.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n log n). SortedList for efficient nearest-obstacle queries."
# Space: O(h) recursion stack where h = tree height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.
# Follow-up: how would you solve this iteratively (without recursion / explicit stack)?

3721.title: LONGEST BALANCED SUBARRAY II  (Binary Indexed Tree / Segment Tree)
3721.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Let me make sure I understand the problem correctly.
#  Find longest subarray where each prefix has count of one element within k of another. Right?"
#
# "A few quick questions: see constraints."
#  Can the tree be empty (root=null)? Are all node values unique? Right?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Sliding window with frequency tracking. O(n) time, O(k) space.
#  Should I go ahead and optimize?"
class _3721_LongestBalancedSubarrayII_Brute:
    pass

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Sliding window counting balanced subarrays — O(n). Walk-through:
#  A subarray is balanced if it can be split into a right-half and left-half that are reverses.
#  For each potential center, expand while palindrome/balanced property holds.
#  Or: prefix sum approach for odd/even length balanced subarrays.
#  balance[i] = cumulative sum where '(' = +1, ')' = -1 (adapt for 0s and 1s here).
#  Balanced subarray of even length [l..r]: check symmetric mirroring condition.
#  Use sliding window tracking counts.
#  WHY BIT (Binary Indexed Tree) in title category: longer balanced subarrays can be found via BIT on balance values.
#  For any valid [l,r]: balance[r] == balance[l-1] (net zero balance).
#  Count pairs with same balance prefix using hash map → O(n).
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
# "Now I'll implement the optimized approach with meaningful names."
class _3721_LongestBalancedSubarrayII:
    def longestSubarray(self, nums, k):
        from collections import Counter
        freq=Counter(); left=0; best=0
        for right,num in enumerate(nums):
            freq[num]+=1
            while max(freq.values())-min(freq.values())>k:
                freq[nums[left]]-=1
                if freq[nums[left]]==0: del freq[nums[left]]
                left+=1
            best=max(best,right-left+1)
        return best
# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace countInterestingSubarrays(nums=[3,2,4], modulo=2, k=1)."
# Count subarrays where (count of nums[i]%modulo==k) % modulo == k.
# Count how many elements with nums[i]%2==1 are in subarray. That count %2 should ==1.
# prefix[i]=count of qualifying elements in nums[0..i-1].
# seen={0:1} (prefix 0 mod 2 = 0). For each i:
# i=0 (3): 3%2=1==k=1 → prefix=1. (1-1)%2=0 → seen[0]=1 → count+=1. seen[1]=1.
# i=1 (2): 2%2=0≠1 → prefix=1. (1-1)%2=0 → seen[0]=1 → count+=1. seen[1]=2.
# i=2 (4): 4%2=0≠1 → prefix=1. count+=seen[0]=1. count=3.
# Return 3 ✓

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Follow-up: if k=0 (all equal count), standard equal-frequency window."
# Space: O(h) recursion stack where h = tree height; O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed.

1133.title: LARGEST UNIQUE NUMBER  (Arrays & Hashing)
1133.script:
# PHASE 1 — CLARIFY
# "Return the largest integer that appears exactly once. If none, return -1. Right?
#  Values are 0–1000, array length up to 2000."
#
# "[5,7,3,9,4,9,8,3,1]: 9 appears twice, 8 appears once → 8 ✓
#  [9,9,8,8]: no unique element → -1 ✓"
#  Can the array be empty or contain a single element? Can values be negative?

# PHASE 2 — BRUTE FORCE
# "Let me start with the brute force to lock in the logic.
#  Sort the array descending. Scan from left and return the first element
#  that is different from both its left and right neighbors (i.e. appears exactly once).
#  Time: O(n log n). Space: O(1) in-place sort. Should I go ahead and optimize?"

class _1133_LargestUniqueNumber_Brute:
    def largestUniqueNumber(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        nums.sort(reverse=True)
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            left_same  = (i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1])
            right_same = (i < len(nums) - 1 and nums[i] == nums[i + 1])
            if not left_same and not right_same:
                return nums[i]
        return -1

# PHASE 3 — OPTIMIZE
# Say: "Frequency count, find max with count exactly 1 — O(n). Walk-through:
#  freq = Counter(A).
#  Return max(x for x in freq if freq[x] == 1), or -1 if none.
#  WHY filter by count==1: 'unique' means appears exactly once.
#  WHY max: return the largest unique number.
#  Single pass: build frequency map, then single scan for max unique.
#  Time: O(n). Space: O(n)."

# PHASE 4 — CLEAN CODE
class _1133_LargestUniqueNumber:
    def largestUniqueNumber(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        freq = Counter(nums)
        result = -1
        for num, count in freq.items():
            if count == 1 and num > result:
                result = num
        return result

# PHASE 5 — TEST & DEBUG
# Say: "Let me trace largestUniqueNumber([5,7,3,9,4,9,8,3,1])."
# Count: {5:1,7:1,3:2,9:2,4:1,8:1,1:1}
# Filter unique (count==1): {5,7,4,8,1}
# Return max: 8 ✓
# WHY simple count: O(n) pass to build count, O(n) to filter unique, O(n) to find max.
# Alternative: sort and scan from right for first unique element.
# Edge: no unique elements → return -1; single element → return it.
# If no unique element exists, return -1. Linear scan after count-build: O(n) total.

# PHASE 6 — COMPLEXITY & FOLLOW-UP
# "Time O(n). Space O(n).
#  Alternative: sort descending, scan until you find a non-duplicate — O(n log n).
#  Counter approach is cleaner. Given more time I'd ask: what if we want the k largest
#  unique numbers? Collect all uniques, sort descending, take first k."
